The recurrent excitatory weights are highly plastic under Hebbian, spike-timing-dependent rules, which is how the pool learns its attractor patterns - and precisely why runaway potentiation, if unchecked by homeostatic scaling, can pathologically raise the network's excitability toward seizure.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a local population from hundreds to many thousands of excitatory cells sharing dense recurrent connectivity, spanning a cortical patch of a few hundred micrometres to a millimetre, together with its embedded interneurons.

In hippocampal area CA3 the recurrent network spans the whole subfield, with each pyramidal cell contacting thousands of others, making it the largest and most explicit single instance of the motif.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Recurrent excitatory pools tile the entire neocortex and the hippocampus, so instances number in the millions if counted by cortical patch, overlapping continuously across the sheet.

They are densest in association and prefrontal cortex and in area CA3, and their recurrent connectivity is a defining structural feature of cortical grey matter everywhere.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The neocortex generally, where recurrent excitation amplifies feedforward input and supports persistent activity in every area.

• The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, where recurrently sustained firing holds items in working memory across a delay.

• The hippocampal area CA3, where dense recurrent collaterals form the autoassociative network for pattern completion.

• The layer 2/3 and layer 5 networks of sensory cortex, where recurrence sharpens and amplifies tuned responses.

• The entorhinal cortex, where recurrent excitation supports grid-cell and persistent-activity dynamics.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete recurrent excitation and the cortex would lose its amplifier and its memory in one stroke: feedforward input would still arrive but could not be magnified, sustained, or completed from a fragment, so the region would react but never reverberate.

A region with recurrent excitation can hold a thought, complete a pattern, and amplify a whisper into a decision; a region without it is a passive filter - and a region whose recurrence outruns its inhibition is a region that seizes.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

In plain words the pool amplifies and can latch: below a critical recurrent gain it multiplies its input by a finite factor and relaxes when input stops, while above that gain it becomes multistable, holding self-sustained activity as an attractor after the input is gone.

The mathematical forms are gain amplification (output equals input divided by one minus the loop gain, for gain below one) and attractor bistability or multistability (for supercritical gain with saturating nonlinearity), the same positive-feedback mathematics as Chapter 4 scaled to a population.

Real numbers: balanced cortical pools hold persistent firing at low rates near 10 to 50 hertz, whereas in seizure the same pools discharge hypersynchronously at far higher, paroxysmal rates - the transition marking the crossing from computation into pathology.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

In the healthy regime the signature is amplified, sustained firing that outlasts the input by seconds (persistent activity), smoothed by the slow NMDA component into a stable plateau.

In the pathological regime the signature is an abrupt, self-accelerating recruitment into hypersynchronous high-frequency discharge - the electrographic seizure - often preceded by a measurable drift of the excitation-inhibition balance toward excitation.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The pool has three broad regimes set by the excitation-inhibition balance: a stable amplifier (subcritical), a memory attractor holding one of several self-sustaining patterns (balanced supercritical with inhibition), and a runaway seizure (excitation exceeding inhibition's control).

The boundaries between these are sharp, which is why small shifts in inhibitory strength, neuromodulator level, or synaptic scaling can flip a computing cortex into an ictal one.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Hebbian potentiation of the recurrent synapses stores attractor patterns - co-active members strengthen their mutual connections, carving stable memory states out of the pool, the mechanism of the autoassociative network of Part Five.

Homeostatic scaling is the essential safety mechanism, multiplying synaptic weights down when average activity runs high to keep the pool off the seizure boundary; failure of this homeostatic control is one route by which networks drift toward chronic epilepsy.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The balanced recurrent pool (excitation matched by fast inhibition) is the computational workhorse; the autoassociative variant (with strongly modifiable recurrent synapses) stores and completes patterns; and the disinhibited or damaged variant (inhibition removed by injury, drug, or channelopathy) is the epileptic focus.

Scaled and specialised, this one motif becomes the point attractor of working memory, the autoassociative attractor of episodic memory, and the ring and line attractors of Part Five - all children of recurrent excitation tamed by inhibition.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Recurrent excitatory networks are built by the growth of local collaterals and their Hebbian stabilisation, with inhibitory (especially parvalbumin) interneurons maturing relatively late to bring the balancing brake online.

This developmental lag in inhibition is one reason the immature cortex is more seizure-prone, and why the maturation of parvalbumin circuits marks the closing of critical periods and the stabilising of the excitatory pool.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Recurrent excitation is the scaling-up of the ancient reciprocal loop, and it expands dramatically in the mammalian and especially the primate cortex, where the sheer density of recurrent connections underlies the cortex's computational power.

The perpetual coexistence of this power with seizure risk is an evolutionary bargain: the same wiring that makes cortex capable of memory and amplification makes it capable of the runaway discharge, so inhibition had to co-evolve step for step with excitation.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes are critical governors here, clearing glutamate and buffering the potassium that recurrent firing dumps into the extracellular space; impaired astrocytic potassium and glutamate clearance is itself a mechanism of seizure, so glia are part of the firebreak.

The high metabolic cost of sustained recurrent firing makes the pool dependent on brisk neurovascular coupling, and metabolic failure can tip a stressed network toward ictal activity.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Epilepsy is the signature disease of this motif: when the excitation-inhibition balance tips toward excitation - through interneuron loss, channelopathy, gliosis, or failed homeostasis - the recurrent pool discharges hypersynchronously, and the amplifier becomes a seizure generator.

At the other pole, weakened or dysregulated recurrent excitation in prefrontal cortex is linked to the working-memory failures of schizophrenia, so both too much and too little recurrent gain are disorders of this one circuit.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Feedforward excitatory drive to the pool 0 to 20 nanosiemens; recurrent excitation from pool members; feedback and feedforward inhibition 0 to 40 nanosiemens.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Amplified, potentially self-sustaining population firing, 10 to 50 hertz in the balanced regime, paroxysmal high-frequency discharge in the ictal regime.

• STATE.

◦ Population activity level, active attractor pattern, recurrent synaptic weights, excitation-inhibition balance, extracellular potassium.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Recurrent excitatory connection probability (a few percent locally); recurrent versus feedforward fraction (recurrent often greater than 50 percent of excitation); NMDA fraction; inhibitory gain.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ NMDA decay near 100 milliseconds; persistence seconds; homeostatic scaling hours to days; Hebbian change minutes.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Epileptic seizure when inhibition fails (interneuron loss, channelopathy, failed homeostatic scaling, impaired astrocytic buffering); working-memory failure in schizophrenia when recurrent excitation is too weak or dysregulated.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named recurrent_amplifier_pool that subscribes to feedforward input and publishes an amplified, optionally self-sustaining population activation, implemented as a positive-feedback pool of excitatory units wrapped in an obligatory inhibitory control loop with an explicit stability governor.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is the recurrent layer of a Hopfield or attractor network and, more broadly, any positive-feedback amplifier with normalisation, where the wrapping inhibition plays the role of a normalisation or gain-control term.

The biological motif differs in that its stability is not guaranteed by construction but must be actively maintained by matched inhibition and slow homeostatic scaling, and its failure mode is a real dynamical catastrophe (the seizure) rather than mere numerical divergence - so a faithful module must expose the excitation-inhibition balance as a monitored, regulated parameter, treating runaway as a first-class failure state to be detected and damped.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to model a pool of mutually exciting cells whose activity is amplified by recurrent excitation and held in check by inhibition, and to flag the runaway state when excitation overwhelms the brake.

Create a number variable called population activity with initial value 0.

Create a number variable called recurrent gain with initial value 1.05.

Create a number variable called inhibition strength with initial value 1.0.

Create a number variable called external input with initial value 0.2.

Create a number variable called runaway threshold with initial value 5.

Repeat the following actions once for each time step.

    Calculate the recurrent drive as recurrent gain times population activity.

    Calculate the inhibitory drive as inhibition strength times population activity.

    Set population activity to external input plus recurrent drive minus inhibitory drive.

    If population activity is less than zero, then set population activity to zero.

    If population activity is greater than runaway threshold is true, then perform the following actions.

        Display the message runaway excitation, seizure regime, to the console.

    Otherwise, perform the following actions.

        Display population activity to the console.

    End the conditional block.

End the repeat block.

The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the knife-edge between stable amplification and runaway is best shown by sweeping the excitation-inhibition balance and watching activity either settle or blow up, which a short loop over a few balance values makes vivid.

# Recurrent excitation with a runaway threshold: a self-amplifying pool that is
# stable when inhibition matches excitation and seizes when it does not
# (Wang, Neuron 2002; Trevelyan et al., J. Neurosci. 2006, on the inhibitory
# restraint that fails at seizure onset).
def run_pool(exc_gain, inh_gain, steps=60, runaway=5.0):
    a = 0.0
    for t in range(steps):
        drive = 0.2 + exc_gain * a - inh_gain * a   # input + recurrence - inhibition
        a = max(0.0, drive)
        if a > runaway:
            return t, "SEIZURE (runaway excitation)"
    return steps, f"stable at {a:.2f} Hz-equivalent"

for exc, inh in [(1.05, 1.10), (1.20, 1.10), (1.50, 1.10)]:
    t, outcome = run_pool(exc, inh)
    print(f"E-gain={exc}  I-gain={inh}  ->  {outcome} (by t={t})")
# Balanced (E<I): the fire is contained and activity settles.
# Excitation exceeding inhibition: the same wiring runs away into seizure.

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A dense pool of excitatory cells all feeding one another, girdled by fast inhibition, that amplifies a spark into sustained firing when balanced and into a spreading blaze when the brake fails - the one circuit that is simultaneously the cortex's memory and its most dangerous fault.


PART TWO. THE INHIBITORY MOTIFS

Inhibition is not the silence between thoughts but a computation in its own right, as active and as expensive as excitation, and the interneurons of the Layer 6 catalogue spend it lavishly.

Every motif in this part takes the same raw material - a cell that says no - and wires it into a different shape, and each shape computes something the others cannot: a narrow window in time, a thermostat on gain, a knife-edge of contrast, a governor on the final motor path, a see-saw between opposing muscles.

The lesson repeated across the five chapters is the framework's own: the diagram is generic, the address gives it meaning, and the personality of the particular interneuron chosen to play the inhibitor colours the whole result.

Two of these motifs (feedforward inhibition, feedback inhibition, and lateral inhibition) earn the cognitive tag because they sculpt information; the last two (the Renshaw loop and reciprocal inhibition) serve the motor substrate and are tagged non-cognitive, though the same wiring reappears in the thinking parts of the brain wearing a different coat.


CHAPTER 7. FEEDFORWARD INHIBITION (Input-Driven Delayed-Brake Motif) (The Coincidence-Window Cutter) (COG)

An excitatory signal arrives at a principal cell and, in the same breath, at an interneuron sitting beside it; the principal cell begins to depolarise, but a heartbeat later the interneuron's brake slams down and closes the door.

The result is that only inputs arriving almost together, within a window sometimes narrower than two thousandths of a second, can push the principal cell to fire before the door shuts.

This is the circuit that makes the cortex fast and the hippocampus precise: it converts a leaky, slow membrane that would otherwise smear signals across tens of milliseconds into a stopwatch that resolves near-simultaneity.

Coincidence names the quantity it measures, whether two inputs truly arrived together.

Window names the brief opening in time it holds ajar.

Cutter names what it does to that window, trimming it shorter as the drive grows stronger.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Feedforward inhibition is a three-node motif in which one upstream source excites both a principal (output) cell and a local inhibitory interneuron, and the interneuron in turn inhibits the same principal cell.

Because the inhibitory path runs through one extra synapse, its signal arrives one to two milliseconds later than the direct excitation, and this fixed delay is the whole trick.

What the motif computes is a coincidence-detection window: the principal cell can only integrate and fire during the sliver of time between the arrival of excitation and the arrival of the delayed inhibition, so it reports whether its excitatory inputs were synchronous rather than merely present.

A millisecond, for the reader new to these scales, is one thousandth of a second, and the fastest human behaviours are built from events separated by just a few of them.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

There are three node roles: the afferent source (S), the principal cell (P), and the feedforward interneuron (I).

Edge one is excitatory, from S to P, a fast glutamatergic contact - this is the signal to be gated.

Edge two is excitatory, from S to I, also glutamatergic and typically stronger and faster than edge one, so that the interneuron is driven reliably even by input that only weakly excites the principal cell.

Edge three is inhibitory, from I to P, a gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) contact placed on or near the principal cell's soma (cell body) or axon initial segment (the spike-launching stub of the axon), where it can veto output.

The topology is a feedforward triad (an open triangle): S drives both P and I, and I drives P, but P sends nothing back to I - the absence of that return edge is exactly what distinguishes this motif from feedback inhibition in the next chapter.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The principal cell is a glutamatergic projection neuron: the L2/3 or L5 pyramidal cell of the neuron catalogue in cortex, or the CA1 pyramidal cell in hippocampus.

The interneuron role is played above all by the parvalbumin-positive fast-spiking basket cell of the neuron catalogue, whose personality is the reason the motif works: it fires with millisecond-precise, non-adapting, high-frequency spikes, has a short membrane time constant, and receives large, fast-rising excitatory currents, so it converts afferent input into an inhibitory pulse with the least possible jitter and delay.

In some regions the bistratified cell and the chandelier cell of the catalogue add feedforward inhibition onto dendrites and the axon initial segment respectively, layering a slower dendritic brake beneath the fast somatic one.

The fast-spiking personality matters because a slow, adapting interneuron would blur the window; only a cell that can fire once, hard, and on time can cut a clean two-millisecond aperture.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The S-to-P and S-to-I edges use glutamate acting on fast AMPA receptors (named for the agonist alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid) with decay near two milliseconds, plus slower NMDA receptors (N-methyl-D-aspartate) on the principal cell.

The S-to-I synapse onto parvalbumin cells is specialised for speed: calcium-permeable AMPA receptors, large unitary currents, and short latency, so the interneuron reaches threshold in under a millisecond.

The I-to-P edge uses GABA acting on fast GABA-A receptors (ionotropic chloride channels) clustered perisomatically, giving an inhibitory pulse that rises in about one millisecond and decays over five to ten.

Characteristic weights favour the inhibitory arm: perisomatic GABA-A conductance can reach tens of nanosiemens, enough to shunt the soma; plasticity here is modest, though the excitatory drive onto parvalbumin cells shows its own long-term potentiation and depression that retune the window over learning.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is small: a single afferent bundle, one to a few principal cells, and one to a handful of feedforward interneurons, spanning tens to a couple of hundred micrometres (a micrometre being a thousandth of a millimetre).

Because a single fast-spiking basket cell contacts hundreds to over a thousand principal cells within its dense local axonal cloud, one interneuron serves as the shared brake for a whole local pool, so the effective instance is one interneuron and its target field.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Uncountable in the literal sense: feedforward inhibition is installed at essentially every glutamatergic relay in the forebrain that receives an organised afferent, so the count scales with the number of parvalbumin interneurons, on the order of hundreds of millions across the human cortex and hippocampus (parvalbumin cells are roughly forty per cent of the cortex's GABAergic population, which is itself about twenty per cent of cortical neurons).

Confidence is high that the motif is ubiquitous and moderate on any precise count, because motifs have no census.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Neocortex, layer 4 and layers 2/3: thalamic and feedforward corticocortical input excites pyramidal cells and parvalbumin basket cells together, sharpening the temporal window of every sensory relay.

• Hippocampus, CA1 and CA3: Schaffer-collateral and perforant-path input drives pyramidal cells and basket cells, enforcing the sub-two-millisecond integration window that underlies phase precision.

• Dentate gyrus: entorhinal input onto granule cells and fast-spiking interneurons, contributing to sparse, precise activation.

• Cerebellar cortex: mossy-fibre and parallel-fibre input onto Golgi and molecular-layer interneurons feeds forward onto granule and Purkinje cells, timing their responses.

• Striatum: corticostriatal input excites medium spiny neurons and fast-spiking interneurons together, gating the entry of cortical commands.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete feedforward inhibition and each hosting region keeps its content but loses its clock: the cortex would still receive its senses and the hippocampus its context, but both would integrate over tens of milliseconds instead of two, smearing distinct inputs into an indiscriminate blur.

Spike timing would lose its meaning, gamma and theta phase codes would degrade, and the region would slide from a precise reporter of coincidence toward a sluggish averager - and, with the perisomatic brake gone, toward runaway excitation and seizure.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is a subtractive-then-shunting temporal gate: the principal cell's effective integration window T is set by the excitation-inhibition delay, and only charge delivered within T counts.

In rat hippocampal pyramidal cells the window is under two milliseconds, and it shrinks as excitatory drive rises from a few synapses to tens of synapses, because stronger input recruits the interneuron faster - a drive-dependent narrowing, not a fixed aperture.

In plain numbers: at weak drive the window may be several milliseconds; at strong drive it collapses toward one, so the cell becomes an ever-stricter coincidence detector precisely when its inputs are strongest.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The signature is the excitatory postsynaptic potential followed one to two milliseconds later by the inhibitory postsynaptic potential, the pair producing a sharp, brief depolarisation with a fast repolarising shoulder.

The disynaptic inhibitory latency is the fingerprint; the whole event is over within ten milliseconds, allowing the circuit to repeat faithfully at high rates that a bare membrane would filter away.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

At rest the motif idles, its interneuron near threshold.

Under strong synchronous drive it operates as a tight coincidence gate; under weak asynchronous drive it passes little.

With repetitive stimulation the excitatory drive onto parvalbumin cells can depress, widening the window transiently, while neuromodulators (acetylcholine, especially) adjust interneuron excitability and so retune the aperture with brain state, opening it in quiet states and tightening it during attention.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The excitatory synapses onto the feedforward interneuron are plastic: they undergo long-term potentiation and depression that change how quickly and strongly the brake is recruited, and hence the window width.

The perisomatic GABA synapse itself shows activity-dependent scaling.

Developmentally, the maturation of parvalbumin feedforward inhibition closes critical periods of cortical plasticity, so the motif's own strengthening is a switch that ends an epoch of learning.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Somatic feedforward inhibition (basket-cell, fast, output-vetoing) versus dendritic feedforward inhibition (bistratified and Martinotti-like, slower, input-selecting).

Axo-axonic feedforward inhibition by chandelier cells at the axon initial segment is the most decisive variant, able to block the spike outright.

A fast-and-slow pairing (parvalbumin plus a slower interneuron class) appears in olfactory and cortical circuits, giving both a sharp edge and a sustained damping.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The interneurons are born in the medial ganglionic eminence of the embryonic forebrain and migrate tangentially into cortex and hippocampus, arriving before their principal-cell partners are fully wired.

Feedforward inhibitory strength matures late, over the first postnatal months to years in humans, and its maturation (with the perineuronal nets that ensheath parvalbumin cells) both times and terminates critical-period plasticity.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Feedforward inhibition is ancient and general, present wherever a nervous system needs to gate a relay in time; the parvalbumin fast-spiking implementation is a vertebrate elaboration, but the open-triad logic (drive a target and its brake together) appears across phyla, including invertebrate sensory circuits.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Parvalbumin interneurons are metabolically demanding fast-spikers, heavily dependent on mitochondria and on astrocytic glutamate clearance and potassium buffering; they are wrapped in perineuronal nets, extracellular-matrix lattices that stabilise their synapses and protect against oxidative stress.

Their high energy use makes them the first casualties of hypoxia and oxidative damage.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Loss of parvalbumin feedforward inhibition is central to schizophrenia (reduced parvalbumin expression and gamma disruption) and to epilepsy (failure of the perisomatic brake), and is implicated in autism-spectrum excitation-inhibition imbalance.

Because the motif times cortical computation, its degradation shows up as impaired temporal precision, degraded gamma rhythms, and lowered seizure threshold.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Afferent glutamatergic drive to principal cell 0 to 20 nanosiemens; parallel drive to interneuron 0 to 30 nanosiemens with sub-millisecond latency.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Timed principal-cell spikes gated to a 1 to 2 millisecond coincidence window; feedforward GABA pulse onto the soma.

• STATE.

◦ Principal-cell somatic voltage; interneuron voltage; current window width (drive-dependent).

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Excitation-inhibition delay 1 to 2 milliseconds; GABA-A rise about 1 millisecond, decay 5 to 10 milliseconds; interneuron divergence hundreds to over 1,000 targets.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ AMPA decay about 2 milliseconds; membrane time constant of fast-spiking interneuron 5 to 10 milliseconds; integration window under 2 milliseconds at strong drive.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ In schizophrenia parvalbumin-cell dysfunction widens the window and degrades gamma; in epilepsy perisomatic feedforward inhibition fails and coincidence gating collapses into runaway excitation.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module coincidence_window_gate.

It would subscribe to an afferent feature stream and, on each message, open a short acceptance window whose width shrinks with input magnitude, publishing the target's output only for inputs whose components arrived inside that window.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a temporal attention gate or a leaky integrator with a fast subtractive reset; the biological motif differs in that its window is not fixed but narrows dynamically with drive, and the brake is delayed by a real conduction latency rather than computed instantaneously.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to decide whether a principal cell fires, given two excitatory inputs that arrive at different times and a delayed inhibitory brake that closes a coincidence window.

Create a number variable called excitation arrival one with a value in milliseconds.
Create a number variable called excitation arrival two with a value in milliseconds.
Create a number variable called drive strength with a value between 0 and 1.
Create a number variable called base window with initial value 2.0.
Create a number variable called window with initial value 0.
Set window to base window minus drive strength times 1.0.
Create a number variable called arrival gap with initial value 0.
Set arrival gap to the absolute difference of excitation arrival one and excitation arrival two.
Create a truth variable called cell fires with initial value false.
If arrival gap is less than or equal to window is true, then perform the following actions.
    Set cell fires to true.
Otherwise, perform the following actions.
    Set cell fires to false.
End the conditional block.
Display cell fires to the console.
The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the point is the shape of the window and how it narrows with drive, and Python shows both in a few honest lines.

# Feedforward inhibition as a coincidence-window gate.
# The disynaptic brake arrives ~1-2 ms after excitation, so only
# near-simultaneous inputs fire the cell; the window narrows with drive.
# (Pouille & Scanziani, Science 2001, "Enforcement of Temporal Fidelity".)
BASE_WINDOW_MS = 2.0   # window at weak drive

def cell_fires(t1_ms, t2_ms, drive):     # drive in [0, 1]
    window = BASE_WINDOW_MS - drive * 1.0   # stronger drive -> tighter window
    return abs(t1_ms - t2_ms) <= window

print("t1  t2  drive  window(ms)  fires")
for gap in (0.5, 1.5, 3.0):
    for drive in (0.1, 0.9):
        w = BASE_WINDOW_MS - drive * 1.0
        print(f"0.0  {gap:.1f}   {drive:.1f}    {w:4.2f}      {cell_fires(0.0, gap, drive)}")
# Weak drive passes a 1.5 ms gap; strong drive rejects it -> stricter detector.

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

An open triangle in which one input drives both a cell and its brake, the brake lagging by one to two milliseconds, so the cell answers not "was there input?" but "did the inputs arrive together?" - and answers more strictly the harder it is driven.


CHAPTER 8. FEEDBACK (RECURRENT) INHIBITION (Self-Braking Interneuron Loop) (The Activity Thermostat) (COG)

A principal cell fires, and its own output loops through a neighbouring interneuron that turns straight back and inhibits it.

The louder the principal cell speaks, the harder the brake presses, so the circuit holds its own activity near a set point exactly as a thermostat holds a room near a chosen temperature.

This is negative feedback in its purest neural form, and it does three jobs at once: it controls gain, it prevents the runaway excitation that becomes seizure, and its round-trip delay sets the tempo of population rhythms.

Activity names the quantity it senses, its own firing rate.

Thermostat names the discipline it enforces, holding that rate near a target by pushing back in proportion to error.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Feedback inhibition is a two-node recurrent loop in which a principal cell excites an interneuron that inhibits the principal cell back, closing a negative-feedback loop.

Unlike feedforward inhibition, where the brake is driven by the input, here the brake is driven by the output, so the circuit responds to what the population is actually doing rather than to what it was told to do.

What it computes is automatic gain control and rate stabilisation: it divides or subtracts from the principal cell's response in proportion to recent population activity, keeping firing within a usable range and, through its loop delay, pacing rhythmic activity.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Two node roles: the principal cell (P) and the feedback interneuron (I).

Edge one is excitatory, from P to I, a glutamatergic collateral of the principal cell's own axon.

Edge two is inhibitory, from I to P, a gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) contact returning onto the principal cell's soma or dendrites.

The topology is a closed two-node loop (a reciprocal pair of opposite sign), and because one interneuron collects excitation from many principal cells and returns inhibition to many, the real diagram is a fan-in-fan-out loop: a pool of principal cells drives a shared interneuron that brakes the whole pool - lateral spread of the brake is what links this motif to the lateral inhibition of the next chapter.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The principal cell is again the pyramidal or granule cell; the classic feedback interneurons differ from the feedforward ones.

In hippocampus the oriens-lacunosum-moleculare cell and the bistratified cell are quintessential feedback cells, driven by local pyramidal collaterals and returning dendritic inhibition; the parvalbumin basket cell also serves feedback duty.

In cortex the somatostatin-positive Martinotti cell of the neuron catalogue is the signature feedback element: it is recruited by sustained pyramidal firing (its excitatory inputs facilitate, growing with each spike), and it returns inhibition onto distal dendrites, so its adapting, facilitating personality makes it a slow, integrating brake that ramps up only when activity persists - a thermostat with a deliberate lag.

The contrast in personalities matters: fast-spiking feedback gives tight, fast rhythm control, while facilitating somatostatin feedback gives slow, accumulating gain control.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The P-to-I edge is glutamatergic (alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)); onto somatostatin cells it is strongly facilitating, meaning release grows with repeated spikes, which is why these cells engage late.

The I-to-P edge is GABA on GABA-A receptors (fast) and, for dendritic feedback, also GABA-B receptors (slow, metabotropic, potassium-mediated) giving inhibition that lasts hundreds of milliseconds.

Placement encodes function: perisomatic feedback controls output gain and timing, dendritic feedback controls the local synaptic integration and calcium spikes.

Weights are set homeostatically, and the P-to-I synapse's short-term facilitation is itself the key dynamic variable.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

A local pool of tens to a few hundred principal cells sharing one or a few feedback interneurons, spanning one to several hundred micrometres.

Because the loop's job is population-level, the natural instance is the pool, not the pair.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

As ubiquitous as excitatory populations themselves: every recurrent excitatory network in the forebrain carries feedback inhibition to stabilise it, so instances number in the hundreds of millions, with high confidence on ubiquity and low confidence on any exact count.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Neocortex, all layers: somatostatin and parvalbumin feedback holds pyramidal-cell gain and paces gamma rhythms.

• Hippocampus, CA3 and CA1: feedback inhibition restrains the powerful recurrent excitation of CA3, the region most prone to seizure without it.

• Dentate gyrus: feedback from basket and hilar cells keeps granule-cell activity sparse.

• Olfactory bulb: granule-cell feedback onto mitral cells (a dendrodendritic special case) sharpens and paces output.

• Cerebellar cortex: Purkinje-cell recurrent collaterals and molecular-layer feedback shape output.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove feedback inhibition and each region loses its stability: gain would run open-loop, responses would saturate, and recurrent excitatory networks - CA3 above all - would drift toward the self-amplifying storm of a seizure.

The region would also lose its rhythm, because the loop delay that generates gamma and other population oscillations would be gone; a cortex without feedback inhibition is both epileptic and arrhythmic.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is divisive-and-subtractive gain control: the principal pool's output rate R settles where excitatory drive is balanced by feedback inhibition proportional to R, giving R approximately equal to drive divided by (one plus a feedback gain term).

This is a first-order negative-feedback controller; with the loop delay it becomes an oscillator, ringing at a frequency set by the round-trip time (about 25 milliseconds round trip yields gamma near 40 cycles per second).

In numbers: doubling the drive raises output far less than twofold, because the brake scales with output - the hallmark of divisive normalisation implemented in time.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

A build-up of principal-cell firing followed, after the loop delay of a few milliseconds, by a wave of inhibition that curtails it, then recovery and repeat - the sawtooth of a self-pacing rhythm.

With facilitating somatostatin feedback the signature is a slow ramp of inhibition that grows over tens to hundreds of milliseconds of sustained activity.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

At low drive the loop is a stabiliser; at moderate drive with short delay it becomes a gamma oscillator (this is the pyramidal-interneuron gamma motif of Part Four in embryo); at high drive it saturates into a hard ceiling on rate.

Neuromodulators shift the set point: acetylcholine and noradrenaline retune interneuron excitability and hence the gain the thermostat enforces.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The excitatory synapse onto the feedback interneuron is plastic, and its facilitation dynamics are themselves subject to change, adjusting how strongly activity recruits its own brake.

Homeostatic plasticity uses this loop to hold long-term average firing near target after perturbation, scaling inhibitory strength up or down over hours to days.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Perisomatic feedback (fast, parvalbumin, gain-and-timing) versus dendritic feedback (somatostatin, slow, input-gating).

A specialised dendrodendritic variant in the olfactory bulb and thalamus dispenses with an axon entirely (treated in Part Eight).

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Feedback interneurons arrive from the ganglionic eminences and wire into local recurrent networks postnatally; the somatostatin feedback system matures on its own schedule, distinct from the parvalbumin feedforward system, giving the developing cortex first a crude then an increasingly disciplined thermostat.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Negative feedback is the oldest control principle in biology, and recurrent inhibition is its neural incarnation, found from invertebrate ganglia upward; it is arguably the most conserved inhibitory motif because every excitatory network that must not explode needs it.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Shares the parvalbumin support requirements (mitochondria, perineuronal nets, astrocytic buffering); somatostatin cells are less metabolically extreme but depend on the same glutamate-clearance and potassium-homeostasis services from astrocytes.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Failure of feedback inhibition is a core mechanism of epilepsy (loss of the CA3 and cortical brake), and altered feedback gain is implicated in schizophrenia and in the excitation-inhibition imbalance of autism; overactive feedback can contribute to the cognitive slowing of some sedative and anaesthetic states.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Recurrent excitation from the principal pool's own axon collaterals 0 to 30 nanosiemens; neuromodulatory set-point signals.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Activity-proportional GABA inhibition returned to the pool; a population rhythm at the loop frequency.

• STATE.

◦ Pool firing rate; interneuron activation; short-term facilitation level of the excitatory drive onto the interneuron.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Feedback gain (dimensionless); loop delay 2 to 5 milliseconds; GABA-A decay 5 to 10 milliseconds, GABA-B decay 100 to 300 milliseconds.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Fast loop about 25 milliseconds round trip (gamma); somatostatin facilitation onset tens to hundreds of milliseconds; homeostatic scaling hours to days.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ In temporal-lobe epilepsy the CA3 feedback brake fails and recurrent excitation runs away; loss of gamma pacing accompanies schizophrenia.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module activity_gain_thermostat.

It would subscribe to the aggregate output of a principal population and publish an inhibitory signal proportional to that output, holding the population's rate near a set point and, with an imposed loop delay, generating a carrier rhythm.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is divisive normalisation or an automatic-gain-control layer, and a recurrent-cell integrator for the rhythmic case; the biological motif differs in that its normalisation emerges from a delayed physical loop (so it oscillates) and its gain is set by short-term synaptic facilitation rather than a fixed learned weight.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to hold a population's firing rate near a target by subtracting inhibition proportional to the population's own recent output, like a thermostat.

Create a number variable called drive with a value representing excitatory input.
Create a number variable called feedback gain with initial value 0.8.
Create a number variable called rate with initial value 0.
Create a number variable called inhibition with initial value 0.
Create a whole number variable called steps with initial value 20.
Repeat the following actions steps times.
    Set inhibition to feedback gain times rate.
    Set rate to drive minus inhibition.
    If rate is less than 0 is true, then perform the following actions.
        Set rate to 0.
    End the conditional block.
    Display rate to the console.
End the repeat block.
The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the point is to watch the loop settle to a stable rate that grows far less than the drive, and a short iteration makes the convergence visible.

# Feedback (recurrent) inhibition as an activity thermostat.
# The brake is proportional to the population's own output, so the
# steady-state rate obeys R ~= drive / (1 + gain): divisive gain control.
# (Isaacson & Scanziani, Neuron 2011, "How inhibition shapes cortical activity".)
FEEDBACK_GAIN = 0.8

def settle(drive, steps=20):
    rate, inh = 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(steps):
        inh = FEEDBACK_GAIN * rate          # brake scales with output
        rate = max(0.0, drive - inh)         # subtract, rectify
    return rate

print("drive  settled_rate  ratio")
for drive in (1.0, 2.0, 4.0):
    r = settle(drive)
    print(f"{drive:4.1f}   {r:6.3f}     {r/drive:5.3f}")
# Doubling drive does NOT double output: the thermostat compresses gain.

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A closed two-cell loop of opposite sign in which the cell drives its own brake, so the harder it fires the harder it is inhibited - a thermostat that compresses gain, prevents seizure, and, given a loop delay, rings the cortex at gamma.


CHAPTER 9. LATERAL INHIBITION (Neighbour-Suppressing Interneuron Motif) (The Contrast-Carving Circuit) (COG)

An active cell reaches sideways, through an interneuron, and quiets the cells around it, so that a strong signal not only reports itself but suppresses its neighbours' claim to be heard.

The winner grows relatively louder and the losers relatively softer, and the difference between them - the edge, the boundary, the contrast - is carved sharper than the raw input ever was.

Named in the framework volumes as the exemplary generic motif, lateral inhibition is installed in the retina to find edges of light, in the dentate gyrus to keep memories from blurring into one another, and in the cortex to sharpen selectivity of every kind.

Neighbour names its reach, sideways to cells nearby in space or in feature.

Suppressing names its sign, turning those neighbours down.

Carving names its product, a sharpened contrast where before there was a gentle gradient.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Lateral inhibition is a motif in which active principal cells inhibit their neighbours by way of interneurons, so that each cell's output is reduced by the activity of its surround.

What it computes is contrast enhancement and competition: it takes a smooth input distribution and sharpens its peaks and edges, implementing a form of spatial (or feature-space) high-pass filtering and, in its strong form, a winner-take-most selection.

In the retina it builds the centre-surround receptive field that is the first computation performed on light; in the dentate gyrus it separates similar input patterns into dissimilar sparse outputs.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Node roles: an array of principal cells (P1, P2, ... Pn) and inhibitory interneurons (I) that connect neighbours.

Each principal cell excites nearby interneurons (excitatory edge, glutamatergic), and each interneuron inhibits principal cells in a surrounding neighbourhood (inhibitory edge, gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)), excluding or weakly including the cell that drove it.

The topology is a spatially organised lateral network: the excitatory-to-inhibitory-to-neighbour path forms a surround of suppression around each active site, so the effective connectivity is a centre (self, net excitatory) minus a weighted surround (neighbours, net inhibitory) - a difference-of-Gaussians kernel in wiring.

In the retina a special dendrodendritic and electrical variant is used: horizontal cells feed inhibition back laterally onto photoreceptor terminals.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

In cortex and hippocampus the interneuron is again the parvalbumin fast-spiking basket cell of the neuron catalogue, whose fast, focal, reliable inhibition makes lateral suppression sharp in both time and space - in the dentate gyrus lateral inhibition by parvalbumin cells is more abundant than in any other studied region.

In the retina the role is played by the horizontal cell of the other-cells catalogue (for the outer retina) and the amacrine cell (for the inner retina); the horizontal cell is a broad, slow, electrically coupled integrator whose wide receptive field sets the scale of the surround.

In the olfactory bulb the granule cell plays the inhibitor through dendrodendritic synapses.

The personality contrast is instructive: the fast-spiking cortical inhibitor carves contrast on a millisecond, cell-by-cell basis, while the slow, gap-junction-coupled horizontal cell carves it as a smooth spatial average - same motif, opposite temporal grain.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Excitatory edges use glutamate on alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors; inhibitory edges use GABA on GABA-A receptors (fast, cortex) or, in the outer retina, a still-debated sign-inverting mechanism at the cone terminal involving GABA, ephaptic (electrical field) effects, and proton signalling.

Horizontal cells are joined to one another by gap junctions (connexin-mediated electrical synapses, largely connexin-57 in horizontal cells) that pool their signals over hundreds of micrometres, setting the surround radius.

Amacrine and granule cells use dendrodendritic reciprocal synapses.

Weights follow the surround kernel and are tuned by adaptation and neuromodulation (dopamine uncouples horizontal-cell gap junctions in bright light, shrinking the surround).

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a local array: in the retina, a photoreceptor with the horizontal-cell surround feeding back over 100 to several hundred micrometres; in cortex, a principal cell and the ring of neighbours reached by one basket cell's axon, tens to a couple of hundred micrometres.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Astronomical: every point in the retina and every feature map in the cortex carries lateral inhibition, so instances tile every sensory sheet and every competitive population - hundreds of millions to billions, high confidence on ubiquity.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Retina (outer plexiform layer): horizontal-cell lateral inhibition builds the centre-surround receptive field and enhances edges - the first computation on light.

• Retina (inner plexiform layer): amacrine-cell lateral inhibition sharpens temporal and directional selectivity.

• Dentate gyrus: parvalbumin lateral inhibition enforces sparse, separated codes for pattern separation, the memory-disambiguation step.

• Neocortex, sensory areas: lateral inhibition sharpens orientation, frequency, and whisker tuning, narrowing receptive fields.

• Olfactory bulb: granule-cell lateral inhibition sharpens odour representations by contrast between glomerular channels.

• Thalamus: reticular-nucleus lateral inhibition sharpens sensory relay.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete lateral inhibition and each sensory sheet loses its edges: the retina would report absolute light levels but not boundaries, so the visual world would go foggy and uniform; the cortex would report that a feature is present but not sharply which one; the dentate gyrus would let similar experiences collapse into one another, and memories would interfere.

The region keeps its signal but loses its selectivity - it can still see the wall but no longer the doorway in it.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is subtractive-to-divisive surround suppression: each cell's output equals its own drive minus a weighted sum of its neighbours' drive (difference-of-Gaussians), which enhances contrast at edges and suppresses uniform regions.

In strong form with recurrent lateral inhibition it becomes divisive and competitive, approaching winner-take-all.

Concretely, a step edge in the input produces overshoot on the bright side and undershoot on the dark side (Mach bands), and a broad uniform patch is suppressed toward baseline while its border is amplified severalfold.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

In the fast cortical form, lateral inhibition follows excitation by the disynaptic delay of one to three milliseconds and sharpens within a single response.

In the retinal horizontal-cell form it is slower and graded (photoreceptors and horizontal cells signal with graded potentials, not spikes), acting over tens of milliseconds, and it produces the sustained surround antagonism of the receptive field.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Weak lateral inhibition gives gentle contrast enhancement; strong recurrent lateral inhibition gives winner-take-all selection (the next part's competitive motifs are lateral inhibition turned up).

Adaptation reshapes the surround with light level (retina) or stimulus statistics (cortex): the surround widens in dim conditions and narrows in bright ones as gap junctions uncouple.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The excitatory drive onto inhibitory neighbours is plastic, tuning who suppresses whom; in cortex, experience shapes the lateral inhibitory kernel, sharpening maps during critical periods.

Retinal surround gain is modulated on a fast timescale by dopamine and light adaptation rather than by long-term synaptic learning.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Feedforward lateral inhibition (input drives the surround directly) versus feedback lateral inhibition (output drives the surround); spatial lateral inhibition (retina, cortex maps) versus feature-space lateral inhibition (tuning-curve sharpening); the electrical-and-dendrodendritic retinal variant versus the chemical synaptic cortical variant.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Retinal horizontal-cell mosaics self-organise during development to tile the sheet evenly; cortical lateral inhibitory kernels are refined by sensory experience over critical periods, with parvalbumin maturation again the gate.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Lateral inhibition is among the most ancient sensory computations, described first in the horseshoe-crab eye (Limulus) by Hartline and Ratliff, and conserved across essentially all image-forming eyes and most sensory systems - the framework's chosen exemplar of a generic motif precisely because it recurs everywhere.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Retinal lateral inhibition depends on Muller glia for potassium and neurotransmitter homeostasis and on the pigment epithelium; cortical lateral inhibition depends on the parvalbumin support systems described earlier.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Loss of retinal lateral inhibition degrades contrast sensitivity (seen in some retinal degenerations and in connexin mutations affecting horizontal-cell coupling); impaired dentate lateral inhibition is linked to pattern-separation deficits in ageing, epilepsy, and Alzheimer disease; weakened cortical lateral inhibition blurs sensory selectivity.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ An array of principal-cell activities across space or feature 0 to 1 normalised; neuromodulatory surround-gain signals (dopamine in retina).

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A contrast-enhanced array in which peaks are amplified and uniform regions suppressed; edges marked by over- and undershoot.

• STATE.

◦ Per-cell activity; horizontal-cell coupling strength (surround radius); adaptation level.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Surround radius 100 to 300 micrometres (retina) or tens to 200 micrometres (cortex); inhibitory weight fraction 0.2 to 0.8 of centre.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Cortical disynaptic delay 1 to 3 milliseconds; retinal surround 10 to 50 milliseconds; adaptation of coupling seconds to minutes.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Connexin-57 or horizontal-cell dysfunction flattens contrast; dentate parvalbumin loss abolishes pattern separation, producing memory interference.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module lateral_inhibition_sharpener.

It would subscribe to an activity array over a spatial or feature map and publish a contrast-enhanced array, each element reduced by a weighted sum of its neighbours (a difference-of-Gaussians kernel), with a strong-mode switch to winner-take-all.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogues are the difference-of-Gaussians edge filter, local response normalisation, and lateral competition in self-organising maps; the biological motif differs in that its surround radius is dynamically re-scaled by neuromodulators and adaptation, and in the retina it is implemented partly through electrical coupling rather than pure arithmetic.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to sharpen contrast across an array of activities by subtracting from each element a weighted average of its two neighbours, then removing any negative results.

Create a list variable called input activities holding numbers across space.
Create a number variable called surround weight with initial value 0.5.
Create an empty list variable called output activities.
Create a whole number variable called index with initial value 0.
Repeat for each element in input activities.
    Create a number variable called centre set to input activities at index.
    Create a number variable called left neighbour set to input activities at index minus 1, or centre if none exists.
    Create a number variable called right neighbour set to input activities at index plus 1, or centre if none exists.
    Create a number variable called surround set to surround weight times the average of left neighbour and right neighbour.
    Create a number variable called result set to centre minus surround.
    If result is less than 0 is true, then perform the following actions.
        Set result to 0.
    End the conditional block.
    Add result to output activities.
    Increase index by 1.
End the repeat block.
Display output activities to the console.
The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because contrast enhancement is a one-line kernel over an array, and printing the input beside the output makes the carved edge unmistakable.

# Lateral inhibition as contrast enhancement across an array.
# Each cell subtracts a weighted average of its neighbours: a difference-of-
# Gaussians / centre-surround kernel that amplifies edges (Mach bands) and
# suppresses flat regions. (Hartline & Ratliff, Limulus retina, 1957.)
SURROUND_W = 0.5

def sharpen(x):
    out = []
    for i, c in enumerate(x):
        left  = x[i-1] if i > 0 else c
        right = x[i+1] if i < len(x)-1 else c
        out.append(max(0.0, c - SURROUND_W * (left + right) / 2))
    return out

edge = [1, 1, 1, 1, 5, 5, 5, 5]     # a step from dim to bright
print("input :", edge)
print("output:", [round(v, 2) for v in sharpen(edge)])
# The flat runs collapse toward 0; the border overshoots -> the edge is carved.

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

An array of cells each reaching sideways through an inhibitor to quiet its neighbours, so a smooth gradient comes out with its edges overshooting and its flats suppressed - the same difference-of-Gaussians signature whether it is carved in the retina by a slow horizontal cell or in the cortex by a fast basket cell.


CHAPTER 10. RECURRENT INHIBITION OF THE RENSHAW TYPE (Motor-Collateral Feedback Interneuron) (The Final-Path Governor) (NON-COG)

A spinal motoneuron sends its command out to the muscle and, at the same moment, drops a copy of that command onto a small interneuron crouched beside it in the ventral horn.

That interneuron - the Renshaw cell, named for its discoverer - fires a fierce high-frequency burst straight back onto the motoneuron and its neighbours, damping the very output that woke it.

Discovered at the spinal motoneuron as the first proven feedback-inhibition circuit in the mammalian cord, it is a governor bolted onto the final common path: it stabilises firing rate, limits synchrony, and smooths the force a muscle produces.

Final path names its address, the motoneuron that is the last neuron before muscle.

Governor names its job, the mechanical regulator that keeps an engine from over-revving.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Recurrent inhibition of the Renshaw type is a feedback-inhibition motif specialised to the spinal (and brainstem) motor system, in which a motoneuron's own axon collateral excites a Renshaw cell that inhibits that motoneuron and its synergists.

Functionally it stabilises the discharge frequency of motoneuron pools, prevents them from firing at excessive rates, limits pathological synchrony, and (by the leading hypotheses) either filters spike timing for smooth force generation or controls the gain of the motoneuron pool.

It is tagged non-cognitive because it regulates motor execution rather than participating in perception, memory, or decision, though its diagram is identical to the cognitive feedback inhibition of Chapter 8.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Node roles: the alpha-motoneuron (M) and the Renshaw cell (R).

Edge one is excitatory, from M's recurrent axon collateral to R, using acetylcholine (the same transmitter the motoneuron uses at the muscle) - a rare central cholinergic excitatory synapse.

Edge two is inhibitory, from R back to M and to synergist motoneurons and to Ia inhibitory interneurons, using glycine (with some gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) co-release).

The topology is a closed feedback loop with lateral spread: one Renshaw cell collects collaterals from many motoneurons of a pool and returns inhibition to that pool and its synergists, and it also inhibits the Ia inhibitory interneurons, thereby modulating reciprocal inhibition (the subject of Chapter 11) - so the Renshaw loop sits partly in control of the next motif.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The principal cell is the alpha-motoneuron of the neuron catalogue, the large ventral-horn cell that is the sole output to skeletal muscle.

The interneuron is the Renshaw cell of the catalogue, whose defining personality is its explosive response: a single motoneuron volley makes it fire a brief, very high-frequency burst (hundreds of spikes per second) that then decays, so its inhibitory feedback is a sharp initial pulse followed by a tail - a fast-onset, rapidly adapting brake perfectly matched to catching the leading edge of motoneuron firing.

Its cholinergic excitation and short-term potentiation mean repeated motoneuron activity recruits it strongly.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The M-to-R synapse is nicotinic-cholinergic (acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors, a fast ionotropic excitation) and shows short-term potentiation, so the loop strengthens within a burst.

The R-to-M synapse is glycinergic (glycine on strychnine-sensitive glycine receptors, fast chloride-mediated inhibition), with GABA co-release; Renshaw cells make a large number of synaptic contacts onto each motoneuron, giving large inhibitory conductances.

Renshaw cells are also electrically coupled to one another by gap junctions in early development.

Weights are large and reliable; plasticity is mainly short-term (potentiation within a burst) rather than the long-term learning of cortical synapses.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a motoneuron pool (the motoneurons innervating one muscle, tens to a few hundred cells) together with the Renshaw cells sharing their collaterals, spanning a few hundred micrometres to a few millimetres along the ventral horn.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Bounded and countable in principle: one loop per motoneuron pool, and there are a few hundred skeletal muscles, so on the order of hundreds of instances in the spinal cord and brainstem - far fewer than the astronomical forebrain motifs, moderate confidence.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Spinal cord, ventral horn (all levels): Renshaw feedback stabilises the motoneuron pools of limb and trunk muscles.

• Brainstem motor nuclei (partial): analogous recurrent inhibition regulates some cranial motoneuron pools.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove the Renshaw loop and the ventral horn loses its governor: motoneuron pools would fire faster and more synchronously, force would come in coarse, jerky increments rather than smoothly graded contractions, and fine control at low force levels would degrade.

The cord keeps its reflexes but loses the smoothing that lets a muscle produce steady, finely graded tension.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is negative-feedback rate stabilisation and desynchronisation: the motoneuron pool's output is fed back as inhibition proportional to recent firing, flattening the pool's frequency-current relationship (reducing gain) and decorrelating individual motoneuron spikes to smooth summed force.

In numbers, recurrent inhibition can reduce motoneuron gain by a modest fraction and measurably lower firing synchrony; the Renshaw burst reaches hundreds of hertz and decays over tens of milliseconds.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Motoneuron spike, then after about one millisecond the Renshaw burst, then a glycinergic inhibitory potential in the motoneuron peaking within a few milliseconds and decaying over tens of milliseconds - a fast recurrent inhibitory postsynaptic potential with a characteristic bursting driver.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Recurrent inhibition is itself under descending control: supraspinal and segmental inputs raise or lower Renshaw excitability to suit the task, reducing it for strong synchronous efforts and raising it for fine steady holds.

During locomotion its gain is modulated phase-by-phase by the central pattern generator.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Mostly short-term (within-burst potentiation of the cholinergic drive); developmentally the loop is refined as motoneuron pools mature, and Renshaw electrical coupling is prominent early then reduced.

Long-term cognitive-style plasticity is not its business.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Limb versus axial motoneuron loops; the degree of synergist spread varies by muscle group; some motoneuron pools (notably certain distal hand muscles in primates) have weak or absent recurrent inhibition, a specialisation for independent finger control.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Renshaw cells are among the earliest-born spinal interneurons, derived from the V1 interneuron class (engrailed-1 lineage), and they wire to motoneurons before birth; their early gap-junction coupling helps synchronise developing motor networks, giving way to the mature chemical feedback loop.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Recurrent inhibition of motor output is an old vertebrate feature, present across tetrapods; its relative weakening in the primate distal-hand system is a derived specialisation permitting fractionated finger movement.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Depends on spinal astrocytes for glycine and potassium homeostasis and on the cholinergic and glycinergic machinery of the ventral horn; Renshaw cells are identifiable by calbindin and by their gephyrin-anchored glycine receptors.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Loss of glycinergic Renshaw inhibition produces hyperexcitability: in tetanus and in strychnine poisoning, block of glycine receptors removes recurrent (and reciprocal) inhibition, causing rigidity and spasm; Renshaw-cell degeneration is implicated in aspects of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, where motoneuron loss and altered recurrent inhibition co-occur.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Cholinergic recurrent collateral drive from the motoneuron pool; descending and segmental modulation of Renshaw excitability.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Glycinergic inhibition to the motoneuron pool, its synergists, and the Ia inhibitory interneurons.

• STATE.

◦ Motoneuron pool firing rate; Renshaw burst level; descending gain-modulation setting.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ M-to-R latency about 1 millisecond; Renshaw burst rate up to several hundred hertz; recurrent inhibitory potential decay tens of milliseconds.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Glycine receptor decay about 5 to 10 milliseconds; burst adaptation tens of milliseconds; modulation over the movement cycle.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Strychnine and tetanus toxin block glycinergic recurrent inhibition, producing convulsive rigidity; recurrent-inhibition changes accompany amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spasticity.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Although non-cognitive, the module would be named motoneuron_output_governor: it would subscribe to a motor pool's output and publish an inhibition proportional to and slightly delayed from that output, flattening the pool's gain and desynchronising its units for smooth force.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is an output-side automatic-gain-control or a rate limiter with decorrelation; the biological motif differs in using a bursting, rapidly adapting inhibitor and in doubling as a controller of the reciprocal-inhibition pathway.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A ventral-horn feedback loop in which the motoneuron's own cholinergic collateral fires a small cell into an explosive high-frequency burst that glycinergically brakes the pool - the one place in the body where the transmitter of muscle command also drives its own governor.


CHAPTER 11. RECIPROCAL INHIBITION (Mutually-Silencing Antagonist Pair) (The Push-Pull Pair) (NON-COG)

Two cells, or two pools, are wired so that each inhibits the other: when one speaks the other falls silent, and they cannot both be loud at once.

In the spinal cord this see-saw is what lets a limb move - as the flexor motoneurons fire to bend the joint, a disynaptic inhibitory path relaxes the extensor that would otherwise fight them, so agonist and antagonist do not waste effort pulling against each other.

The same push-pull diagram, given fatigue, becomes the half-centre oscillator that drives walking, and given a different address it flips the brain between sleep and waking - one see-saw, many destinies.

Push-pull names its logic, one side up forces the other down.

Pair names its minimal form, two opposed elements locked in mutual veto.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Reciprocal inhibition is a motif in which two cells or populations inhibit each other, so that activity in one enforces silence in the other.

In its canonical spinal form it computes antagonist relaxation: when a muscle's motoneurons are driven, an interneuron path simultaneously inhibits the motoneurons of the opposing muscle, coordinating the joint.

It is tagged non-cognitive for its principal sensorimotor role, with the honest note that the identical diagram, elsewhere, powers oscillators (the half-centre) and bistable decision and state switches (sleep-wake, winner-take-all) that are cognitive.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The canonical spinal diagram has these node roles: the Ia afferent (A) from the muscle spindle, the agonist motoneuron (Ma), the Ia inhibitory interneuron (Iia), and the antagonist motoneuron (Mn).

Edge one is excitatory, from A to Ma (glutamatergic, monosynaptic - the stretch reflex).

Edge two is excitatory, from A to Iia (glutamatergic).

Edge three is inhibitory, from Iia to Mn (glycinergic), one synapse beyond the excitation, hence disynaptic.

For a symmetric pair the antagonist's own Ia afferent drives its own Ia inhibitory interneuron that inhibits the agonist, giving the mutual, cross-coupled topology; the two Ia inhibitory interneurons also inhibit each other, and Renshaw cells (Chapter 10) inhibit the Ia interneurons, so the see-saw is itself governed.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The motoneurons are the alpha-motoneurons of the neuron catalogue.

The pivotal cell is the Ia inhibitory interneuron of the catalogue, a glycinergic ventral-horn interneuron whose personality is speed and reliability: it converts spindle input into antagonist inhibition with a single interposed synapse, producing an inhibitory potential in the antagonist that lags the agonist's excitatory potential by only about 0.8 milliseconds.

Its fast, faithful relay is what makes reciprocal inhibition tight enough to be useful during rapid movement.

In half-centre and flip-flop variants the mutually inhibiting elements are the relevant projection or pattern-generator neurons, and the addition of spike-frequency adaptation or synaptic depression to each side is what turns the static see-saw into an alternating oscillator.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The afferent-to-neuron and afferent-to-interneuron edges are glutamatergic (alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA)).

The Ia inhibitory interneuron-to-motoneuron edge is glycinergic (glycine on strychnine-sensitive receptors, fast chloride inhibition), the same fast inhibition as the Renshaw synapse.

In half-centre oscillators the mutual inhibition may be glycinergic or GABAergic, and each side carries an adaptation or depression mechanism (calcium-activated potassium currents, synaptic depression) that provides the fatigue enabling escape.

Weights are strong and reliable; plasticity is mostly short-term and modulatory rather than long-term learning.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance spans an agonist-antagonist motoneuron pair with their Ia interneurons at a single spinal segment, a few hundred micrometres to a couple of millimetres.

The half-centre and flip-flop variants scale to the pattern-generator or hypothalamic populations they serve.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

In the spinal form, one reciprocal pair per antagonist muscle pairing at each relevant segment - on the order of hundreds of instances; the broader push-pull family (opponent channels, half-centres, flip-flops) recurs widely, but the antagonist-relaxation instance itself is bounded and countable, moderate confidence.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Spinal cord, ventral horn: Ia reciprocal inhibition relaxes the antagonist during voluntary and reflex movement at every joint.

• Spinal and brainstem central pattern generators: reciprocal inhibition between flexor and extensor half-centres generates locomotor and respiratory alternation.

• Hypothalamus and brainstem (as flip-flop): mutually inhibiting sleep-promoting and arousal populations form the sleep-wake switch (this reappears as a Part Five motif).

• Vestibular and oculomotor nuclei: reciprocal inhibition coordinates push-pull eye-muscle control.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove reciprocal inhibition from the cord and every movement becomes a tug-of-war: agonist and antagonist would co-contract, wasting force and stiffening the joint, and smooth flexion or extension would be impossible.

Remove it from a central pattern generator and rhythmic alternation collapses; remove it from the sleep-wake switch and the brain would drift and dither between states instead of committing cleanly - the region loses its ability to choose one of two opposites.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is mutual (cross) subtraction enforcing exclusivity: each side's output is its drive minus the other side's activity, so with sufficient mutual gain the pair becomes bistable (one high, one low) and, with added fatigue, oscillatory (the two sides alternate).

In the spinal reflex the concrete number is the 0.8-millisecond lag of the antagonist inhibitory potential behind the agonist excitatory potential; in the half-centre the period is set by the adaptation time constant, from hundreds of milliseconds (fast locomotion) to seconds (slow rhythms).

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Agonist excitatory potential followed about 0.8 milliseconds later by the antagonist inhibitory potential (the disynaptic fingerprint); in the oscillatory variant, a clean alternation with a duty cycle set by the fatigue of each half-centre.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Static reciprocal inhibition (antagonist relaxation) is the resting regime; add fatigue and it becomes a half-centre oscillator; raise the mutual gain and it becomes a hard bistable flip-flop.

The spinal pathway's gain is modulated by descending commands and by presynaptic inhibition, and is deliberately reduced during co-contraction tasks (stiffening a joint) - so the see-saw can be locked when stiffness is wanted.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Chiefly short-term and modulatory; the spinal reciprocal pathway's gain is adjustable by training (its modulation is impaired in spasticity and dystonia), but it does not store patterns the way cognitive attractors do.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Antagonist-relaxation reciprocal inhibition (spinal, static) versus the half-centre oscillator (with fatigue) versus the mutual-inhibition flip-flop (high gain, bistable) versus opponent sensory channels (ON-OFF).

The framework treats these as one diagram at different operating points and addresses.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The Ia inhibitory interneurons derive from the same ventral interneuron programmes as other spinal inhibitory cells and wire to their motoneuron pairs before and shortly after birth; reciprocal circuits are refined by early motor activity, and their balance matures over the first years.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Reciprocal inhibition between antagonists (Sherrington's reciprocal innervation) is a fundamental vertebrate motor principle, and mutual inhibition as an oscillator and switch is even older and more general, appearing in invertebrate pattern generators and throughout nervous systems as the elementary way to make two things mutually exclusive.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Depends on spinal glycinergic machinery and astrocytic homeostasis, as for the Renshaw loop; the Ia interneurons and their gephyrin-anchored glycine receptors are the identifiable substrate.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Impaired reciprocal inhibition is a signature of spasticity (reduced disynaptic reciprocal Ia inhibition during movement in spastic multiple sclerosis and stroke) and of dystonia (abnormal reciprocal inhibition producing co-contraction); strychnine and tetanus, by blocking glycine, abolish it along with recurrent inhibition, causing rigidity.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Ia spindle afferent drive to agonist motoneuron and Ia interneuron; descending commands setting reciprocal versus co-contraction mode.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Glycinergic inhibition of the antagonist motoneuron pool; in oscillatory mode, alternating drive to the two sides.

• STATE.

◦ Activity of each side; mode (reciprocal, co-contraction, oscillatory); adaptation level in half-centre variants.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Disynaptic lag about 0.8 milliseconds; mutual inhibitory gain (dimensionless); half-centre adaptation time constant hundreds of milliseconds to seconds.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Glycine receptor decay 5 to 10 milliseconds; oscillation period set by adaptation, 0.1 to several seconds; modulation over the movement.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Reduced reciprocal Ia inhibition in spasticity and stroke; abnormal reciprocal inhibition in dystonia; glycine block (strychnine, tetanus) abolishing it entirely.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Although non-cognitive in its spinal role, the module would be named mutual_exclusion_pair: it would subscribe to the drives of two opposed channels and publish outputs in which each channel is suppressed by the other, exposing a mode parameter that selects static exclusivity, oscillation (with fatigue), or hard bistability (high gain).

The closest artificial-intelligence analogues are a two-unit softmax or lateral-inhibition winner-take-all and a coupled relaxation oscillator; the biological motif differs in that a single wiring pattern is reused across three operating regimes selected by adaptation and gain rather than by separate architectures.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

Two opposed elements each holding the other silent through a fast glycinergic interneuron, so that in the cord one muscle relaxes exactly as its antagonist contracts - the elementary see-saw that, with fatigue added, becomes the rhythm of walking and, with gain added, the switch between sleep and waking.


CHAPTER 12. PRESYNAPTIC INHIBITION (Axo-Axonic Terminal Gating Motif) (The Input Tap) (NON-COG)

Every other brake in this manuscript acts on a cell; this one acts on a wire.

An inhibitory terminal reaches forward and clamps onto the very tip of an incoming axon, turning down that single input line before its message is ever delivered, while every other line into the same target keeps flowing at full strength.

It is the only inhibitory motif in the nervous system that can silence one voice in a choir without touching the singer beside it.

The spinal cord uses it in vast numbers to mute the flood of sensation from a limb at the instant that limb begins to move.

Input names the target: not a cell, but one arriving connection.

Tap names the action: a valve on the pipe, dialled between open and shut rather than switched.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Presynaptic inhibition is a wiring motif in which one neuron's axon terminal forms a synapse onto another neuron's axon terminal, so that transmitter release from the second terminal is reduced at the moment it would otherwise fire.

The computation is selective gain control on a single input line: the receiving cell is not inhibited, and its other inputs are untouched, but the one gated line delivers a fraction of its normal signal.

Because it multiplies the strength of one input by a number between zero and one, it is a divisive gate applied per-connection rather than a subtraction applied to the whole cell.

Its principal job in the body is not thought but filtering: it suppresses predictable or self-generated sensory signals, most famously the barrage of touch and stretch information that a moving limb would otherwise send back to the cord.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

There are three nodes and they form a short open chain with one special junction.

The first node is the primary afferent or input axon, an excitatory fibre (glutamatergic) running toward a target cell, for example a muscle-spindle sensory fibre running to a motoneuron.

The second node is a gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) releasing interneuron, called a GABAergic axo-axonic interneuron, whose axon terminal lands not on the target cell's dendrite or soma but directly on the input axon's own terminal - this is the defining axo-axonic edge, and its sign is inhibitory-by-depolarisation, explained below.
