The operating point k is state-dependent: novelty and acetylcholine loosen inhibition to admit more winners (encoding mode), while familiarity tightens it; adult neurogenesis adds a special regime in which young, hyperexcitable granule cells compete on easier terms for a few weeks, refreshing the code.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Perforant-path synapses onto the winning granule cells undergo long-term potentiation, entrenching each committee for its context; inhibitory plasticity tunes the brake to hold the target sparseness; and adult neurogenesis in the dentate gyrus, one of the two accepted human neurogenic niches, continually inserts new competitors, which modelling and experiment link to improved separation of similar memories.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Hard k equals 1 recovers Chapter 16; the dentate variant adds neurogenesis; the cerebellar variant adds the Golgi cell's slower loop and enormous expansion; the piriform variant runs distributed, non-topographic sparse codes; and neocortical soft-WTA keeps a graded margin rather than a crisp k.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Granule cells are born late and continue to be born in adulthood in the dentate; the inhibitory thermostat calibrates during postnatal life through activity-dependent inhibitory plasticity, and the characteristic sparseness emerges only as the GABA system matures from its early depolarising phase to mature hyperpolarising inhibition.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The expansion-plus-global-inhibition diagram is one of evolution's favourites, implemented independently in the insect mushroom body (Kenyon cells with one giant inhibitory neuron as thermostat), the fish cerebellum-like electrosensory lobes and the mammalian dentate and cerebellum: the same sparse-coding solution rediscovered at least three times.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Sparseness is an energy policy as much as a coding policy: silent cells burn little, letting the brain afford billions of granule cells; astrocytes in the neurogenic niche double as stem-cell nursemaids, and radial glia-like precursors supply the new competitors.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

In temporal-lobe epilepsy the dentate brake fails and mossy fibres sprout recurrent excitatory collaterals, converting the sparsifier into an amplifier, and the dentate's normal role as a seizure gate is lost.

Reduced neurogenesis and degraded pattern separation are implicated in the overgeneralised fear of post-traumatic stress disorder and the discrimination deficits of ageing and early Alzheimer disease.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Dense afferent vectors (entorhinal grid and object codes; mossy-fibre state vectors), individual synaptic conductances under 1 nanosiemens.

◦ Cholinergic and noradrenergic novelty signals adjusting the sparseness set point by tens of percent.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A sparse code: 2 to 5 percent of cells active, winners bursting at 10 to 40 hertz for tens of milliseconds.

• STATE.

◦ Current winner set; interneuron pool rate; slowly, the age distribution of adult-born competitors.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Target active fraction 0.02 to 0.05; expansion ratio about 4 to 5 (dentate) up to hundreds (cerebellum); granule threshold near minus 45 millivolts from rest near minus 85.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Feedback inhibition loop 5 to 15 milliseconds; theta frame 125 to 250 milliseconds; potentiation minutes to hours; neurogenesis weeks.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Temporal-lobe epilepsy with mossy-fibre sprouting (lost sparseness); overgeneralisation of fear memories; pattern-separation decline in ageing and early Alzheimer disease.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module sparse_code_pattern_separator, subscribing to a dense feature-vector topic and a sparseness set-point topic, and publishing a k-hot sparse vector plus an overlap statistic.

The closest artificial intelligence analogues are k-winners-take-all layers, top-k sparse autoencoders and locality-sensitive hashing by random expansion; the biological motif differs in that k is a live, neuromodulator-set parameter, the coding field slowly gains new units (neurogenesis) rather than being fixed, and the expansion weights are sparse and largely random rather than learned end to end.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to keep only the k most strongly driven cells active by raising a global inhibition level, producing a sparse code.
Create a number variable called k with initial value 3.
Create a list variable called drives holding the input drive of each of one hundred cells.
Create a number variable called inhibition with initial value 0.
Repeat the following actions until the number of active cells equals k.
    Create a number variable called active count with initial value 0.
    For each cell, perform the following actions.
        Calculate the difference of that cell's drive and inhibition.
        If the result is greater than 0 is true, then add 1 to active count and mark the cell active.
        Otherwise, mark the cell inactive.
        End the conditional block.
    End the loop over cells.
    If active count is greater than k is true, then increase inhibition by a small step.
    Else if active count is less than k is true, then decrease inhibition by a small step.
    End the conditional block.
End the repetition block.
Display the list of active cells as the sparse code.
The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the claim to demonstrate is numerical, that sparsening two similar inputs reduces their overlap, and a few lines of array arithmetic prove it directly.

# k-winners sparse coding and pattern separation, dentate-gyrus style.
# Only ~2-5 percent of granule cells fire per context (Chawla et al.,
# Hippocampus 2005; Cayco-Gajic and Silver, Neuron 2019 on expansion).
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

N_IN, N_OUT, K = 100, 1000, 30            # expansion, then 3 percent winners
W = (rng.random((N_OUT, N_IN)) < 0.1) * rng.random((N_OUT, N_IN))

def k_winners(x, k=K):
    drive = W @ x
    out = np.zeros(N_OUT)
    out[np.argsort(drive)[-k:]] = 1.0      # global inhibition spares top k
    return out

def overlap(a, b):
    return (a @ b) / np.sqrt((a @ a) * (b @ b))

x1 = rng.random(N_IN)                      # context A
x2 = x1.copy()
flip = rng.choice(N_IN, 20, replace=False) # context B: 80 percent similar
x2[flip] = rng.random(20)

y1, y2 = k_winners(x1), k_winners(x2)
print(f"input overlap  = {overlap(x1, x2):.2f}")
print(f"output overlap = {overlap(y1, y2):.2f}  (separated)")
print(f"active fraction = {y1.mean():.3f}")
# Output overlap falls well below input overlap: similar experiences
# are written onto largely different sparse committees of cells.

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A vast, mostly silent expansion population under one cheap global brake, an active fraction of a few percent, and the measurable signature that its outputs overlap less than its inputs: it is the only motif whose product is distance between memories.


CHAPTER 18. DIVISIVE NORMALIZATION (Pooled-Activity Divisive Scaling Motif) (The Fair-Share Circuit) (COG)

Step from a dim hallway into noon sunlight and the light flooding your retina multiplies ten-thousand-fold, yet the scene looks merely brighter, not obliterated: something divided.

Divisive normalisation is that something, a motif in which each neuron's response is divided by the summed activity of a pool of its neighbours, so that every cell reports not its raw drive but its share of the local conversation.

Carandini and Heeger crowned it a canonical neural computation because the same equation keeps reappearing, in retina, cortex, olfaction, audition and attention, wherever biology needs ratios instead of raw amounts.

It is arithmetic's quietest gift to the brain: division, implemented in wetware, and with it invariance.

Fair names the outcome: each response is scaled relative to the whole pool, so no signal can hog the dynamic range.

Share names the operation: output equals a cell's drive divided by drive-plus-everyone-else's, a normalised fraction.

Circuit marks it as a wiring motif, installed at many addresses, not a cell or a region.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Divisive normalisation is a circuit operation in which a neuron's output equals its driving input raised to a power, divided by the sum of a semisaturation constant and the pooled activity of a normalisation pool, the classic form R = c to the n over (sigma to the n plus the sum of pool activity to the n), with n near 2.

The computation is dynamic-range management and ratio coding: it produces contrast invariance in vision (orientation tuning keeps its shape as contrast varies), concentration invariance in olfaction, and the multiplicative response changes wrought by attention, which the normalisation model of attention explains by letting attention weight the numerator or the pool.

It converts absolute codes into relative ones, which is why a grey patch looks the same at dawn and at noon.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Node roles: a set of driven principal cells (the reporters), a pooling stage that sums activity across many reporters (the tax assessor), and a divisive feedback path onto each reporter.

Each reporter receives its private excitatory (glutamatergic) driving edge from upstream.

Every reporter contributes an excitatory edge to the pooling node, which in cortex is realised by broadly tuned inhibitory interneurons and, in part, by shared synaptic depression and network-level balanced amplification.

The pooling node returns an edge to each reporter whose effect is divisive rather than subtractive: implemented by shunting (conductance-increasing) inhibition on soma and proximal dendrites, by presynaptic depression scaling with pool rate, and in invertebrate olfaction by lateral presynaptic inhibition of afferent terminals.

Topology: all-to-one convergence onto the pool, one-to-all divergence back, a fully shared tax with no favourites.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The reporters in the flagship cortical instance are the pyramidal cells of primary visual cortex, chiefly layer 4 and layer 2/3 cells of the neuron catalogue, whose tuned, adapting personalities supply the selective numerator.

The tax assessor is dominated by the parvalbumin basket cell of the neuron catalogue: broadly tuned, fast-spiking and untiring, it fires in proportion to the summed local drive regardless of stimulus identity, which is precisely the untuned pool signal division requires, and its perisomatic synapses deliver the shunting conductance that makes the arithmetic divisive rather than subtractive.

Somatostatin Martinotti cells contribute a slower, surround-gathering component that extends the pool beyond the local column, colouring normalisation with its spatial-surround flavour.

In the retina the roles are played by bipolar cells (reporters) and horizontal plus amacrine cells (pool), and in the olfactory bulb by mitral cells with granule and periglomerular cells as the assessors.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Driving edges are glutamatergic alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) plus N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) synapses on reporter dendrites.

The divisive return path uses gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A shunting synapses clustered perisomatically, where an open chloride conductance raises total membrane conductance and scales down the voltage response per unit current, the biophysical form of division.

Short-term synaptic depression on thalamocortical and recurrent synapses, scaling with pool rate, supplies a second divisive mechanism with time constants of 50 to 300 milliseconds.

GABA-B receptor-mediated presynaptic inhibition implements normalisation at afferent terminals in the olfactory system, and gap junctions among the basket-cell pool (connexin 36) homogenise the tax.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

A cortical normalisation pool spans roughly one hypercolumn, 0.5 to 1 millimetre, pooling on the order of 10,000 to 100,000 neurons' activity onto each reporter; retinal and bulbar instances pool over 100 to 500 micrometres.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Effectively co-extensive with sensory and associative grey matter: every cortical column, retinal patch and glomerular neighbourhood runs one, so the count is in the millions of overlapping instances, and Carandini and Heeger's survey finds the same equation from fly antennal lobe to primate parietal cortex.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Retina, where photoreceptor and bipolar-stage normalisation implements light adaptation across ten log units of intensity.

• Primary visual cortex, where it produces contrast-invariant orientation tuning, cross-orientation suppression and surround suppression.

• Olfactory bulb and piriform cortex, where it yields concentration-invariant odour identity codes.

• Auditory cortex, where it underlies intensity-invariant tuning and forward suppression.

• Lateral intraparietal area and extrastriate cortex, where the normalisation model of attention accounts for attention's multiplicative and contrast-gain effects.

• Ventromedial prefrontal and orbitofrontal valuation circuits, where value signals are normalised by the value of the choice set, producing context-dependent economic choice.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove the divider and every hosting region loses its invariances: visual cortex would confuse contrast with orientation, the olfactory system would smell concentration instead of identity, valuation circuits would be seduced by absolute rather than relative worth, and all of them would saturate, their limited firing ranges crushed against the ceiling by strong inputs.

Normalisation is why a region's code means the same thing across the enormous dynamic range of the world.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transfer function is the ratio R equals R max times c to the n, divided by (sigma to the n plus c to the n plus pooled drive to the n), with exponent n typically 1.5 to 2.5 and semisaturation constant sigma corresponding to roughly 10 to 30 percent contrast in primary visual cortex.

Its fingerprints: response versus log contrast is a saturating sigmoid; adding a second, orthogonal stimulus suppresses the response to the first (cross-orientation suppression of 30 to 50 percent); and enlarging the pool shifts the curve rightward (contrast-gain change) rather than crushing it downward.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Fast: shunting components act within 5 to 20 milliseconds, depression components over 50 to 300 milliseconds, and slow adaptation extends the same arithmetic over seconds, so normalisation operates as a nested family of dividers from the frame rate of perception to the timescale of light adaptation.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The strength of normalisation is state-dependent: arousal and attention reweight the pool (attention effectively multiplies the attended input's contribution to numerator and denominator), and adaptation retunes sigma to recent statistics, keeping the operating point centred on the current scene.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Sigma and pool weights adapt over seconds to minutes through short-term plasticity and over days through inhibitory plasticity that matches inhibition to average excitation; contrast adaptation, the psychophysicist's oldest tool, is largely this motif re-tuning itself.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Feedforward normalisation (retina, fly antennal lobe), feedback normalisation (cortical recurrent form), surround normalisation (pool larger than the receptive field), feature-space normalisation (pool defined over tuning similarity rather than distance) and value normalisation in decision circuits.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Normalisation strength matures with the inhibitory system: surround suppression and cross-orientation suppression sharpen through the critical period as parvalbumin cells and their perineuronal nets mature, and visual deprivation weakens it, showing the divider is calibrated by experience.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Among the most ancient computations documented: the fruit fly antennal lobe performs textbook divisive normalisation through presynaptic lateral inhibition, and the invariance problem it solves, coding ratios in a world of absolute magnitudes, is as old as sensing itself.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Shunting inhibition moves large chloride fluxes, and the potassium-chloride cotransporter KCC2 plus astrocytic potassium buffering maintain the gradients that keep inhibition divisive rather than depolarising; the basket-cell pool's high metabolic rate is supported by dense perineuronal nets and mitochondria.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Weakened normalisation is a leading circuit hypothesis for autism spectrum condition, where reduced inhibitory tone predicts the observed reductions in surround suppression and the reported sensory overload; abnormal normalisation is also documented in schizophrenia (weakened surround suppression of contrast) and in migraine visual cortex between attacks.

Because division fails gracefully, these are disorders of degree: percepts become too absolute, too intense, too little contextualised.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Private driving inputs per reporter, 0 to 100 percent contrast equivalent.

◦ Pooled activity of 10,000 to 100,000 neighbours; attention and arousal weights scaling pool contributions by 10 to 50 percent.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Normalised rates, 0 to about 100 hertz, following R max times c to the n over (sigma to the n plus c to the n) with n about 2.

• STATE.

◦ Current pool activity; adaptation level of sigma; attention weights.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Exponent n 1.5 to 2.5; sigma equivalent to 10 to 30 percent contrast; R max 30 to 100 hertz; pool radius 0.5 to 1 millimetre in cortex.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Shunting 5 to 20 milliseconds; synaptic depression 50 to 300 milliseconds; contrast adaptation seconds to tens of seconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Reduced surround and cross-orientation suppression in autism spectrum condition and schizophrenia; sensory overload; saturation of codes under strong stimulation.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module divisive_normalization_scaler, subscribing to a raw feature-activity topic and an attention-weight topic, and publishing the same vector rescaled so that each element is divided by a constant plus the weighted pool sum.

The direct analogy for the artificial intelligence engineer is softmax and the normalisation layers of deep learning: softmax is exactly a divisive normalisation with an exponential numerator, and layer normalisation, batch normalisation and the softmax inside attention heads all divide unit activity by pooled statistics just as this motif does; the biological version differs in being local, continuous-time, implemented by shunting conductance with its own dynamics, and tunable on the fly by neuromodulators rather than fixed by architecture.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to compute a neuron's normalised response by dividing its drive by the pooled activity of its neighbours.
Create a number variable called maximum response with initial value 100.
Create a number variable called sigma with initial value 0.15.
Create a number variable called exponent with initial value 2.
Create a number variable called own drive holding the neuron's input contrast.
Create a list variable called pool drives holding the input contrasts of the neighbouring neurons.
Create a number variable called pool sum with initial value 0.
For each value in pool drives, perform the following actions.
    Raise the value to the power of exponent.
    Add the result to pool sum.
End the loop over pool drives.
Raise own drive to the power of exponent and call the result numerator.
Raise sigma to the power of exponent.
Calculate the sum of that result, numerator, and pool sum, and call it denominator.
Calculate the quotient of numerator and denominator.
Multiply the result by maximum response.
Set the neuron's response to the result.
Display the neuron's response to the console.
The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the proof is a curve, the saturating contrast-response function and its suppression by a busy pool, and a short loop prints that curve beyond argument.

# Divisive normalization: R = Rmax * c^n / (sigma^n + c^n + pool^n).
# Canonical computation per Carandini and Heeger, Nature Reviews
# Neuroscience 2012; explains contrast saturation and cross-suppression.
RMAX, SIGMA, N = 100.0, 0.15, 2.0

def response(c, pool=0.0):
    num = c ** N
    return RMAX * num / (SIGMA ** N + num + pool ** N)

print("contrast   alone   with busy pool (0.5)")
for c in (0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 1.0):
    print(f"{c:7.2f}  {response(c):6.1f}   {response(c, pool=0.5):6.1f}")

# Two signatures appear: response saturates with contrast (a sigmoid on
# log axes), and pooled neighbour activity divides the whole curve down,
# the cross-orientation suppression measured in visual cortex.
r_lo = response(0.1); r_hi = response(1.0)
print(f"tuning ratio preserved: {response(0.1, 0.5)/response(1.0, 0.5):.2f}"
      f" vs {r_lo/r_hi:.2f} without pool")

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A saturating response curve that slides sideways, not downward, when the neighbourhood gets busy, suppression by stimuli the cell does not even prefer, and invariance of tuning across intensity: wherever responses behave like fractions of a conversation rather than absolute shouts, this motif is the arithmetic underneath.


CHAPTER 19. GAIN MODULATION (Multiplicative Slope-Control Motif) (The Multiplier) (COG)

A whisper in an empty library and a shout at a concert can carry the same word, and your cortex hears both because something turned the volume knob without touching the tune.

Gain modulation is that knob: a modulatory input that changes the slope of a neuron's input-output curve rather than its threshold, multiplying responses instead of adding to them.

It is how attention brightens a location, arousal sharpens a moment, and posture-tracking signals rescale a retinal map into a body-centred one, all without rewriting the content of any signal.

Where the previous motif divides, this one multiplies, and between them the brain owns both halves of arithmetic's second row.

The names the definite article of a singular role: among the motifs, this is the designated multiplier.

Multiplier names the operation precisely: output equals input times gain, a change of slope, not of offset, distinguishing it from every additive influence.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

Gain modulation is a circuit and biophysical motif in which a second, modulatory input scales the sensitivity of a neuron or population to its driving input, multiplying the input-output function by a factor typically between roughly 0.5 and 2 without shifting its threshold.

The computation is multiplication of two signals, the operation underlying coordinate transformation (gain fields in parietal cortex multiply retinal position by eye position), attentional selection (attended stimuli gain 20 to 40 percent response amplification in extrastriate cortex), and state-dependent processing (arousal rescaling whole cortical maps).

Because a multiplicative interaction is exactly what a basis-function network needs, gain modulation is the brain's general mechanism for computing with context: content stays in the driving pathway, relevance arrives through the gain.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Node roles: a driven principal cell (the carrier), a driving input pathway (the content), and one or more modulatory pathways (the knob), plus in the disinhibitory variant a two-interneuron chain.

The content edge is a conventional excitatory glutamatergic projection onto the carrier's dendrites.

The knob is implemented by three interchangeable edge types: a neuromodulatory paracrine edge (acetylcholine, noradrenaline, serotonin, dopamine, released from brainstem and basal forebrain nuclei and acting through G-protein-coupled receptors on the carrier's conductances); a balanced background edge that raises excitatory and inhibitory bombardment together, changing slope through noise and conductance effects; and a disinhibitory chain in which a vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneuron inhibits a somatostatin interneuron, whose release of the carrier's distal dendrites multiplies dendritic responsiveness.

Topology: content edges are point-to-point and topographic; knob edges are diffuse and one-to-many, one modulatory nucleus scaling millions of carriers at once, which is why the motif can retune an entire map in a heartbeat.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The carriers are pyramidal cells throughout cortex, the layer 2/3 and layer 5 cells of the neuron catalogue, whose apical dendrites, electrically remote from the soma, form a natural multiplication site: dendritic calcium and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) nonlinearities mean that releasing or facilitating the apical compartment multiplies the somatic response to basal content.

The knob's neuromodulatory sources are the cholinergic neuron of the nucleus basalis and the noradrenergic neuron of the locus coeruleus (other-cells and neuron catalogues), slow-firing, broadly projecting cells whose tonic-versus-phasic personalities set background gain and deliver moment-of-import surges respectively.

The disinhibitory chain casts the VIP interneuron, an irregular-spiking cell activated by attention, movement and reinforcement signals, against the somatostatin Martinotti cell, whose adapting dendrite-targeting inhibition it silences: two inhibitory personalities in series making a positive knob.

Acetylcholine's mechanism is characteristically intimate, closing leak and M-type potassium channels to raise the carrier's input resistance, so the same synaptic current now buys more voltage, multiplication at the membrane.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Content synapses are alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and NMDA glutamatergic contacts on spines.

Cholinergic edges act through muscarinic M1 receptors (closing potassium channels, gain up) and nicotinic receptors on interneurons; noradrenergic edges act through alpha and beta adrenergic receptors, with alpha-2 activation reducing and beta activation enhancing responsiveness, allowing bidirectional gain by the same transmitter at different concentrations.

Both are largely volume transmission, released from en-passant varicosities into the extracellular space rather than at private synapses, matching the knob's one-to-many topology.

The disinhibitory chain uses conventional gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A synapses: VIP onto somatostatin somata, somatostatin onto pyramidal distal dendrites.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

The smallest instance is a single pyramidal neuron with its apical compartment and local VIP-somatostatin pair, within 100 micrometres; the largest is the whole cortical mantle rescaled by one locus coeruleus of only about 30,000 to 50,000 noradrenergic neurons per side, the most extreme fan-out in the nervous system.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Every cortical pyramidal cell is a multiplication site, so the count is on the order of 10 billion carrier instances, served by a handful of modulatory nuclei and by VIP-somatostatin pairs distributed through every cortical area.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Posterior parietal cortex, where eye-position and body-position gain fields multiply retinal signals to build head- and body-centred coordinates for reaching.

• Extrastriate visual cortex (V4, MT), where attention multiplies responses to the attended stimulus by 20 to 40 percent.

• Primary sensory cortices, where arousal state and locomotion rescale response gain, in visual cortex famously doubling visual responses during running.

• Prefrontal cortex, where dopaminergic gain control sets the signal-to-noise of working-memory representations along an inverted-U.

• Thalamus, where brainstem cholinergic input switches relay neurons from burst to tonic mode, a gain and format change for everything passing through.

• Locus coeruleus and nucleus basalis themselves, the transmitting ends of the knob, whose firing modes are the master gain settings of the forebrain.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this motif each region would speak at a single fixed volume: parietal cortex could not convert maps between reference frames, visual cortex could not favour the attended over the ignored, prefrontal cortex could not protect a memory against distraction, and the whole cortex would process the world identically whether the animal were drowsy or hunted.

Gain modulation is why the same anatomy can be a different machine from one second to the next.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transfer function is output rate equals gain g times f(driving input), where f is the neuron's threshold-linear or sigmoid curve and g moves between about 0.5 and 2: on logarithmic axes the curve shifts vertically, and against an additive influence the diagnostic is that a modulator's effect grows in proportion to the response instead of being constant.

Measured examples: attention multiplies V4 contrast-response curves consistent with contrast gain of 20 to 50 percent, eye-position gain fields scale parietal visual responses linearly over the oculomotor range, and acetylcholine can roughly double the slope of cortical frequency-current curves without moving threshold.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The knob is slower than the content: G-protein-coupled effects develop over 100 milliseconds to seconds, phasic locus coeruleus bursts sharpen gain within a few hundred milliseconds of salient events, and tonic state changes (sleep to waking, quiet to aroused) unfold over seconds to minutes, so gain is a slowly varying coefficient on a fast signal.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Gain follows the classic inverted-U: too little (drowsiness) and signals sink into noise, an intermediate optimum sharpens signal-to-noise, and too much (stress, panic) amplifies noise and locks circuits into over-responsive states, the Yerkes-Dodson law written in conductances.

Network models show that raising gain shifts cortex from segregated to integrated global dynamics, so the knob also tunes how much the brain acts as one machine versus many.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The knob gates the pen: acetylcholine and noradrenaline are permissive signals for cortical map plasticity, and pairing a tone with nucleus basalis stimulation retunes auditory cortex to that tone, so gain modulation decides not only what is amplified now but what is learned next.

Receptor densities themselves adapt, with chronic stress and stimulant exposure re-setting adrenergic and dopaminergic gain.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Neuromodulatory gain (diffuse, slow), balanced-background gain (fast, local, mediated by synaptic bombardment statistics), dendritic-disinhibition gain (VIP-somatostatin, targetable to specific columns), gain fields (multiplication by a second sensory or postural variable) and thalamic mode switching.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Modulatory axons invade the cortex early and their receptors are prerequisites for critical-period plasticity; the VIP-somatostatin disinhibitory chain matures through adolescence alongside the maturation of attention, and juvenile cortex runs at higher baseline plasticity-gain that the adult brake systems later cap.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The modulatory nuclei are among the most conserved structures in the vertebrate brainstem, with homologues of the locus coeruleus and cholinergic systems in fish, and multiplicative modulation by amines is documented in invertebrates (octopamine, the insect analogue of noradrenaline, rescales sensory gain during flight), making the multiplier at least half a billion years old.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Volume transmission depends on the extracellular matrix and on transporter-equipped astrocytes that set neuromodulator dwell time; the noradrenergic system also commands the brain's vasculature and, during sleep, the glymphatic clearance cycle, so the gain system moonlights as the janitorial scheduler.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder is treated almost entirely through this motif, with methylphenidate and atomoxetine raising catecholaminergic gain toward the optimum of the inverted-U.

Degeneration of the locus coeruleus and nucleus basalis is among the earliest events in Alzheimer disease and Parkinson disease, presenting as failing attention and processing speed before memory collapses, and delirium is acutely disordered gain, its cholinergic basis betrayed by its precipitation by anticholinergic drugs.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Driving content signals (topographic glutamatergic afferents, 0 to 100 hertz equivalent).

◦ Modulatory state signals: locus coeruleus tonic 1 to 3 hertz and phasic bursts to 10 to 15 hertz; basal forebrain cholinergic tone; VIP-interneuron attention and movement signals.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ The content signal rescaled by gain 0.5 to 2, with tuning shape preserved.

• STATE.

◦ Current gain per region; receptor occupancy; behavioural state (sleep, quiet waking, aroused).

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Gain range 0.5 to 2; inverted-U optimum at intermediate modulator concentration; muscarinic and adrenergic receptor densities.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Disinhibitory gain 10 to 50 milliseconds; G-protein-coupled effects 100 milliseconds to seconds; tonic state shifts seconds to minutes.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder (catecholaminergic gain too low or unstable); delirium (cholinergic gain collapse); early Alzheimer and Parkinson disease (degenerating modulatory nuclei); stress-induced over-gain.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module context_gain_multiplier, subscribing to a content-signal topic and a scalar-or-field gain topic (published by arousal, attention and task-relevance modules), and publishing the content multiplied element-wise by gain.

The closest artificial intelligence analogues are multiplicative attention weights, feature-wise linear modulation (the FiLM layer, which learns per-channel scale and shift) and the temperature parameter of a softmax; the biological motif differs in that one low-dimensional broadcast signal rescales billions of units at once, the multiplier doubles as the plasticity gate deciding what may be learned, and gain has its own slow dynamics and an inverted-U optimum rather than being a free per-example parameter.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to show that a modulator multiplies the slope of a neuron's input-output curve, unlike an additive input which shifts it.
Create a number variable called threshold with initial value 10.
Create a number variable called baseline slope with initial value 1.
Create a number variable called gain with initial value 1.8.
Create a number variable called additive shift with initial value 5.
For each input drive from 0 to 50 in steps of 10, perform the following actions.
    Calculate the difference of the input drive and threshold.
    If the result is less than 0 is true, then set the result to 0.
    End the conditional block.
    Multiply the result by baseline slope and call it the plain response.
    Multiply the plain response by gain and call it the multiplied response.
    Calculate the sum of the plain response and additive shift and call it the shifted response.
    Display the input drive, the plain response, the multiplied response, and the shifted response on one line.
End the loop over input drives.
Observe that the multiplied response grows faster with input while the shifted response stays a constant distance above the plain response.
The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the distinction to demonstrate is between two columns of numbers, a slope change versus an offset, and a printed table settles it instantly.

# Gain modulation multiplies the slope of the input-output curve;
# an additive input merely shifts it (multiplicative gain by ACh/NA:
# Ferguson and Cardin, Nature Reviews Neuroscience 2020).
THRESH = 10.0

def f(drive):                       # threshold-linear neuron
    return max(drive - THRESH, 0.0)

print("drive   plain   gain x1.8   additive +5   (gain effect grows)")
for drive in range(0, 60, 10):
    plain = f(drive)
    multiplied = 1.8 * plain        # neuromodulatory gain: slope change
    shifted = plain + 5.0           # additive input: offset change
    print(f"{drive:5.0f}  {plain:6.1f}  {multiplied:9.1f}  {shifted:11.1f}"
          f"   diff = {multiplied - plain:5.1f}")

# The gain effect (last column) is proportional to the response itself,
# zero below threshold and growing with drive, while the additive shift
# is constant: the experimental diagnostic for multiplication in cortex.

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

An influence whose size is proportional to the response it influences, vanishing below threshold and swelling with drive; tuning curves that change height but never shape; and a source anatomy of tiny nuclei fanning out to the whole forebrain: no other motif changes what the brain does without changing what its signals say.


CHAPTER 20. THE PUSH-PULL (OPPONENT) MOTIF (Sign-Splitting Dual-Channel Motif) (The Two-Handed Circuit) (NON-COG)

A neuron that can only fire faster is a trumpet that can only get louder: half the music is out of reach.

The push-pull motif solves this by splitting every signal into two channels of opposite sign, one that fires for more and one that fires for less, ON against OFF in the retina, flexor against extensor at the joint, insulin against glucagon in the blood.

Each channel rests at a low rate and devotes its whole range to its own half of the world, and when one is pushed the other is actively pulled down, doubling both the range and the speed of the code.

It is tagged non-cognitive for its front-end sensory, motor and hormonal role, though its opponent logic echoes upward into cognition as opposing value channels.

Two names the invariant: every installation is a pair of channels carrying the same variable with opposite signs.

Handed names the reciprocity: like two hands on one rope, when one pulls the other yields, each movement being both a push and a release.

Circuit marks it as a wiring motif, installed from the retina to the pancreas, not a cell or a region.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The push-pull motif is a paired-channel architecture in which one signal is encoded by two populations with opposite sign conventions, each excited by what inhibits the other, so that the difference between the channels carries the signal and their sum carries almost nothing.

The computation is range doubling, speed doubling and offset removal: neither channel wastes firing on a resting baseline, decrements are signalled as actively and as fast as increments, and common-mode disturbances (overall light level, overall hormone clearance) cancel in the difference.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Node roles: a shared source (the measured variable's transducer), a push channel, a pull channel, and often a cross-coupling inhibitory bridge.

In the retinal flagship: the cone photoreceptor makes a sign-conserving glutamatergic edge onto the OFF bipolar cell (ionotropic receptors, depolarised by darkness together with the cone) and a sign-inverting edge onto the ON bipolar cell through the metabotropic glutamate receptor 6 (mGluR6), whose G-protein cascade closes the TRPM1 cation channel so that light, by silencing the cone, opens the ON cell.

Each channel then runs in parallel through its own bipolar and ganglion cells, and sign-inverting amacrine cells form crossover-inhibition bridges between the channels, pulling each down when the other is pushed.

In the spinal instance the two channels are flexor and extensor motor pools bridged by the reciprocal Ia-inhibitory interneurons of entry 11; in the endocrine instance they are the beta and alpha cells of the pancreatic islet, coupled by paracrine edges (insulin and somatostatin suppressing glucagon release, and falling glucose releasing the alpha cell).

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The ON bipolar cell and OFF bipolar cell of the neuron catalogue are twin specialists distinguished by a single receptor choice, metabotropic versus ionotropic, the entire opponency resting on that molecular fork; their graded, non-spiking personalities transmit smooth analogue halves of the light axis.

The AII and other glycinergic amacrine cells contribute the crossover bridges, fast graded cells whose sign-inverting personality keeps the two channels honestly reciprocal.

In the islet instance, the beta cell (Chapter 69 of the other-cells catalogue) is a bursting, electrically coupled glucose sensor that pushes insulin as glucose rises, while the alpha cell's opposite dose-response pulls glucagon up as glucose falls, two secretory personalities tuned to opposite flanks of one set point near 5 millimoles per litre.

Alpha motor neurons of flexor and extensor pools, with the Ia inhibitory interneuron between them, supply the motor casting.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The retinal fork: one glutamate transmitter read by two receptor families, ionotropic alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and kainate receptors on OFF bipolar dendrites (sign-conserving) and mGluR6 coupled through the G-protein Go to TRPM1 closure on ON bipolar dendrites (sign-inverting), all within the single synaptic invagination of the cone pedicle.

Crossover inhibition uses glycine (AII amacrine) and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA); the spinal bridge uses glycinergic Ia-interneuron synapses on antagonist motor neurons; the islet uses paracrine insulin, somatostatin and glucagon signalling plus connexin 36 gap junctions synchronising the beta-cell push.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One retinal instance is a single cone pedicle and its 8 to 10 bipolar partners within 10 micrometres; one spinal instance spans an agonist-antagonist pair of motor pools over several segments; one islet instance is a 100 to 200 micrometre islet of 1,000 to 2,000 cells.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Roughly 4 to 5 million cone pedicles per retina each run the fork; every one of the body's several hundred antagonist muscle pairs runs the spinal form; and about one million pancreatic islets run the hormonal form, high confidence on orders of magnitude.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Retina, where ON and OFF pathways born at the cone synapse give vision equal speed for brightening and darkening.

• Dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus and primary visual cortex, which inherit and recombine the two channels, with push-pull synaptic organisation documented in simple-cell receptive fields.

• Spinal cord ventral horn, where flexor-extensor opponency with reciprocal inhibition makes joints controllable by a difference signal.

• Pancreatic islets of Langerhans, where insulin and glucagon form a hormonal push-pull holding blood glucose near 5 millimoles per litre.

• Autonomic nervous system as a whole, sympathetic against parasympathetic, the largest single installation of opponency in the body.

• Vestibular system, where paired canals on opposite sides of the head signal each rotation as a push on one side and a pull on the other.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without the fork, the retina would signal darkening only by the slow decay of an excited channel, and reaction to shadow, the oldest predator alarm, would lag; joints would be controllable only by co-contraction against a spring; and glucose would be defended on one side only, with hypoglycaemia unguarded, which is precisely the deficit seen when diabetic alpha-cell counter-regulation fails.

Every hosting system owes to this motif its symmetry: equal authority over up and down.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

Each channel applies a rectified half-range code, ON approximately max(signal, 0) and OFF approximately max(minus signal, 0) about the adaptation point, and the downstream difference reconstructs the full signed variable with roughly double the dynamic range and no wasted baseline firing.

In the islet version the two dose-response curves are opposed sigmoids crossing near 5 millimoles per litre glucose, insulin rising above and glucagon rising below, yielding bidirectional proportional control.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Retinal ON and OFF responses both begin within 20 to 50 milliseconds of their preferred transition, with the OFF pathway typically a few milliseconds faster; hormonal push-pull operates over minutes; spinal reciprocal action operates within the 20 to 40 millisecond reflex loop.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The crossing point (the adaptation level, the joint's equilibrium, the glycaemic set point) is itself regulated, so the motif is a difference amplifier riding on a movable pivot; in pathology the pivot drifts, as in the raised glucose set point of diabetes.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Mostly calibration rather than learning: retinal opponency adapts its pivot to mean luminance within seconds, spinal reciprocal inhibition is retuned by motor training, and islet mass slowly remodels to demand, but the sign assignments themselves are developmentally fixed.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Sensory opponency (ON-OFF, vestibular left-right, colour-opponent red-green and blue-yellow channels), motor opponency (flexor-extensor), hormonal opponency (insulin-glucagon, parathyroid hormone against calcitonin), autonomic opponency (sympathetic-parasympathetic) and the cognitive echo of opponent appetitive and aversive value channels.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The retinal fork is set by transcription-factor choice of receptor: developing bipolar cells expressing mGluR6 wire to the ON stratum of the inner plexiform layer and ionotropic-receptor cells to the OFF stratum, laminating the two channels before vision begins, and spontaneous retinal waves rehearse both before eye opening.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Opponency is among the oldest tricks in signalling: ON- and OFF-type photoreceptor pathways exist in invertebrate eyes, agonist-antagonist muscle control is universal in articulated animals, and paired counter-regulatory hormones predate vertebrates, evidence that half-range coding around a set point is a convergent optimum.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The cone pedicle's fork depends on Mueller glia for glutamate clearance fast enough to keep two receptor systems honestly informed; islet opponency depends on a dense fenestrated capillary bed and on delta-cell somatostatin refereeing between alpha and beta cells.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Congenital stationary night blindness of the complete type is a clean lesion of one channel: mutations in the mGluR6-TRPM1 cascade silence the ON pathway while OFF vision survives, abolishing the electroretinogram b-wave.

In diabetes mellitus both hands fail, the beta-cell push lost and, insidiously, the alpha-cell pull impaired, leaving patients open to iatrogenic hypoglycaemia; spasticity after stroke or spinal injury reflects disordered reciprocal inhibition, the two hands pulling against each other.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ One signed physical variable: luminance change (up to 10 log units with adaptation), joint torque command, blood glucose 3 to 15 millimoles per litre.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Two rectified half-range channels: ON and OFF firing 0 to about 200 hertz at the ganglion-cell stage; insulin and glucagon secretion in opposed sigmoids crossing near 5 millimoles per litre.

• STATE.

◦ The adaptation pivot; the two channels' current activities; crossover-inhibition tone.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Crossing point (set point); per-channel gain; rectification threshold at the pivot.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Retinal fork 10 to 50 milliseconds; spinal reciprocal loop 20 to 40 milliseconds; hormonal loop 5 to 30 minutes; pivot adaptation seconds (retina) to years (glycaemic set point).

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Congenital stationary night blindness (ON channel loss via mGluR6-TRPM1 mutations); diabetes mellitus with failed counter-regulation; post-stroke spasticity from broken reciprocal inhibition.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module opponent_channel_splitter, subscribing to any signed scalar topic and publishing paired rectified topics (variable_increase_channel and variable_decrease_channel) plus the current pivot; downstream modules subscribe to the difference for the full signed signal or to one channel for a cheap half-range alarm.

The closest artificial intelligence analogues are on-centre and off-centre filter pairs in early vision models, the positive and negative parts of a rectified linear unit pair, and the advantage decomposition of opponent value learning; the biological motif differs in that the pivot is itself an adaptive, regulated state and the two channels actively inhibit each other rather than merely being complementary rectifications.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

Two mirror-image channels born from one source at a single sign-inverting synapse or receptor fork, resting quietly at a shared pivot and each surging for its own half of the world: wherever a lesion of one pathway blinds an organism to increments but not decrements, or to pushing but not pulling, this motif is what was cut.


PART FOUR. THE TEMPORAL AND OSCILLATORY MOTIFS

The motifs of the earlier parts computed values: a contrast, a maximum, a normalised ratio.

The motifs of this part compute something stranger and harder to hold in the hand, which is a rhythm or a timing relationship.

Their output is not how much but when, and their currency is the microsecond, the millisecond and the phase of a wave.

Here the nervous system stops asking what a signal is worth and starts asking exactly when it arrived and how it lines up against a shared clock, because a great deal of biological meaning lives not in the size of a spike but in its moment.

Four motifs open the part: a detector that reads the difference between two arrival times down to millionths of a second, two engines that manufacture the cortex's gamma clock, and a nesting scheme that packs an ordered sequence into the beats of a slower wave.


CHAPTER 21. COINCIDENCE DETECTION WITH DELAY LINES (The Jeffress Interaural-Time Comparator) (The Microsecond Stopwatch) (NON-COG)

Snap your fingers to one side of your head and, without turning, you know which side, because the sound reached the near ear a few ten-millionths of a second before the far ear.

That impossibly small gap is measured by a sheet of cells in the brainstem that fire only when two signals land at the very same instant, one from each ear, sent down wires cut to deliberately different lengths.

It is the most precise timing measurement the nervous system ever makes, finer than the duration of a single nerve impulse.

Coincidence names the rule: fire only when inputs arrive together.

Delay Lines names the trick: give each input a wire of chosen length so that "together" means a particular difference in arrival time at the ears.

Microsecond names the resolution, a microsecond being a millionth of a second.

Stopwatch names the job, the reading-out of a tiny time difference.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The motif is a bank of coincidence-detecting neurons, each receiving one excitatory input from the left ear and one from the right, with the two inputs travelling along axons (nerve fibres) of systematically different length and therefore different conduction delay.

A cell fires maximally when the external interaural time difference (the gap between when a sound reaches the two ears, abbreviated ITD) exactly cancels the internal wiring delay, so that the two spikes collide inside the cell at the same moment.

Because different cells carry different internal delays, the population lays out a map of sound-source azimuth (left-right angle): which cell fires tells the brain where the sound is.

The human head gives a maximum ITD of only about 700 microseconds ear to ear, yet the system resolves changes near 10 microseconds, which corresponds to roughly one degree of angle.

This is the classic Jeffress model, proposed in 1948 and later found, with mammalian modifications, in tissue.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Two source nodes feed the circuit: the left and right anteroventral cochlear nucleus, each holding spherical bushy cells that relay ear signals with extreme temporal fidelity.

Each bushy cell sends an excitatory (glutamate) axon to the coincidence-detector node, the principal neurons of the medial superior olive (MSO), but the axons are cut to graded lengths so that the same firing event arrives at different MSO cells at different times: these are the delay lines.

The topology is a ladder: contralateral axons enter from one end and run along the MSO nucleus while ipsilateral axons enter from the other end and run the opposite way, so that position along the nucleus reads out internal delay.

Each MSO principal cell is a two-input excitatory coincidence gate: left-excitatory edge plus right-excitatory edge, firing on their temporal product.

Two further inhibitory (glycine, a fast inhibitory transmitter) edges land on the MSO soma, one driven by each ear via the medial and lateral nuclei of the trapezoid body, and this precisely timed inhibition sharpens and shifts the best delay, a mammalian addition beyond pure Jeffress.

The output edge is an excitatory projection from MSO up to the inferior colliculus of the midbrain, where the place code is read.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The spherical bushy cell of the anteroventral cochlear nucleus is a fidelity specialist: its giant endbulb-of-Held synapses and fast membrane let it lock its spikes to the phase of a sound wave (phase-locking), so the delay lines carry a clean temporal signal rather than a smeared one.

The principal neuron of the medial superior olive is the coincidence detector proper, a bipolar cell with one dendrite reaching toward each ear's inputs; its personality is defined by breathtakingly fast membrane dynamics, a very low input resistance and a low-threshold potassium current (Kv1) that shuts the integration window to well under a millisecond, so it counts only near-simultaneous spikes and ignores those that straggle.

The globular bushy cells feeding the trapezoid-body nuclei are speed-and-timing cells too, driving the glycinergic interneurons fast enough that inhibition arrives inside the same sub-millisecond window it must shape.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Excitatory inputs use glutamate acting on fast alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors with unusually quick kinetics, placed on the two opposing dendrites of the MSO cell.

Inhibition uses glycine acting on chloride-permeable glycine receptors placed on and near the soma, timed to precede or coincide with excitation.

There are no functionally important gap junctions in the mature mammalian detector; the computation is chemical and its precision comes from receptor and channel speed, not electrical coupling.

Characteristic membrane time constants are extraordinarily short, on the order of a few hundred microseconds, which is what makes microsecond arithmetic possible in cells whose spikes last a millisecond.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One human medial superior olive holds on the order of a few thousand to about ten thousand principal neurons per side, arranged as a thin vertical sheet a few millimetres tall.

The delay-line axons add up to a compact ladder only millimetres across, yet encode the full physiological ITD range of roughly plus or minus 700 microseconds.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

There is essentially one instance per side, the left and right medial superior olive, so two per person.

The motif is not repeated elsewhere in the brain in this exact microsecond form; its cousin for interaural level differences (the lateral superior olive) uses a different, non-delay-line computation.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Medial superior olive (left and right), in the superior olivary complex of the pons: the sole home of the microsecond ITD comparator, computing horizontal sound-source angle.

• Anteroventral cochlear nucleus (left and right): supplies the phase-locked delay-line inputs, so it is part of the installed fabric.

• Medial and lateral nuclei of the trapezoid body: supply the fast glycinergic inhibition that tunes best delay.

• Inferior colliculus of the midbrain: the immediate downstream reader of the MSO place code, where ITD maps are refined.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete this motif and the superior olive loses low-frequency sound localisation entirely: a person could still tell a loud sound from a soft one and could still use level differences for high pitches, but the ability to place a low or broadband sound in the horizontal plane, and much of the ability to pick one voice out of a noisy room, would vanish.

The brainstem would keep its volume knob and lose its compass.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is a running cross-correlation of the two ears' spike trains: each cell outputs a firing rate proportional to the coincidence of left and right inputs at its own internal delay, so the population computes correlation as a function of delay.

In plain words, it multiplies two time-shifted signals and integrates, and the peak of the resulting curve marks the sound's ITD.

The real numbers: internal delays span roughly 0 to 700 microseconds, the coincidence window is under about 400 microseconds, and behavioural resolution reaches near 10 microseconds.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The motif has no rhythm of its own; its signature is latency precision, firing sharply tuned to sub-millisecond arrival differences and following sound envelopes up into the hundreds of hertz.

Its output is a firing-rate hill across the population that shifts position as a sound moves in azimuth.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

In its normal regime the cell sits as a fast, leaky coincidence gate with a fixed narrow window.

Glycinergic inhibition provides a slow-timescale gain and best-delay adjustment, and strong background sound can broaden apparent tuning; there is no bistable or oscillatory state here, only sharper or blunter timing.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The circuit is calibrated during development and early life to each individual's head size and ear spacing, since the ITD range depends on the distance between the ears, which grows.

In adulthood it is comparatively hard-wired, with the main adjustable element being the timing and strength of glycinergic inhibition; this is a measuring instrument, and instruments are built to hold their calibration rather than to keep learning.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The mammalian medial superior olive realises the motif with cochlear delay contributions and fast glycinergic inhibition refining the effective delays, whereas the avian nucleus laminaris realises a purer Jeffress form with orderly anatomical delay-line ladders - two engineering solutions to the same microsecond problem.

A second variant family uses the same delayed-coincidence logic on other carriers: the electrosensory timing circuits of electric fish, and the cortical coincidence detectors that read spike synchrony on the millisecond rather than microsecond scale.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Delay-line axon lengths and inhibitory timing are refined by sound-driven activity in the first months and years, with the glycinergic inputs shifting from an early diffuse, partly excitatory pattern to the mature, precisely somatic, fast inhibitory pattern.

Correct assembly requires patterned auditory experience; deprivation during the sensitive period leaves the map coarse.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Coincidence detection for sound localisation is ancient and convergent, present in an analogous but independently evolved form in birds (nucleus laminaris) and in mammals (medial superior olive).

The mammalian version added strong, precisely timed glycinergic inhibition, which is why the pure avian Jeffress delay-line picture had to be revised for mammals.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Specialised astrocytes and a rich blood supply support the very high metabolic cost of fast-spiking, low-input-resistance cells that must run large ion currents to reset quickly.

Myelinated, large-calibre delay-line axons depend on healthy oligodendrocytes, because conduction velocity, and therefore the delays themselves, hinges on intact myelin.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder, in which spike timing is degraded while audibility is spared, wrecks ITD processing and with it sound localisation and speech-in-noise ability.

Demyelinating disease and ageing both smear conduction timing and blunt the map, and congenital or early conductive hearing loss during the sensitive period can leave binaural timing permanently coarse.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Phase-locked excitatory spike trains from left and right anteroventral cochlear nucleus, one per ear, per frequency channel.

◦ Fast glycinergic inhibition from the trapezoid-body nuclei, per ear.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A population firing-rate hill encoding interaural time difference over roughly 0 to 700 microseconds, sent to the inferior colliculus.

• STATE.

◦ Per-cell internal delay (fixed by wiring), instantaneous coincidence level, inhibitory tone.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Coincidence window under about 400 microseconds; membrane time constant a few hundred microseconds; ITD range plus or minus about 700 microseconds; behavioural resolution near 10 microseconds.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Membrane roughly 0.1 to 0.3 milliseconds; AMPA decay well under 1 millisecond; glycine decay a few milliseconds; developmental calibration months to years.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Auditory neuropathy, demyelination and ageing degrade spike timing and destroy sound localisation and speech-in-noise performance.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named interaural_time_difference_comparator would subscribe to two time-stamped event streams (left and right) and publish a source-angle estimate plus confidence.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a cross-correlation layer or a time-delay-and-sum beamformer, and the point of difference is that the biology reaches microsecond resolution using cells whose own events last a thousand times longer, by exploiting membrane speed and precisely timed inhibition rather than a fast digital clock.

Engineers should note that the coincidence window, not the spike width, sets the resolution.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A thin brainstem sheet of bipolar cells, one dendrite pointed at each ear, fed by axons cut to graded lengths, firing only on collisions timed to millionths of a second - the single place in the body where the nervous system does microsecond arithmetic.


CHAPTER 22. THE GAMMA OSCILLATOR, PYRAMIDAL-INTERNEURON TYPE (Pyramidal-Interneuron Network Gamma, PING) (The Cortical Metronome) (COG)

Watch a patch of cortex with the right instrument while it does something demanding and you will see it flicker, thirty to ninety times a second, a fast shimmer called the gamma rhythm.

That shimmer is made by a two-step conversation: excitatory principal cells shout, a squad of fast inhibitory cells shouts back a beat later and silences everyone, the silence lifts, and the shout comes again.

The loop rings like a bell, and every cell caught in the ring is stamped with the same beat, which is how the cortex decides that scattered signals belong to the same thought.

Pyramidal-Interneuron names the two players, excitatory pyramids and inhibitory interneurons.

Network Gamma names the emergent product, a network rhythm in the gamma band.

Metronome names the function: a shared beat that active cells are pinned to.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The PING motif is a delayed negative-feedback loop between an excitatory population and a fast-spiking inhibitory population that, when driven hard enough, oscillates at gamma frequency, roughly 30 to 90 cycles per second.

It computes a shared clock: the cells that are active in a given cycle fire together within a few milliseconds, and this common time-stamp lets downstream readers treat them as one ensemble (binding by synchrony) while cells not on the beat are relatively suppressed.

It also implements a fast winner-favouring competition, because the most strongly driven pyramidal cells fire first each cycle and their recruited inhibition silences the laggards, so gamma is both a clock and a sharpener.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Two nodes: an excitatory pyramidal population (E) and a fast-spiking inhibitory interneuron population (I).

Edge one is excitatory (glutamate, alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA)) from E to I: pyramids drive the interneurons.

Edge two is inhibitory (gamma-aminobutyric acid, the brain's main inhibitory transmitter, abbreviated GABA, acting on fast GABA-A receptors) from I back to E: interneurons silence the pyramids.

Edge three is inhibitory from I to I, mutual inhibition among the interneurons, which regularises the beat.

There is usually recurrent excitation E to E as well, feeding the ring.

The loop's period is set mainly by the delay around E to I to E plus the decay time of the GABA-A inhibition: excite, wait a synaptic delay, inhibit, wait for inhibition to decay, fire again.

An external excitatory drive (from thalamus or other cortex) is the throttle that turns the oscillator on and sets its frequency.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The pyramidal cell (for example the cortical excitatory pyramids catalogued in the neuron corpus) plays the excitatory node; its adapting, integrating personality means the strongest-driven pyramids reliably fire earliest each cycle, which is what gives gamma its rank-ordering-by-strength flavour.

The parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking basket cell (the parvalbumin basket cell of the neuron catalogue) plays the inhibitory node, and it is the indispensable engine: its very fast, non-adapting spiking, its perisomatic synapses right on the pyramidal soma and axon initial segment, and its short membrane time constant let it deliver a hard, synchronous, well-timed brake to thousands of pyramids at once.

The tight, brief GABA-A inhibition of these basket cells sets the gamma period almost single-handedly, which is why anything that weakens parvalbumin cells weakens gamma.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The E to I synapse is glutamatergic on AMPA receptors, fast and depressing.

The I to E synapse is GABAergic on GABA-A receptors placed perisomatically, with a decay time constant of roughly 5 to 10 milliseconds that is the single most important number setting gamma frequency.

Parvalbumin basket cells are also coupled to each other by gap junctions built from connexin-36, which helps synchronise the inhibitory volley.

Weights are plastic: E to I and I to E synapses show activity-dependent changes, and the strength of the drive scales the amplitude and frequency of the rhythm.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

A single gamma-generating patch is roughly a cortical column or a local network a few hundred micrometres across, holding on the order of tens of thousands of pyramidal cells and a few thousand fast-spiking interneurons.

One parvalbumin basket cell contacts hundreds to over a thousand pyramids, so a small inhibitory population can clamp a large excitatory one, which is essential to making a coherent beat.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The motif is installed almost everywhere in neocortex and in the hippocampus, essentially once per local column-sized patch, so there are on the order of millions of overlapping instances across the human cortical sheet.

Gamma is not confined to one address; it is a generic cortical operating mode wherever pyramids and parvalbumin cells sit together.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Neocortex, all sensory, association and frontal areas: local gamma binds co-active feature ensembles and tags attended inputs.

• Hippocampus (CA1 and CA3): gamma organises cell assemblies within each theta cycle for memory encoding and retrieval.

• Entorhinal cortex: fast-spiking interneurons generate gamma that structures grid- and spatial-cell activity.

• Amygdala and prefrontal cortex: gamma synchrony coordinates emotional and cognitive ensembles across regions.

• Olfactory bulb and piriform cortex: gamma organises odour-coding assemblies.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove functional PING and a cortical area keeps its cells and its wiring but loses its shared clock: feature signals that should bind into one perceived object no longer fire together, attention loses its mechanism for boosting selected ensembles, and the region degrades from an orchestra with a conductor into a crowd of soloists.

Much of what we call cortical "coordination" is this beat.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is oscillation: a tonic (steady) excitatory input is converted into a periodic output at gamma frequency whose frequency rises modestly with drive strength and whose phase carries information.

In plain words, steady in, rhythmic out, with the most strongly driven cells assigned the earliest phase (a rate-to-phase conversion).

Real numbers: gamma period roughly 11 to 33 milliseconds (30 to 90 hertz), set largely by a GABA-A decay near 5 to 10 milliseconds plus a synaptic loop delay of a few milliseconds.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

A fast, roughly sinusoidal population rhythm at 30 to 90 hertz, with pyramidal spikes clustered just before the inhibitory volley and a near-silent trough between volleys.

Bursts of gamma typically wax and wane over tens to a few hundred milliseconds, often riding on slower rhythms.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Below a drive threshold the loop is quiet or fires irregularly; above it, the loop locks into rhythmic gamma.

With stronger drive frequency climbs and the regime is firmly PING (excitation-paced); with weak excitation and strong mutual inhibition the same cells can slip into a faster, interneuron-paced ING regime (the subject of Chapter 23).

Neuromodulators (acetylcholine especially) and network state gate whether gamma appears.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Spike-timing-dependent plasticity is powerfully shaped by gamma phase, because a presynaptic pyramid that fires at the excitatory peak lands its spike just before the postsynaptic one, favouring strengthening.

Thus gamma does not just read out ensembles, it helps write them: the rhythm creates repeated, tightly timed windows in which Hebbian learning ("cells that fire together wire together") is most effective.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The motif runs in at least three recognised bands: slow gamma (roughly 30 to 50 cycles per second), fast gamma (roughly 60 to 90), and the epsilon or high-gamma range above 90, with slow and fast gamma in the hippocampus routing information from different upstream sources.

A second axis of variation is drive: visually induced gamma in the cortex, optogenetically driven gamma in experiment, and the spontaneous gamma bursts of the idling network are the same loop under different forcing, and the theta-nested version of the loop is treated in Chapter 24.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Gamma matures late, tracking the protracted maturation of parvalbumin fast-spiking interneurons and their perineuronal nets through childhood and adolescence.

Early sensory experience tunes the interneuron network, and disrupted maturation of parvalbumin cells yields weak or disorganised gamma, a change linked to neurodevelopmental disorders.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The E-I feedback loop is one of the oldest and most reused motifs in nervous systems, and gamma-band rhythms generated this way appear across mammals and in analogous form in other vertebrates and even insects.

The parvalbumin fast-spiking cell that paces mammalian cortical gamma is an evolutionary refinement that made the beat fast, hard and reliable.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Fast-spiking parvalbumin cells are metabolically expensive and oxidatively stressed, and they depend on perineuronal nets (a specialised extracellular scaffold) for their fast firing and on a robust blood and antioxidant supply.

Astrocytes clear the heavy glutamate and GABA traffic, and gamma power is a large part of the cortex's energy budget, which is why functional imaging that tracks blood flow tracks gamma so well.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Schizophrenia is associated with reduced parvalbumin-cell function and reduced task-evoked gamma, thought to underlie disorganised binding and cognition.

Gamma abnormalities also appear in autism spectrum disorder, in epilepsy (where runaway synchrony becomes seizure), and in Alzheimer's disease, where reduced gamma has motivated experimental 40-hertz sensory-stimulation therapies.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Tonic excitatory drive from thalamus and other cortex, 0 to tens of nanosiemens; neuromodulatory tone (acetylcholine) gating the oscillator.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A gamma-rhythmic population signal (30 to 90 hertz) that time-stamps active pyramidal ensembles for downstream readers and for cross-region synchrony.

• STATE.

◦ Excitatory-population phase, inhibitory-population phase, drive level, per-synapse weights.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ GABA-A decay 5 to 10 milliseconds; loop delay a few milliseconds; drive threshold for oscillation; connexin-36 coupling strength among interneurons.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ AMPA decay about 2 milliseconds; GABA-A decay 5 to 10 milliseconds; gamma period 11 to 33 milliseconds; burst envelope tens to hundreds of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Weakened parvalbumin cells reduce gamma (schizophrenia); loss of inhibitory control turns synchrony into seizure (epilepsy).

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named gamma_synchrony_clock would subscribe to a set of active feature or ensemble signals plus a drive level, and publish a shared phase reference (a time-stamp) plus a synchronised, rank-ordered ensemble.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a global attention or gating signal that binds a subset of features, or a recurrent oscillatory reservoir, and the point of difference is that the biological clock is not imposed from outside but generated by the same excitatory-inhibitory loop it coordinates, and it doubles as a plasticity-timing window.

Engineers building binding-by-synchrony should pace the loop with a hard, fast, mutually coupled inhibitory unit, because inhibition sets the beat.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to make an excitatory population and a fast inhibitory population ring together at gamma frequency by delayed negative feedback.

Create a number variable called excitatory activity with initial value 0.1.

Create a number variable called inhibitory activity with initial value 0.

Create a number variable called external drive with initial value 1.0.

Create a number variable called inhibition decay per step with initial value 0.6.

Create a number variable called excitation feedback gain with initial value 1.5.

Create a number variable called inhibition feedback gain with initial value 2.0.

Create a list called history to record the excitatory activity over time.

Create a number variable called step counter with initial value 0.

Repeat the following actions while step counter is less than 400.

    Calculate a new excitatory activity as external drive plus excitation feedback gain times the previous excitatory activity minus inhibition feedback gain times the inhibitory activity.

    If the new excitatory activity is less than 0, then set the new excitatory activity to 0.

    Calculate a new inhibitory activity as the previous inhibitory activity times inhibition decay per step plus the previous excitatory activity.

    Set excitatory activity to the new excitatory activity.

    Set inhibitory activity to the new inhibitory activity.

    Add excitatory activity to the history list.

    Add 1 to step counter.

End the repeat block.

Report that the history list oscillates, rising and falling at a gamma-like rhythm.

The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because a handful of coupled difference equations show the ring of PING oscillation clearly, and the standard scientific stack plots the beat with no ceremony.

# Minimal two-population (E-I) rate model of PING gamma.
# Excitation drives inhibition, delayed inhibition silences excitation,
# and the loop rings at gamma. Wilson-Cowan style, after Borgers &
# Kopell (Neural Computation 2003) and Wilson & Cowan (Biophys J 1972).
import numpy as np

dt = 0.001                 # 1 ms steps
T  = np.arange(0, 0.4, dt) # 400 ms
E = np.zeros(len(T)); I = np.zeros(len(T))
E[0] = 0.1
drive = 1.0                # tonic excitatory throttle
tau_I = 0.008              # 8 ms GABA-A decay sets the gamma period

def relu(x): return np.maximum(x, 0.0)

for t in range(1, len(T)):
    # E rises with drive and recurrent E, falls with inhibition
    E[t] = relu(drive + 1.5*E[t-1] - 2.0*I[t-1])
    # I integrates E and decays with the GABA-A time constant
    I[t] = I[t-1] + dt*(-I[t-1] + 5.0*E[t-1]) / tau_I

# count peaks to estimate frequency
peaks = np.where((E[1:-1] > E[:-2]) & (E[1:-1] > E[2:]))[0]
freq = len(peaks) / (T[-1] - T[0])
print(f"approx gamma frequency: {freq:.0f} Hz over {len(peaks)} cycles")

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A two-node ring of excitatory pyramids and fast-spiking parvalbumin basket cells whose GABA-A decay time sets a 30-to-90-hertz beat, stamping every active cell with the same phase - the cortex's built-in metronome, paced by its brake.


CHAPTER 23. THE GAMMA OSCILLATOR, INTERNEURON-ONLY TYPE (Interneuron Network Gamma, ING) (The Self-Ringing Brake) (COG)

Take away the pyramidal cells entirely and a network of fast inhibitory neurons will still find a beat, ringing among themselves at gamma frequency, each cell silencing its neighbours, recovering, and firing again in unison.

It is the same gamma clock as the previous chapter but stripped to its inhibitory skeleton, a rhythm that needs no excitatory shout to keep time.

The brake, it turns out, can beat on its own.

Interneuron-Only names the cast: fast inhibitory cells and no principal cells required.

Network Gamma names the product, a gamma-band network rhythm.

Self-Ringing Brake names the paradox at its heart, an inhibitory system that generates rather than merely stops activity.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:
