The ING motif is a population of mutually inhibiting fast-spiking interneurons that, given enough tonic excitatory drive to keep spiking, synchronise into a gamma rhythm through their shared inhibition alone.

It computes a pure timing signal: a fast, regular inhibitory beat that can pace pyramidal cells downstream without depending on a moment-to-moment excitatory feedback loop.

Because it does not need patterned excitatory input, ING is a robust background clock and tends to run faster than PING, often into the 60-to-140-hertz range when drive is weak, transitioning toward PING frequencies as excitatory drive grows.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

One functional node: a population of fast-spiking inhibitory interneurons (I).

The defining edge is mutual inhibition, I to I, using gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) acting on fast GABA-A receptors: every interneuron inhibits many others.

A second, electrical edge couples the interneurons through gap junctions (connexin-36), which promotes synchrony by letting subthreshold voltages equalise.

The driving edge is a tonic, non-rhythmic excitatory input onto the interneurons (from principal cells or afferents) that simply keeps them firing; unlike PING, this drive carries no beat, it is a throttle, not a partner.

The output edge is inhibitory, I onto principal cells, delivering the gamma beat to the wider network.

The period is set by the interneurons' firing tendency and the decay of their mutual GABA-A inhibition: fire together, mutually silence, recover as inhibition decays, fire together again.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The parvalbumin-expressing fast-spiking basket cell (the parvalbumin basket cell of the neuron catalogue) is again the star, but here it plays every role: its fast, non-adapting spiking lets it keep a rapid beat, and its mutual GABA-A synapses onto sister basket cells are the whole oscillator.

The gap-junction coupling among these cells, built from connexin-36, is more important here than in PING, because with no excitatory partner to enforce common timing, the electrical coupling is what pulls the interneurons into unison rather than into anti-phase splitting.

Some axo-axonic (chandelier) and other fast interneuron types can join the mutually inhibiting pool, and their shared trait, fast recovery and tight perisomatic inhibition, is what makes a purely inhibitory clock possible.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The core synapse is GABAergic, I to I, on GABA-A receptors with a decay near 5 to 10 milliseconds that sets the beat, placed on somata and dendrites of neighbouring interneurons.

Gap junctions of connexin-36 provide fast electrical coupling that synchronises subthreshold membrane potentials and is essential to coherent ING.

The excitatory drive uses glutamate on alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors but need not be patterned.

Plasticity of the I-I synapses and of the drive tunes frequency and coherence.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

An ING instance is a local interneuron network of hundreds to a few thousand fast-spiking cells within a column-sized volume a few hundred micrometres across, the same territory that hosts PING.

Because the oscillator lives entirely in the interneuron population, the effective circuit is smaller and more compact than the full excitatory-inhibitory PING network.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

ING is co-installed with PING throughout neocortex, hippocampus and entorhinal cortex, so it shares the same millions of column-scale addresses.

In practice the same interneurons can operate in ING or PING mode depending on drive, so ING is best thought of as a regime of the gamma machinery that is available wherever fast-spiking interneurons are densely mutually coupled, rather than a separately located circuit.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Hippocampus (CA1, CA3, dentate gyrus): interneuron networks generate fast gamma that can persist even when excitatory transmission is blocked, showing pure ING.

• Entorhinal cortex: fast-spiking interneurons autonomously generate fast gamma, with excitation strength tuning the ING-to-PING transition.

• Neocortex, all areas: the mutually inhibiting fast-spiking network provides the fast, drive-robust component of local gamma.

• Thalamic reticular nucleus: a sheet of mutually inhibiting GABA cells that produces its own rhythmic patterning by a related mechanism.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without the ING mode, a region loses its most robust, excitation-independent gamma component, the part of the clock that keeps ticking when principal-cell firing is sparse or when the excitatory loop is unreliable.

The region would still manage stimulus-driven PING gamma but would lose the steady fast background beat that helps maintain timing and, in the hippocampus, keeps fast-gamma assemblies organised during quiet or offline states.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is oscillation from tonic drive: a steady excitatory current into the interneuron pool is converted into a regular inhibitory gamma output, with frequency rising as drive rises within the fast-gamma band.

In plain words, steady drive in, fast inhibitory beat out, with weak drive giving the fastest rhythms (up to about 100 to 140 hertz) and stronger drive slowing and blending it toward PING.

Real numbers: ING frequencies typically 60 to 140 hertz, GABA-A decay 5 to 10 milliseconds, gap-junction coupling essential for coherence.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

A fast, very regular inhibitory rhythm, generally at the high end of or above the classic gamma band, more metronomic and less bursty than PING because it is not gated by fluctuating excitatory ensembles.

Its trough is defined by synchronous inhibition rather than by an excitatory volley.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

With adequate tonic drive and strong gap-junction coupling, the interneuron pool locks into coherent fast ING.

As excitatory drive to the interneurons strengthens, the system transitions smoothly into pyramidal-paced PING at somewhat lower frequency; with too little drive or weak coupling it falls into asynchronous or clustered firing rather than a clean beat.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The interneuron-to-interneuron synapses and the strength of the excitatory drive are adjustable, and these set the coherence and frequency of the beat rather than storing content.

Gap-junction coupling can itself be modulated, tuning how tightly the network synchronises; as in PING, the resulting rhythm shapes the timing windows in which downstream plasticity occurs.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The pure form - interneurons alone, driven by tonic excitation - is most cleanly demonstrated in pharmacological preparations in which fast excitatory transmission is blocked and the rhythm persists.

In the intact brain the motif grades continuously into the pyramidal-interneuron form of Chapter 22, and a distinct gap-junction-dominant variant appears wherever electrically coupled interneuron networks (parvalbumin cells joined by connexin-36) carry the beat with minimal chemical excitation.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Like PING, ING matures with the protracted development of fast-spiking parvalbumin cells and, importantly, with the establishment of connexin-36 gap-junction networks, which are prominent early and refined through development.

A properly coupled interneuron syncytium is a prerequisite for coherent ING.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Mutual inhibition among coupled cells is an ancient rhythm-making motif, and electrically coupled inhibitory networks producing fast rhythms are found widely, including in structures like the thalamic reticular nucleus.

The specialised fast-spiking, gap-junction-coupled cortical interneuron is a mammalian refinement that made a purely inhibitory gamma clock fast and coherent.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The same demanding support as PING applies: perineuronal nets, high metabolic and antioxidant demand, and astrocytic clearance of GABA, with the added dependence on intact connexin-36 gap junctions.

Anything that damages the gap-junction network or the parvalbumin cells preferentially degrades the ING mode.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Because ING shares its cellular substrate with PING, it is compromised in schizophrenia (parvalbumin-cell dysfunction) and in conditions that disrupt gap junctions.

Abnormal fast inhibitory synchrony contributes to certain fast-oscillation phenomena in epilepsy, where the pathologically synchronous inhibitory network is part of the seizure machinery.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Tonic (non-rhythmic) excitatory drive onto the interneuron pool, 0 to tens of nanosiemens; neuromodulatory tone setting excitability.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A fast inhibitory gamma beat (roughly 60 to 140 hertz) delivered to principal cells as a timing reference.

• STATE.

◦ Interneuron-population phase, coupling coherence, drive level.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ GABA-A decay 5 to 10 milliseconds; connexin-36 coupling strength; drive level (sets frequency and the ING-to-PING transition).

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ GABA-A decay 5 to 10 milliseconds; membrane a few milliseconds; ING period roughly 7 to 17 milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Loss of parvalbumin-cell function or gap-junction coupling abolishes coherent fast gamma; pathological inhibitory synchrony feeds fast oscillations in epilepsy.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named inhibitory_pacemaker_clock would subscribe only to a scalar drive level and publish a fast, regular phase reference, independent of any content stream.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a free-running clock or a coupled-oscillator layer whose rate is set by a single gain, and the difference from PING is that this clock needs no excitatory feedback partner, so it is more robust but carries no rate-to-phase content of its own; it is timing without message.

Engineers wanting a stable background beat rather than a content-bound one should build a mutually inhibiting, electrically coupled unit and drive it tonically.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to make a ring of mutually inhibiting interneurons synchronise into a fast gamma beat driven by steady input.

Create a list called interneuron voltages with four numbers, each a small random value between 0 and 1.

Create a number variable called steady drive with initial value 1.0.

Create a number variable called inhibition strength with initial value 0.5.

Create a number variable called recovery rate with initial value 0.2.

Create a list called population output to record the total firing over time.

Create a number variable called step counter with initial value 0.

Repeat the following actions while step counter is less than 400.

    Create a number variable called total inhibition with value equal to the sum of all interneuron voltages times inhibition strength.

    For each interneuron in the list, perform the following actions.

        Calculate a new voltage as the old voltage plus recovery rate times steady drive minus total inhibition times the old voltage.

        If the new voltage is less than 0, then set it to 0.

        Set the interneuron's voltage to the new voltage.

    End the for-each block.

    Add the sum of all interneuron voltages to the population output list.

    Add 1 to step counter.

End the repeat block.

Report that the population output rises and falls together at a fast, regular rhythm.

The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because a small array of mutually inhibiting units, coupled and driven, shows ING synchrony emerging with almost no code.

# Minimal interneuron-network-gamma (ING) model: a pool of mutually
# inhibiting fast-spiking cells, tonically driven, synchronise into a
# fast gamma beat via shared inhibition and gap-junction coupling.
# After Whittington, Traub & Jefferys (Nature 1995) and Wang & Buzsaki
# (J Neurosci 1996).
import numpy as np

dt = 0.001                      # 1 ms steps
T  = np.arange(0, 0.3, dt)      # 300 ms
N  = 20                         # fast-spiking interneurons
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
v = rng.random(N) * 0.5         # heterogeneous start
drive = 1.2                     # tonic throttle
g_inh = 0.9                     # mutual inhibition strength
g_gap = 0.15                    # connexin-36 electrical coupling
tau_I = 0.008                   # 8 ms GABA-A decay
I = np.zeros(N)
pop = []

for t in T:
    mean_v = v.mean()
    shared_inh = I.sum()                       # every cell inhibits all
    dv = drive - shared_inh + g_gap*(mean_v - v)
    v = np.maximum(v + dt*dv/tau_I, 0.0)
    I = I + dt*(-I + g_inh*v)/tau_I            # inhibition tracks firing
    pop.append(v.sum())

pop = np.array(pop)
peaks = np.where((pop[1:-1] > pop[:-2]) & (pop[1:-1] > pop[2:]))[0]
print(f"approx ING frequency: {len(peaks)/(T[-1]-T[0]):.0f} Hz")

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A pool of fast-spiking, gap-junction-coupled interneurons that rings at fast gamma with no principal cell in the loop - a brake that beats, timing without a message, the purely inhibitory face of the cortical clock.


CHAPTER 24. THETA-GAMMA NESTING (Cross-Frequency Phase-Amplitude Coupling) (The Phase Coder) (COG)

A slow wave rolls through the hippocampus four to eight times a second, and riding on its back is the fast gamma flicker of the previous chapters.

Each slow cycle is carved into a handful of fast slots, and the brain drops one item into each slot in order, so that a single roll of the slow wave carries a short ordered list: this, then this, then this.

It is time-division multiplexing in wet tissue, the trick by which the hippocampus writes a sequence of places or events into the phase of a rhythm, and it is widely held to be the temporal skeleton of episodic memory.

Theta-Gamma names the two rhythms, a slow theta wave carrying a fast gamma one.

Nesting names the relationship, fast cycles packed inside each slow cycle.

Phase Coder names the function: information carried by which phase of the slow wave a cell fires on, not merely by how fast it fires.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The motif is a cross-frequency coupling in which the phase of a slow theta oscillation (about 4 to 8 cycles per second) controls the amplitude and timing of fast gamma oscillations (about 30 to 100 cycles per second), so that each theta cycle contains an ordered series of gamma sub-cycles, each a discrete "slot."

It computes a phase code: it converts an ordered set of items into a sequence of activations at successive phases of theta, so that order is represented by position within the slow cycle, and it packs roughly seven (the often-cited 7 plus or minus 2) items into one theta cycle.

This turns a rhythm into a data structure, a short ordered buffer that repeats every theta cycle and can be written into memory by synaptic plasticity.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Three functional elements: a theta pacemaker, a gamma generator, and the principal cells whose spikes are being sorted.

The theta rhythm is imposed on the network by a slow oscillatory drive: in the hippocampus this comes from the medial septum (rhythmic cholinergic and GABAergic input) and from entorhinal input, providing a slow excitatory-inhibitory wave across the principal-cell population.

The gamma generator is the local PING or ING motif of Chapters 22 and 23, running fast on top of the slow wave.

The coupling edge is that the slow theta depolarisation gates the fast gamma: gamma amplitude is largest at a particular theta phase and suppressed at the opposite phase (phase-amplitude coupling), so gamma slots exist only in the permissive half of each theta cycle.

The ordering edge is provided by a depolarisation gradient across cells, so that the most excited cell reaches threshold at the earliest gamma slot and successively less excited cells fire at later slots, laying the items out in order; recurrent and feedforward inhibition enforces one-assembly-per-slot.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The hippocampal pyramidal cell (of area CA1 and CA3) is the item-carrier, and its slow ramping depolarisation and after-depolarisation let its firing phase advance across successive theta cycles (phase precession), which is the single-cell face of this code.

The parvalbumin fast-spiking basket cell (the parvalbumin basket cell of the neuron catalogue) supplies the gamma slotting exactly as in Chapters 22 and 23, chopping each theta cycle into discrete inhibitory windows.

Oriens-lacunosum-moleculare and other dendrite-targeting interneurons, together with septal GABAergic cells, help pace and shape the theta rhythm itself, their slower, rhythmic inhibition setting the frame within which gamma slots sit; the cholinergic septal input sets the regime that makes theta appear.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Theta pacing uses rhythmic gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-A inhibition from septal and local interneurons plus cholinergic modulation (acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors) that promotes the theta state, with slower kinetics than the gamma machinery.

Gamma slotting uses the fast GABA-A perisomatic inhibition and gap junctions described in Chapters 22 and 23.

The excitatory items ride glutamatergic alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and, crucially, N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) synapses on principal-cell dendrites, and the NMDA receptor's coincidence-detecting, slow kinetics make it the substrate that reads the phase code into synaptic weight during learning.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

An instance spans a local hippocampal network, a slice of the CA1 or CA3 sheet perhaps a millimetre or so along the long axis, in which one coherent theta wave organises several gamma sub-networks.

Within one theta cycle, on the order of five to nine gamma slots each recruit a distinct assembly of tens to hundreds of pyramidal cells.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The theta-gamma code is most strongly and clearly installed in the hippocampal formation and adjacent entorhinal cortex, essentially as one traveling theta organisation per hippocampus with many nested gamma instances.

Related phase-amplitude coupling appears in neocortex (for example prefrontal cortex during working memory), so the motif is repeated in weaker or task-specific form at multiple cortical addresses.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• Hippocampus (CA1 and CA3): the canonical site, where theta-gamma nesting orders place-cell and event assemblies for episodic-memory encoding and retrieval.

• Entorhinal cortex: provides theta-paced input and hosts grid-cell sequences organised by the same nesting.

• Medial septum and diagonal band: the theta pacemaker that imposes the slow frame on the hippocampus.

• Prefrontal cortex: theta-gamma phase-amplitude coupling supports the ordering and maintenance of items in working memory.

• Striatum and other cortical areas: weaker phase-amplitude coupling coordinates sequenced activity during learning and action.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Strip the nesting away and the hippocampus keeps its gamma clock and its slow theta wave but loses their marriage, and with it the ability to lay several items out in order within a single slow cycle: the region could still tag co-active cells as one ensemble but could no longer represent this-before-that in a compact repeating buffer.

Episodic memory, which is fundamentally about sequence and order, would lose its temporal scaffolding, and phase precession, the read-write mechanism of that scaffolding, would disappear.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is a serialisation: a set of simultaneously active items, ranked by excitation, is converted into a time-ordered sequence of gamma-slot activations within each theta cycle (a rate-to-phase and set-to-sequence conversion).

In plain words, several things that are true at once are laid out one after another in slots, in order of strength, and repeated every theta cycle.

Real numbers: theta period roughly 125 to 250 milliseconds (4 to 8 hertz), gamma slot roughly 10 to 25 milliseconds, giving about 5 to 9 slots, matching the classic 7 plus or minus 2 capacity of short-term memory.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

A slow 4-to-8-hertz wave whose depolarising phase is filled with a burst of several gamma cycles and whose opposite phase is comparatively silent, with successive assemblies firing at successively later theta phases and, across cycles, advancing to earlier phases (phase precession).

The signature is not one frequency but the fixed relationship between two.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The nested code appears in the theta state (active exploration, rapid-eye-movement sleep, attentive behaviour) driven by cholinergic and septal tone, and dissolves in the non-theta state, where the hippocampus instead produces sharp-wave ripples for memory replay.

Coupling strength varies sub-second by sub-second and with task demand, and stronger coupling accompanies better working-memory performance.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

This is the motif's deepest purpose: the ordered, theta-phase-separated firing creates exactly the tens-of-milliseconds timing offsets that spike-timing-dependent plasticity needs, so that an assembly firing in an earlier slot strengthens its synapses onto the assembly in the next slot, writing the sequence into the recurrent network.

Phase precession ensures that within-sequence pairs are repeatedly presented in the correct order at learnable intervals, which is why theta-gamma nesting is regarded as the encoding mechanism for episodic sequences.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The hippocampal original nests slow or fast gamma into theta depending on whether area CA1 is listening to area CA3 (memory) or to the entorhinal cortex (the present), so the variant in play reports which conversation the region is having.

Cortical cousins nest gamma into slower carriers of their own: alpha-gamma coupling in sensory cortex during attention, and the frontal theta-gamma coupling that scales with working memory load in humans - same nesting logic, different carrier and cargo.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Theta and its coupling to gamma emerge as the hippocampal circuitry, the septal pacemaker, and the parvalbumin interneuron network mature during early postnatal life, with theta-organised activity appearing before reliable spatial behaviour.

Proper cholinergic innervation and interneuron maturation are prerequisites for the nested code.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Hippocampal theta and its nesting of gamma are conserved across mammals and have analogues in other vertebrates, reflecting the ancient role of the hippocampal formation in spatial and sequential memory.

The specific 7-slot phase code is a general property of coupling a slow oscillator to a fast one, a scheme evolution appears to have reused wherever ordered sequences must be buffered.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The motif depends on the support systems of both its rhythms: the metabolically demanding parvalbumin gamma machinery of Chapters 22 and 23, and the cholinergic and GABAergic septal projection that sets the theta state.

Astrocytic support, healthy cholinergic tone, and intact long-range septo-hippocampal fibres are all required; degeneration of cholinergic input flattens theta and its coupling.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Alzheimer's disease, with its early loss of cholinergic input and hippocampal circuitry, degrades theta-gamma coupling and is thought to contribute to episodic-memory failure.

Schizophrenia shows abnormal theta-gamma coupling tied to working-memory deficits, and temporal-lobe epilepsy disrupts the hippocampal rhythms that the code depends on; disordered coupling is also reported in some developmental disorders.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ A slow theta drive from medial septum and entorhinal cortex (4 to 8 hertz); a set of excitatory item signals ranked by strength; cholinergic tone selecting the theta state.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ An ordered sequence of gamma-slot assembly activations, roughly 5 to 9 per theta cycle, encoding item order by theta phase.

• STATE.

◦ Theta phase, gamma slot index, per-item excitation rank, phase-precession offset, coupling strength.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Theta period 125 to 250 milliseconds; gamma slot 10 to 25 milliseconds; slots per cycle about 5 to 9; NMDA-based learning window.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Theta cycle 125 to 250 milliseconds; gamma cycle 10 to 25 milliseconds; NMDA decay about 100 milliseconds; plasticity window tens of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Loss of cholinergic tone or interneuron function weakens coupling (Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia), degrading sequence memory and working memory.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named theta_gamma_sequence_buffer would subscribe to a slow clock signal and a ranked set of active items and publish a repeating, time-ordered sequence of item activations, one item per gamma slot.

The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a positional-encoding scheme feeding a short ordered buffer, or the time-division multiplexing that lets one channel carry several ordered messages, and the point of difference is that the biological code both represents order and, through spike-timing plasticity in the same cycles, writes that order into memory, so it is a buffer and a learning rule fused into one rhythm.

Engineers should note the fixed capacity near seven and the fact that order, not exact spike time, carries the message.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

The purpose of this procedure is to place an ordered list of items into successive gamma slots within one slow theta cycle, so that item order is encoded by theta phase.

Create a list called items to encode with the values first, second, third, fourth and fifth.

Create a number variable called slots per theta cycle with initial value 7.

Create a number variable called theta period milliseconds with initial value 200.

Create a number variable called gamma slot milliseconds equal to theta period milliseconds divided by slots per theta cycle.

Create an empty list called phase code.

Create a number variable called slot index with initial value 0.

For each item in the items to encode list, perform the following actions.

    Calculate the slot start time as slot index times gamma slot milliseconds.

    Calculate the theta phase as 360 times slot start time divided by theta period milliseconds.

    Add to the phase code list a pair holding the item and its theta phase in degrees.

    Add 1 to slot index.

    If slot index is equal to slots per theta cycle, then stop adding items because the theta cycle is full.

End the for-each block.

Display each item next to the theta phase at which it fires.

The procedure is complete.

CODE SAMPLE:

Python is chosen because the essence of the code is the mapping from item order to theta phase, and a short loop over a gated fast oscillation shows the nesting and the ordering at once.

# Theta-gamma nesting: a slow theta wave gates fast gamma into slots,
# and an ordered set of items is dropped into successive slots so that
# order is read out as theta phase. After Lisman & Idiart (Science 1995)
# and Lisman & Jensen (Neuron 2013).
import numpy as np

theta_hz, gamma_hz = 6.0, 60.0          # 6 Hz theta, 60 Hz gamma
slots = int(round(gamma_hz / theta_hz)) # ~10 gamma cycles per theta cycle
items = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]       # an ordered sequence to store

fs = 2000                                # sampling rate, Hz
t  = np.arange(0, 1/theta_hz, 1/fs)      # one theta cycle
theta = np.sin(2*np.pi*theta_hz*t)       # slow wave
gate  = np.clip(theta, 0, None)          # gamma allowed on the rising half
gamma = gate * np.sin(2*np.pi*gamma_hz*t)  # amplitude-coupled gamma

print(f"{slots} gamma slots per theta cycle; storing {len(items)} items")
for i, item in enumerate(items):
    phase_deg = 360.0 * i / slots        # each item at a later theta phase
    print(f"  item {item}: theta phase {phase_deg:5.1f} deg (slot {i})")
# the ordered phases ARE the code: read the items back by ascending phase

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A slow 4-to-8-hertz wave carved into a handful of fast gamma slots, each holding one ordered item and repeating every cycle, with single cells advancing their firing phase as an animal crosses a place - time-division multiplexing in living tissue, the temporal skeleton of episodic memory.


CHAPTER 25. THE HALF-CENTRE OSCILLATOR (Reciprocal-Inhibition Alternator with Fatigue) (The Take-Turns Engine) (NON-COG)

Two crowds of cells that hate each other, wired so that whichever crowd is shouting silences the other, until the shouting crowd tires, falls quiet, and the silenced crowd surges up to take its turn.

Out of that endless handover comes a rhythm, and out of that rhythm comes the alternation of your left leg and your right, your in-breath and your out-breath, the flexing and the extending of every limb that moves in time.

The half-centre oscillator is the smallest machine in biology that can turn a steady push into a beat.

Half-centre names the anatomy: each of the two mutually inhibiting pools is one half of a centre, a term coined by Thomas Graham Brown in 1911 for the spinal machinery that makes a limb step.

Oscillator names the output: not a value but a repeating swing between two states.

Alternator, in the plain-English coinage, names the essential trick - two outputs that are never on at once and always take turns.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The half-centre oscillator is a two-node circuit that converts a constant, non-rhythmic drive into a rhythmic alternation between two mutually exclusive outputs.

It is the elementary rhythm machine: give it a steady excitatory input, tonic and featureless, and it produces a clean back-and-forth beat with no rhythmic input anywhere.

The computation is generation of a rhythm from no rhythm, plus enforcement of strict anti-phase - when output A is high, output B is guaranteed low, and the two swap on every cycle.

Flexor-extensor alternation in a stepping limb is the purest installation: one pool commands the muscle that bends the joint, the other commands the muscle that straightens it, and the animal cannot command both at once because the circuit forbids it.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

There are exactly two nodes, each a pool of neurons: call them half-centre A and half-centre B.

The defining edges are two inhibitory connections in a symmetric loop: A sends an inhibitory edge onto B, and B sends an inhibitory edge onto A - this is reciprocal (mutual) inhibition, the push-pull pair of entry 11 closed into a two-cycle.

A tonic excitatory drive edge enters both A and B from outside the circuit, supplying the energy the oscillator spends; without it the circuit is silent.

Each node carries a hidden internal edge that is the secret of the whole device: a slow negative feedback onto itself, meaning that a pool which has been firing for a while progressively weakens its own output.

That self-weakening comes in two interchangeable flavours - spike-frequency adaptation (a slow potassium current that builds up and quietens a cell that has been active), or post-inhibitory rebound (a pool that has just been released from inhibition surges extra hard, then settles).

Each node's output edge drives a motoneuron pool or downstream effector, and in the moving limb the two output edges also drive reciprocal inhibition at the muscle level, so the mechanical antagonists relax as their partners contract.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The half-centres are built from spinal commissural and ipsilateral inhibitory interneurons, principally the glycinergic and gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)-releasing interneuron classes of the ventral cord, with the V0, V1, V2 and V2b interneuron families of the developmental catalogue playing the alternation roles.

The V1 and V2b inhibitory interneurons are the flexor-extensor alternation enforcers: their fast, reliable inhibition is what guarantees that a limb never tries to flex and extend at the same instant, and losing both together collapses alternation into co-contraction.

The personality that matters most here is adaptation: an adapting cell is one whose firing rate sags the longer it is driven, and it is precisely this sag, this built-in fatigue, that hands the baton from one half-centre to the other - a non-adapting cell would lock the circuit into one state forever.

Where post-inhibitory rebound carries the rhythm instead, the cast favours cells rich in the slow calcium and hyperpolarisation-activated currents that make a neuron fire a rebound burst the moment inhibition lifts, so that release from the partner's veto is itself the trigger to fire.

The motoneurons downstream are pure followers, plateau-capable cells that faithfully broadcast whichever half-centre currently holds the floor.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The reciprocal edges are fast chemical inhibitory synapses using glycine and GABA, acting on glycine receptors and GABA type A receptors, both of which open chloride channels and clamp the target near its resting voltage.

These inhibitory contacts land on the soma and proximal dendrites of the opposing pool, close to the spike-initiation zone where a veto is most effective.

The tonic excitatory drive is glutamatergic, acting on fast alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and slower N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, the latter contributing a voltage-dependent boost that helps sustain plateau firing.

The self-weakening is not a synapse at all but an intrinsic membrane property: calcium-activated and sodium-activated potassium currents that accumulate during a burst (adaptation), or the hyperpolarisation-activated current together with low-threshold calcium currents that build a rebound (post-inhibitory rebound).

Characteristic inhibitory weights are strong enough that one active half-centre fully silences the other, and the plasticity of these weights is slow, tuned during development and by neuromodulators rather than moment to moment.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One half-centre oscillator controlling a single joint's flexor-extensor pair comprises on the order of tens to a few hundred interneurons per pool in a mammal, plus the motoneuron pools they drive.

The whole two-node unit spans a few millimetres of spinal grey matter, small enough that a single lumbar segment holds several, and the coupled set that runs one limb is a stacked assembly of such units.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

There is no census, but the count is large: every joint that alternates flexion and extension in every limb has at least one half-centre unit, and the breathing and chewing rhythms add more in the brainstem.

The lumbar and cervical enlargements of the spinal cord, which serve the legs and arms, hold the densest concentration, with further units in the brainstem for the muscles of the jaw and airway.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The lumbar spinal cord, where flexor and extensor half-centres alternate to step the legs and form the core of the locomotor central pattern generator.

• The cervical spinal cord, where the same motif alternates the muscles of the arms for reaching and rhythmic upper-limb movement.

• The brainstem pre-Bötzinger and adjacent respiratory groups, where inspiratory and expiratory populations alternate to shape the breath (covered in full at Chapter 26).

• The brainstem masticatory central pattern generator of the pons, where jaw-opening and jaw-closing half-centres alternate to chew.

• Invertebrate and vertebrate scratch and swim circuits, where the same two-pool alternation drives fictive scratching and swimming, a favourite laboratory preparation.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete this motif from the lumbar cord and stepping becomes impossible: not weak, but structurally unavailable, because there is no longer anything to alternate the legs; the limb would either freeze or co-contract into rigidity.

A region that hosts a half-centre oscillator gains the ability to produce a self-timed beat without a clock upstream, freeing the brain from having to command every muscle twitch of a rhythmic act - the reason walking does not require thinking about walking.

Strip it out and every rhythmic motor behaviour would need moment-by-moment supervision from higher centres, an impossible bandwidth demand.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transfer function is oscillation: a scalar tonic input maps to a periodic square-ish alternation of two anti-phase outputs.

Crucially, the input controls the frequency - raising the tonic drive shortens each half-centre's time to fatigue and speeds the handover, so the beat quickens, which is how a steady descending command sets walking speed without itself being rhythmic.

Real numbers: locomotor rhythms run from roughly 0.5 to a few cycles per second in mammals, with each half-centre holding the floor for a few hundred milliseconds to about a second; the duty cycle (the fraction of the cycle one pool is active) can be biased away from fifty-fifty so that, for instance, the extension phase of stance lasts longer than the flexion phase of swing.

The mathematics is that of a relaxation oscillator: slow build-up of fatigue to a threshold, fast switch, repeat.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Cycle periods of roughly 0.3 to 2 seconds for locomotion; sharp anti-phase transitions with brief co-activation gaps at the switch.

The signature diagnostic is that the frequency tracks tonic drive smoothly while the alternation stays strictly out of phase - and that after a momentary perturbation or a dropped burst (a motor deletion), the rhythm resumes at its previous cycle frequency, a fingerprint recently used as evidence for a human locomotor central pattern generator in a case of complete spinal cord injury.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Below a threshold drive the circuit sits silent or in tonic co-activation; above it, it oscillates.

Two distinct rhythmogenic regimes exist: an escape regime, where the suppressed pool escapes inhibition through its own rebound, and a release regime, where the active pool releases the other by fatiguing - the two give different sensitivities to perturbation and modulation.

Neuromodulators such as serotonin and noradrenaline, and drugs acting on the persistent sodium current, shift the circuit between regimes and set whether it oscillates at all.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The half-centre is largely a hardwired substrate machine, tuned in development and re-tuned slowly by neuromodulation rather than learning specific sequences.

Spinal locomotor circuits do show use-dependent plasticity - treadmill training after spinal injury can strengthen the rhythm - but this is calibration of an existing oscillator, not the storage of new patterns.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The two great variants are the adaptation-driven (release) half-centre and the rebound-driven (escape) half-centre, distinguished by which intrinsic current carries the handover.

A further variant adds intrinsic pacemaker (bursting) cells inside each pool, blurring the line with the pure pacemaker network of Chapter 27 and yielding hybrid circuits that can oscillate by network alternation, by cellular bursting, or by both.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The alternation interneurons are specified early by transcription-factor codes (the V0, V1, V2 identities) that assign each class its role and its left-right or flexor-extensor wiring.

Genetic deletion of specific classes produces telltale gait failures - losing certain commissural interneurons switches an animal from alternating to hopping - proving that the anti-phase wiring is built to a molecular blueprint before experience.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The half-centre is ancient, present in the swimming circuits of lampreys and the crawling of worms, and conserved across the vertebrate line.

It is one of the oldest computational motifs in the nervous system, predating limbs themselves, repurposed from undulatory swimming to legged walking - old parts solving a new problem.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes clear the glycine and GABA and buffer the potassium that adaptation currents shed; the persistent sodium and calcium currents that carry rhythmogenesis depend on stable ionic gradients maintained by glial and vascular support.

Neuromodulatory fibres from the brainstem supply the serotonin and noradrenaline that keep the oscillator in its working regime.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Spinal cord injury severs descending drive and can leave the half-centre machinery intact but unpowered - the basis of efforts to restore stepping by electrically or pharmacologically re-supplying the missing tonic drive.

Spasticity and clonus reflect disordered alternation and loss of inhibitory balance; disruption of glycinergic inhibition (as in hyperekplexia, the startle disease) corrupts the reciprocal edges; and in respiratory and other rhythms, failure of the alternation motif produces apnoeas and dysrhythmias.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Tonic excitatory (glutamatergic) drive, 0 to full scale, setting frequency; sensory afferent feedback that entrains and corrects the phase.

◦ Neuromodulatory inputs (serotonin, noradrenaline) setting regime and excitability.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Two anti-phase motor commands (for example flexor drive and extensor drive), each active for a few hundred milliseconds per cycle.

• STATE.

◦ Which half-centre currently holds the floor; the accumulated fatigue (adaptation) level of each pool.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Reciprocal inhibitory weight (strong, fully suppressing); adaptation or rebound time constant; tonic drive amplitude; duty-cycle bias.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Cycle period 0.3 to 2 seconds; adaptation build-up hundreds of milliseconds; inhibitory synaptic decay a few to tens of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Loss of reciprocal inhibition yields co-contraction and rigidity; loss of tonic drive (spinal injury) yields silence; corrupted glycinergic inhibition yields hyperekplexia; respiratory installation failure yields apnoea.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module name take_turns_alternator. It would subscribe to a scalar drive channel and an optional phase-correction channel, and publish two mutually exclusive gated outputs plus a phase state. The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a relaxation oscillator or a pair of cross-coupled inhibitory units with leaky adaptation, akin to a two-state recurrent cell forced to alternate; it differs from a software clock in that its period is not fixed but rides continuously on the input drive, and its alternation is enforced by mutual inhibition rather than by a counter.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

Two pools that inhibit each other, each carrying its own slow fatigue, powered by a drive that carries no rhythm, producing a strict take-turns beat whose speed is set by that drive - the minimal circuit that makes a steady push into a walk.


CHAPTER 26. THE CENTRAL PATTERN GENERATOR (Coupled Rhythm-and-Pattern Network) (The Autopilot for Muscles) (NON-COG)

Somewhere in your lower spine sits a machine that already knows how to walk, and in your brainstem sits another that already knows how to breathe, and neither of them needs you.

Cut them off from the brain entirely and they will still, given only a steady wake-up signal, produce the full ordered choreography of a stride or a breath - rhythm and shape together, the right muscles in the right order at the right moments.

The central pattern generator is the nervous system's autopilot: a network that plays a complete motor program from memory, so that the conscious brain need only press start and steer.

Central names its location and its self-sufficiency: the pattern is generated centrally, inside the cord or brainstem, not imported from sensors or from thought.

Pattern names what it produces: not just a beat but a full spatiotemporal pattern - which muscle, how hard, in what phase.

Generator names the crucial fact that it makes this pattern from a non-rhythmic input, needing no rhythmic command to copy.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

A central pattern generator (CPG) is a network of neurons that produces a coordinated, rhythmic, multi-muscle motor program without requiring rhythmic input, and often without any sensory feedback at all.

It computes two things at once: a rhythm (the timing of the cycle, the province of a rhythm-generating layer) and a pattern (the sequence and amplitude of activation across many muscles, the province of a pattern-forming layer).

The canonical demonstration is fictive locomotion - an isolated spinal cord, chemically driven, generates the alternating flexor-extensor bursts of walking with no limbs attached and no sensory input.

This is why walking, breathing, chewing and swallowing run without moment-to-moment conscious command: the program is pre-wired and self-timing, and the brain contributes go, stop, faster and steer.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The CPG is a composite, assembled from the motifs of earlier chapters into a two-tier architecture.

The rhythm-generating tier is one or more half-centre oscillators (Chapter 25) - reciprocally inhibiting pools with intrinsic fatigue or bursting - that set the cycle period and the basic alternation.

The pattern-forming tier is a layer of interneurons downstream of the rhythm tier that distributes and shapes the timing, so that within one cycle many different muscles are recruited in the correct phase and amplitude; this tier can drop the activation of one muscle (a deletion) without disturbing the underlying rhythm, which is the strongest evidence for the two-tier design.

Coupling edges link the CPGs of the several limbs and joints: commissural (left-right) inhibitory and excitatory connections enforce the left-right alternation of walking and can be reconfigured for the left-right synchrony of hopping, while longitudinal edges coordinate fore and hind limbs.

Sensory afferent edges feed in from muscle spindles and skin, not to create the rhythm but to entrain it, correct its phase, and adjust it to the ground.

Excitatory drive from the brainstem locomotor regions enters as a tonic on-switch and speed dial.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The cast is the full developmental interneuron palette of the ventral cord: the excitatory V2a interneurons that help drive and stabilise the rhythm and secure left-right alternation at speed; the inhibitory V0 commissural interneurons that enforce left-right alternation (losing them forces a hopping gait); the V1 and V2b inhibitory interneurons that enforce flexor-extensor alternation; and glutamatergic rhythm-generating interneurons, some carrying a persistent sodium current that gives them intrinsic bursting.

The persistent-sodium bursters are the beating heart: their personality is conditional autonomy - under enough drive they will oscillate on their own, so the rhythm tier does not depend on any single mechanism.

The V2a excitatory cells are speed-dependent recruiters: they are dispensable slowly but essential fast, which is why gait breaks down at high speed when they are removed - their fast, reliable excitation is what holds a quick rhythm together.

The commissural inhibitory cells are the left-right referees, and their fast glycinergic veto is the difference between a walk and a hop.

The motoneurons are plateau-capable followers that amplify and broadcast the finished pattern.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Fast excitation is glutamatergic on alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, the NMDA component and a persistent sodium current together supporting the plateaus and bursts of rhythmogenesis.

Fast inhibition is glycinergic and GABAergic on chloride-permeable receptors, providing both the reciprocal alternation and the left-right coordination.

Gap junctions couple some interneuron and motoneuron populations electrically, tightening synchrony within a pool, especially early in development.

Neuromodulators - serotonin, dopamine and noradrenaline from descending brainstem fibres - reconfigure weights and intrinsic currents on the fly, changing gait, speed and even the direction of coordination; this is a heavily neuromodulated fabric whose effective wiring is state-dependent.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

A locomotor CPG for one limb is a stacked set of rhythm and pattern modules spanning a spinal enlargement of a few segments and a few centimetres; the respiratory CPG core, the pre-Bötzinger complex, is a compact bilateral kernel of roughly 800 to a few thousand glutamatergic neurons per side in a small mammal.

The full walking network of a quadruped links four such limb controllers plus axial modules into one coordinated whole.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

A handful of great CPGs serve the body: one locomotor network in the cord (regionally divided among the limbs), one respiratory network in the brainstem, one masticatory network for chewing, one for swallowing, and smaller ones for other rhythmic acts.

Unlike the elementary motifs there are not astronomically many - the CPG is a large composite, installed a small number of times, each a major named engine.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The lumbar and cervical spinal enlargements, hosting the locomotor CPG that walks the legs and moves the arms.

• The pre-Bötzinger complex of the ventrolateral medulla, hosting the inspiratory rhythm generator that is necessary and sufficient for the drive to breathe in.

• The adjacent parafacial and post-inspiratory complexes of the brainstem, hosting the expiratory and post-inspiratory phases that complete the breathing pattern.

• The pontine and medullary reticular formation, hosting the masticatory (chewing) and swallowing CPGs.

• The brainstem circuits for other rhythmic behaviours - coughing, sneezing, whisking in rodents - each a CPG variant.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete the locomotor CPG and the cord can still reflex but can no longer walk: the region loses its capacity to produce ordered, self-timed movement, leaving only isolated jerks.

Delete the respiratory CPG - specifically ablate the pre-Bötzinger complex - and breathing stops; this is a region whose motif is the literal difference between life and death.

A region that hosts a CPG gains autonomy: it can execute a complex behaviour on a single command, so the brain governs by policy rather than by micromanagement.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is: tonic scalar drive in, full spatiotemporal motor program out - a rhythm whose frequency scales with drive, carrying a fixed-order pattern of multi-muscle activation whose amplitudes and phase durations can be independently biased.

Real numbers: human and mammalian locomotor rhythms run from about 0.5 to a few strides per second, with the stance phase lengthening more than the swing phase as speed drops; breathing runs near 0.2 to 0.3 cycles per second at rest (about 12 to 18 breaths a minute) and pre-Bötzinger pacemaker cells span an intrinsic bursting range of roughly 0.05 to 1 cycle per second; chewing runs near 1 to 2 cycles per second.

The two-tier structure means frequency and pattern are separately controllable - the same rhythm can drive different muscle patterns, and the same pattern can run at different rhythms.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Sustained, self-terminating rhythmicity with a stereotyped intra-cycle sequence; the giveaway is a spontaneous deletion, where one muscle's burst drops out for a cycle or two and then rejoins at exactly the phase the ongoing rhythm predicts, proving that timing is generated separately from pattern.

The rhythm persists at its own frequency when sensory feedback is removed, and resumes at its pre-perturbation frequency after a disturbance.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Off (silent) below drive threshold; rhythmic above it; and within the rhythmic range, multiple gaits (walk, trot, gallop, hop) selected by the level of drive and by neuromodulatory state through reconfiguration of the commissural coupling.

The respiratory network shifts among eupnoea (normal breathing), sighing, and gasping regimes depending on oxygen state and neuromodulation, with gasping falling back onto the most intrinsic pacemaker mechanism.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

CPGs are substrate machines, but adaptable: spinal locomotor networks show training-dependent recovery after injury, and respiratory networks show long-term facilitation, a lasting increase in output after intermittent low-oxygen episodes.

This is calibration and gain-setting of a pre-wired program, not the learning of new sequences (contrast the synfire chain of Chapter 28, which is a sequence learner).

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

By behaviour: locomotor, respiratory, masticatory, deglutitive (swallowing), and more.

By mechanism: network-driven CPGs (rhythm from reciprocal inhibition), pacemaker-driven CPGs (rhythm from intrinsic bursting cells), and the common hybrid that uses both for robustness - the respiratory kernel is the exemplar hybrid, mixing pacemaker cells with network synchronisation and a heavy-tailed distribution of synaptic weights.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The interneuron classes are specified by transcription-factor codes before birth, and functional rhythmicity appears embryonically - fictive locomotor and respiratory rhythms can be recorded in the isolated embryonic cord and brainstem.

The pre-Bötzinger complex is assembled from Dbx1-derived interneurons whose progressive ablation slows and then halts breathing, confirming them as the rhythmogenic core.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

CPGs are among the most ancient and universal neural circuits, found in every animal with organised movement, from the swimmerets of crustaceans and the swim circuit of the lamprey to the human breath.

The vertebrate locomotor CPG descends from the undulatory swimming networks of early fish, re-tiled segment by segment and repurposed for limbs; the deep conservation is a textbook case of old parts serving new problems.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes shape respiratory rhythm actively - they sense carbon dioxide and release signals that stimulate breathing - so glia are not mere support here but participants; astrocytes and the vasculature also maintain the ionic and metabolic conditions the persistent-sodium bursters require.

Descending serotonergic, noradrenergic and dopaminergic modulation from the brainstem keeps the networks in their operating regimes.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Spinal cord injury disconnects the locomotor CPG from descending drive, motivating epidural stimulation and drug therapies that aim to re-power the intact network and restore stepping.

Congenital central hypoventilation syndrome (Ondine's curse), linked to PHOX2B mutations, is a failure of the automatic respiratory CPG so that breathing does not run on autopilot; sudden infant death syndrome has been linked to pre-Bötzinger and brainstem dysfunction; and dysphagia (disordered swallowing) after stroke reflects damage to the swallowing CPG.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Tonic excitatory drive from brainstem command regions (on-switch and speed, 0 to full scale); sensory afferent feedback from spindles, tendon organs and skin for entrainment and phase correction; chemosensory drive (carbon dioxide, oxygen) for the respiratory installation.

◦ Neuromodulatory inputs selecting gait and regime.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A full multi-muscle motor program: phased, amplitude-graded activation commands to many motoneuron pools per cycle.

• STATE.

◦ Cycle phase; current gait or regime; per-pool fatigue and burst state; separable rhythm-tier and pattern-tier states.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Drive amplitude; reciprocal and commissural inhibitory weights; persistent-sodium and adaptation conductances; duty-cycle and amplitude biases per muscle.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Locomotor cycle 0.3 to 2 seconds; respiratory cycle roughly 3 to 5 seconds at rest; masticatory cycle 0.5 to 1 second; synaptic decays a few to tens of milliseconds; respiratory long-term facilitation minutes to hours.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Loss of drive (spinal injury) silences locomotion; pre-Bötzinger failure stops breathing (Ondine's curse, links to sudden infant death); commissural interneuron loss forces hopping; swallowing CPG damage causes dysphagia.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module name motor_autopilot_sequencer. It would subscribe to a scalar go-and-speed channel, a regime or gait selector, and an optional sensory-entrainment channel, and publish a timed vector of per-effector activation commands. The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a parameterised motion primitive or a recurrent policy that emits an action sequence from a single latent command - but the CPG differs by splitting timing from content into two explicit tiers, so that the rhythm and the pattern can be reprogrammed independently, and by generating its own clock rather than stepping on an external one.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A network that, cut off from the brain and from all sensation, still plays the complete ordered score of a stride or a breath from a single steady go-signal - rhythm and pattern generated centrally, deletions in the pattern leaving the rhythm untouched.


CHAPTER 27. THE PACEMAKER NETWORK (Coupled Cellular Oscillators Pulled to Synchrony) (The Chorus of Clocks) (NON-COG)

Take thousands of cells, each a tiny clock ticking at its own slightly wrong rate, and wire them so that each nudges its neighbours; before long the whole crowd is ticking as one, and the shared tick is steadier and truer than any single clock alone.

That is the pacemaker network - a democracy of oscillators that votes itself into a chorus, and it is how a scatter of imperfect cellular clocks becomes the one master rhythm that times a day, or paces a pulse of insulin, or beats a heart.

Pacemaker names the members: each cell is an autonomous oscillator, a clock that runs whether or not it is connected.

Network names the trick: the members are coupled, and coupling is what turns a noisy scatter into a single coherent beat.

Chorus of clocks, the plain-English coinage, names the emergent result - many voices, each imperfect, singing one clean note.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The pacemaker network is a population of individually oscillating cells, coupled to one another, that synchronise into a single coherent, robust, tissue-level rhythm.

Its computation is synchronisation: it takes many independent, noisy, differently-timed oscillators and, through mutual coupling, produces one shared phase and one shared, far more precise period - an emergent clock that no single cell could hold alone.

The output is not a value or a motor program but a clean, self-sustaining pulse, whose great virtue is robustness: because the rhythm is distributed across thousands of coupled cells, it survives the loss or misbehaviour of any few, and it is steadier than the sum of its shaky parts.

The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the hypothalamus is the master installation - tens of thousands of neuronal clocks coupled into the body's central circadian timekeeper - and the same diagram, in gap-junction form, paces the insulin pulses of the pancreatic islet.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

Every node is itself an oscillator - a cell that cycles on its own through some intrinsic mechanism (a molecular transcription-translation feedback loop in the circadian case, an electrical bursting mechanism in the islet case).

The edges are coupling connections between oscillators, and their sign and type is what distinguishes the variants: in the suprachiasmatic nucleus the coupling is chemical and paracrine, carried by the neuropeptide vasoactive intestinal polypeptide (vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)) acting on its VPAC2 receptor and by gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA); in the pancreatic islet the coupling is electrical, carried by connexin-36 gap junctions that fuse the cells into one electrical sheet.

The topology is dense local coupling with a heterogeneous, small-world flavour: not every cell connects to every other, but the network is connected enough that phase information spreads across the whole tissue.

A minority of highly connected, highly excitable cells act as hubs (in the islet) or as a strongly coupling core region (the VIP-rich core of the suprachiasmatic nucleus), leading the waves and pulling the followers into line.

External entraining edges enter - light information via the retinohypothalamic tract sets the circadian phase; glucose sets the islet's excitability - so the network is a coupled oscillator that can be reset by the world.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

In the suprachiasmatic nucleus the cast splits into two great classes: the VIP-releasing neurons of the ventral core, which are the synchronisers, and the arginine-vasopressin (AVP)-releasing neurons of the dorsal shell, which are strongly rhythmic followers and amplifiers.

The VIP neurons' personality is that of a reliable coupler: they are the single most important contributor to keeping the cellular clocks in step, and without VIP or its receptor the population desynchronises into a scatter of free-running cells with different periods - the chorus falls into cacophony.

Each suprachiasmatic neuron is a self-contained molecular oscillator built on the clock genes (a feedback loop of BMAL1 and CLOCK driving PER and CRY, which then repress them), giving a cell-autonomous period near 24 hours that coupling then sharpens and unifies.

In the pancreatic islet the cast is the beta cell of the other-cells catalogue, whose bursting electrical personality makes each an intrinsic oscillator, with a minority of hub beta cells - unusually excitable and highly connected - that lead the calcium waves, and follower beta cells that fall in behind.

The delta and alpha cells sit alongside as paracrine regulators rather than core oscillators.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Circadian coupling is chemical and largely paracrine: VIP released onto VPAC2 receptors (a slow, G-protein-coupled, second-messenger signal) plus GABA acting on GABA type A receptors, the latter able to synchronise or, in some states, to loosen the network - a tunable brake and clutch.

Islet coupling is electrical: connexin-36 gap junctions form direct pores between beta cells, sharing current and calcium so that depolarisation spreads as a wave and the whole islet pulses together.

Characteristic of both is that coupling strength is a controlled variable: too little and the cells desynchronise; the right amount produces robust, coherent, precisely-timed pulses.

Plasticity is slow and state-dependent - seasonal changes in day length reconfigure suprachiasmatic coupling, and metabolic state and disease modulate islet gap-junction coupling.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

The human suprachiasmatic nucleus holds roughly 20,000 neurons per side (about 100,000 cells counted more broadly), a pair of rice-grain nuclei just above the optic chiasm.

A pancreatic islet holds hundreds to a few thousand cells, of which the majority are beta cells, forming a coupled cluster a fraction of a millimetre across; the pancreas contains on the order of a million such islets.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

One master circadian pacemaker network (the paired suprachiasmatic nuclei) sits at the top; on the order of a million islet pacemaker networks are distributed through the pancreas; and the heart's sinoatrial node is a third great installation of coupled cellular oscillators.

Peripheral clock tissues throughout the body are weaker coupled-oscillator networks entrained by the master.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The suprachiasmatic nucleus of the anterior hypothalamus, the master circadian clock that times sleep, hormone release, temperature and metabolism, and synchronises every peripheral clock (its grandest form is entry 63 of the outline).

• The islets of Langerhans of the pancreas, where connexin-36-coupled beta cells pulse insulin in coordinated waves (the islet syncytium, entry 64).

• The sinoatrial node of the heart, where coupled pacemaker myocytes synchronise into the heartbeat (the physiological archetype of the coupled cellular oscillator).

• Peripheral tissue clocks (liver, adrenal and others), coupled-oscillator networks entrained by the suprachiasmatic master.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete the coupling from the suprachiasmatic nucleus and the region keeps thousands of clocks but loses its single voice: behaviour and hormones lose their coherent daily rhythm and drift into a desynchronised scatter - the tissue can no longer tell the body what time it is.

Delete the coupling from the islet and insulin release loses its clean pulsatility, becoming ragged and less effective, which impairs glucose control.

A region that hosts a pacemaker network gains a robust, precise, self-repairing rhythm that no single cell could provide - the whole point is that the chorus is steadier than any chorister.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is synchronisation of phase and sharpening of period: many oscillators with a spread of natural frequencies map, through coupling above a critical strength, onto one shared frequency and phase (mathematically the Kuramoto transition, where coupled oscillators lock).

The emergent period is more precise than any individual's, and the output is a robust pulse at that period: roughly one cycle per 24 hours for the circadian network, one insulin pulse every 5 to 10 minutes for the islet, and about one beat per second for the sinoatrial node.

Below the critical coupling the population stays incoherent (no shared rhythm); above it the population locks - a genuine phase transition, so the presence or absence of a tissue rhythm can flip sharply with coupling strength.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Very slow, extremely regular, self-sustaining oscillation whose defining feature is coherence across a whole population and robustness to the loss of members.

The circadian signature is a near-24-hour free-running period that persists in constant darkness and can be phase-shifted by light; the islet signature is minute-scale calcium waves sweeping across the tissue from hub regions; the shared signature is that decoupling the cells abolishes the coherent tissue rhythm while leaving individual cells still ticking.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Two great regimes: synchronised (coupling above critical, one coherent rhythm) and desynchronised (coupling too weak, a scatter of free-runners).

The suprachiasmatic network also shifts its internal phase relationships with season and day length, and switches GABA between synchronising and loosening roles depending on prior lighting; the islet switches between coupled pulsing at high glucose and quiescence at low glucose.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

This is a regulatory oscillator, not a learning circuit, but it is adaptable: the circadian network re-entrains its phase to shifted light schedules over days (the slow recovery from jet lag is exactly this re-synchronisation), and seasonal plasticity reconfigures coupling.

Islet coupling is modulated over the longer term by metabolic state and is degraded in disease.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

By coupling type: chemically/paracrine-coupled networks (the suprachiasmatic nucleus, via VIP and GABA) and electrically/gap-junction-coupled networks (the islet and the sinoatrial node, via connexins).

By oscillator mechanism: transcription-translation molecular clocks (circadian) versus membrane-electrical bursters (islet, heart) - the same synchronisation motif built on very different single-cell engines.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Cellular oscillators appear before their coupling matures, so synchrony develops gradually: in the suprachiasmatic nucleus individual clock cells are present early and the coupling that unifies them, and the network's synchrony, strengthens through late development.

Connexin-36 coupling in the islet likewise matures to produce coordinated pulsatile secretion.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Cell-autonomous circadian clocks are ancient, present even in single-celled cyanobacteria, and the strategy of coupling many cellular clocks into a robust tissue clock is a conserved solution reused wherever biology needs a reliable slow rhythm.

Electrical coupling of pacemaker cells is the equally ancient mechanism of the heartbeat, redeployed in the islet - one synchronisation motif serving day-timing, insulin pulses and the pulse itself.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes are active timekeepers in the suprachiasmatic nucleus, carrying their own clock and contributing to the rhythm through daily changes in glutamate handling, so glia help set the network's phase rather than merely support it.

The vasculature delivers the glucose that sets islet excitability and the hormonal and light-derived signals that entrain the circadian network.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Circadian rhythm disorders - jet lag, shift-work disorder, advanced and delayed sleep-phase syndromes, and the circadian disruption of ageing and neurodegeneration - are failures or misalignments of the suprachiasmatic pacemaker network.

Loss of islet beta-cell coupling contributes to type 2 diabetes by degrading pulsatile insulin release; and failure of sinoatrial coupling produces sick-sinus syndrome and arrhythmias.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Entraining signals: light via the retinohypothalamic tract for the circadian network (a phase-setting input, not a rhythm); glucose concentration for the islet; autonomic and hormonal drive for the sinoatrial node.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A robust, coherent, tissue-level rhythmic pulse: a near-24-hour timing signal broadcast to the whole body (circadian); pulses of insulin every 5 to 10 minutes (islet); the heartbeat (sinoatrial node).

• STATE.

◦ Population phase; coherence (order parameter, 0 for scattered to 1 for fully locked); coupling strength; current period.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Coupling strength (must exceed a critical value to lock); spread of natural cell frequencies; hub-cell excitability and connectivity; entrainment sensitivity.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Circadian period about 24 hours, re-entrainment over days; islet pulse period 5 to 10 minutes; sinoatrial period about 1 second; coupling signals (VIP second-messenger) seconds to minutes, gap-junction coupling near-instant electrically.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Sub-critical coupling desynchronises the population: circadian disruption and sleep-phase disorders (loss of VIP/VPAC2), degraded pulsatile insulin and type 2 diabetes (loss of connexin-36), sick-sinus syndrome and arrhythmia (sinoatrial decoupling).

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose the module name coupled_clock_synchroniser. It would subscribe to an entrainment/phase-setting channel and publish a single coherent phase-and-period signal plus a coherence measure, serving as a robust distributed clock other modules can time themselves against. The closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a population of coupled phase oscillators (a Kuramoto layer) or an ensemble whose members vote toward a consensus phase - it differs from a software clock in that its rhythm is emergent and fault-tolerant, degrading gracefully as members drop out rather than failing at a single point, and its period is genuinely produced by the population, not read from a crystal.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

Thousands of cells that each keep their own clock, coupled so tightly that they lock into one coherent tissue-wide beat - a rhythm that is steadier than any single member and survives the loss of many, whether it is timing a day or pulsing insulin.


CHAPTER 28. THE SYNFIRE CHAIN (Feedforward Wave Sequence Generator) (The Bucket-Brigade of Spikes) (COG)

Imagine a line of buckets of water passed hand to hand down a bucket-brigade, each bucket handed on the instant it arrives, so that a single splash travels the whole line in perfect step - and if a few hands are clumsy, the splash still arrives, because many hands carry each bucket together.

The synfire chain is that brigade built from neurons: pools of cells wired in feedforward waves so that a packet of synchronous spikes marches pool to pool, keeping its sharp timing across the whole chain, and this travelling packet is a leading candidate for how the brain stores and plays a learned sequence - the proven case is birdsong, and human speech and skilled action plausibly ride on the same motif.

Synfire is a contraction of synchronous firing: the members of each pool fire together, in a tight volley.

Chain names the architecture: pools linked one after another in a one-way line, so the volley has somewhere to travel.

Bucket-brigade, the plain-English coinage, names the essence - a signal passed intact from group to group, robust because many carriers share each hand-off.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

A synfire chain is a feedforward network of excitatory neurons organised into successive pools (layers), each pool connected to the next, so that a synchronous volley of spikes propagates stably from pool to pool while preserving its tight temporal precision.

Its computation is the generation and faithful transmission of a precisely-timed sequence: it turns a single trigger into an ordered, stereotyped, millisecond-precise cascade of activations, a clock and a script rolled into one.

Because the timing is carried by synchrony and by convergent redundancy, the chain is robust: some cells in a pool may fail, some spikes may be dropped, yet the volley still ignites the next pool - dropout tolerance is a defining virtue, not an afterthought.

The proven biological case is the premotor nucleus HVC of the songbird, where sparse, precisely-timed bursts march through a chain to clock out the notes of the song; the hypothesis extended to humans is that learned sequences - speech, typing, playing an instrument, any skilled serial act - are clocked by chains of this kind.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are pools of excitatory principal neurons, arranged in an ordered series: pool 1, pool 2, pool 3, and so on down the chain.

The essential edges are strong, convergent, divergent excitatory connections from every (or most) cells of one pool onto the cells of the next pool - many-to-many feedforward wiring, so that each downstream cell receives coincident input from a large fraction of the upstream pool.

That convergence is the redundancy that makes synchrony self-correcting: a downstream cell fires only when many upstream cells fire together, which both sharpens timing (jitter averages out) and tolerates the loss of individual senders.

A background of inhibition runs alongside the excitatory chain - feedforward and feedback inhibitory interneurons that keep each pool's activation brief and sparse, prevent the volley from spreading sideways into non-chain cells, and stop runaway excitation; in the songbird this inhibitory scaffold is essential to keep the sequence sharp.

The chain may be a simple line, a loop (for a repeating sequence), or a branching structure, and multiple chains can be embedded in one recurrent network, sharing neurons, so that different sequences reuse overlapping hardware.

The entry point is a trigger edge onto pool 1 (a start command), and the exit edges are the outputs of successive pools onto downstream targets (in the songbird, onto the motor nucleus that shapes the syllables).

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The chain principals are excitatory glutamatergic projection neurons - in the songbird, the HVC neurons that project to the song motor nucleus, which fire a single sparse, precisely-timed burst per song and are silent otherwise; in the mammalian analogue, cortical pyramidal cells such as the layer 5 and layer 2/3 excitatory neurons of the neuron catalogue.

The signature personality is sparse, bursting, time-locked firing: each principal fires once, hard, at its appointed millisecond and not otherwise, and this all-or-nothing burst is exactly what makes a clean, unambiguous link in the chain - a bursting cell, unlike a steadily-firing one, marks a moment.

Intrinsic bursting adds robustness: a cell that answers input with a short high-frequency burst rather than a single spike drives the next pool more reliably and helps the volley survive noise, which is why bursting enhances the robustness of sequence propagation.

The inhibitory cast is the fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive interneuron (the basket cell of the catalogue), whose rapid, reliable, perisomatic inhibition sharpens each pool's window and quenches it promptly - its fast-spiking, non-adapting personality is what keeps the volley brief and stops it smearing.

Where the chain forms and is learned, the plastic excitatory synapses between pools (see below) carry the story, and the slow neuromodulatory cells that gate that plasticity (dopaminergic and cholinergic inputs) act as the teachers that decide which connections become chain links.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The chain links are glutamatergic excitatory synapses on alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors, placed on the dendrites of the next pool; their strength is high and their number convergent, so coincident arrival readily crosses threshold.

The inhibitory scaffold is GABAergic, on gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) type A receptors, placed perisomatically by fast-spiking interneurons for timing and gain control.

The load-bearing plasticity is spike-timing-dependent plasticity (STDP): because a chain requires that upstream firing reliably precedes and causes downstream firing, the millisecond-scale pre-before-post timing rule strengthens exactly the forward links and weakens the wrong-way ones, which is the leading account of how a synfire chain self-organises out of an initially unstructured recurrent network.

NMDA-receptor-dependent long-term potentiation supplies the coincidence detection that STDP needs, and homeostatic scaling keeps the whole chain from saturating.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:
