CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A single painful input that produces mirror-image opposites in the two legs - one bending away, one stiffening to bear weight - is the fingerprint of this crossed, polysynaptic program and of no other reflex.


CHAPTER 45. THE GOLGI TENDON (FORCE-LIMITING) ARC (Ib Autogenic Inhibition Reflex) (The Tension Governor) (NON-COG)

Grip something as hard as you can and, at the limit, your hand seems to give way of its own accord - a built-in circuit refusing to let you tear your own muscle from its bone.

That circuit measures force, not length, at the muscle-tendon junction, and when the force runs high it quietly turns the muscle down.

It is the antagonist of the stretch reflex: where the spindle loop resists lengthening, this loop resists excessive force.

Tension names the variable it senses, the pull the muscle exerts on its tendon.

Governor names its job, a negative-feedback regulator that caps and smooths force the way a mechanical governor caps an engine's speed.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The Golgi tendon arc computes muscle force and feeds it back with negative sign onto the muscle producing it - autogenic (self) inhibition proportional to tension.

Its classic textbook role is protective, a safety cut-out preventing damaging forces, but its everyday role is subtler: continuous force feedback that smooths and regulates muscle tension across the whole working range, distributing load and stabilising limb stiffness.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The graph has three nodes and one changed sign relative to the stretch reflex.

Node one is the Ib afferent from a Golgi tendon organ, the force sensor at the muscle-tendon junction.

Node two is the Ib inhibitory interneuron in the spinal intermediate zone.

Node three is the alpha motoneuron of the same (homonymous) muscle.

The edges are: excitatory (glutamatergic) from Ib afferent to the Ib inhibitory interneuron, then inhibitory (glycinergic) from that interneuron onto the homonymous motoneuron - so rising force inhibits the muscle that produced it.

Branches of the same interneuron network diverge to excite the antagonist's motoneurons (via further interneurons) and to receive convergent input from cutaneous, joint, and descending sources, making the Ib interneuron a small integrating hub rather than a pure relay; the essential motif, though, is the single interposed inhibitory neuron that flips the feedback sign.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The Ib afferent is a large, fast, myelinated fibre, one per tendon organ, whose personality is force-proportionality: it is relatively deaf to passive stretch but fires in near-linear proportion to active contractile force, making it a clean tension meter.

The Ib inhibitory interneuron is an integrating cell that pools force information with other modalities, so the reflex it drives is context-dependent, not a fixed cut-out; its interposition is exactly what turns positive muscle force into negative motoneuron drive.

The alpha motoneuron is the same faithful summing output cell as in the stretch reflex, here receiving the inhibitory vote that trims its firing.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The Ib-to-interneuron synapse is glutamatergic on alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors; the interneuron-to-motoneuron synapse is glycinergic (with gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA)), placed on the motoneuron to subtract from its excitation.

The Ib interneuron's convergent inputs are a mix of glutamatergic (afferent, descending) and inhibitory contacts, and presynaptic inhibition regulates the Ib afferent's own gain, so the reflex's strength is set moment to moment.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance runs from a tendon organ, through an afferent up to a metre long, across two central synapses, and back down a motor axon to the same muscle - the same limb-spanning scale as the stretch reflex but with one extra synapse in the middle.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Golgi tendon organs number in the tens of thousands across the body's muscles, on the order of a tenth to a half the spindle count in a given muscle, so this arc runs in hundreds of parallel muscle-specific copies, densest where force must be finely graded.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The intermediate zone and ventral horn of every spinal segment, housing the Ib interneurons and homonymous motoneuron pools.

• The muscle-tendon junction as a peripheral Layer 9 address, where the tendon organ sensor is embedded in series with the muscle fibres.

• The brainstem motor nuclei, where analogous force feedback operates for the jaw and other cranial muscles.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this arc a spinal segment loses its sense of how hard its muscles are pulling, and motor output becomes force-blind - prone to jerky, poorly graded contractions and, at the extreme, to self-inflicted muscle or tendon damage.

The segment would keep length control from the spindle loop but lose the complementary force control that lets it hold a delicate grip or share load smoothly across a joint.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is negative-feedback, threshold-linear on force: motoneuron inhibition rises roughly in proportion to whole-muscle tension, subtracting from excitatory drive and thereby clamping force toward a regulated level.

Under normal loads it operates continuously and gently; at very high forces its gain effectively rises (recruiting the protective give-way), and it can reverse sign under some locomotor conditions, when Ib input transiently reinforces rather than inhibits extension to support body weight.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

With two central synapses the central delay is a small number of milliseconds, longer than the monosynaptic stretch reflex but still fast; the loop tracks force changes on a timescale of tens of milliseconds.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The reflex is state-dependent: inhibitory (autogenic) during quiet standing and static holds, but reversed to excitatory during the stance phase of locomotion, when force feedback from extensors helps hold the leg stiff against the ground.

Descending and interneuronal control switch it between these regimes, making the Golgi arc a reconfigurable feedback element rather than a fixed protective circuit.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The Ib pathways are subject to task-dependent modulation and motor learning, with their gain adjusted by training and by the behavioural context, though they are less classically studied for plasticity than the monosynaptic reflex.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The reflex is named by muscle and segment like the stretch reflex, and its most important functional variant is the locomotor sign-reversal, distinguishing the static protective mode from the dynamic weight-support mode.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Ib afferents and their interneurons form during spinal development alongside the other proprioceptive circuits, wiring with muscle-specific selectivity so that force feedback returns to the correct motor pool.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Force feedback via tendon organs is a conserved vertebrate feature complementing spindle length feedback; together they realise the two variables - length and tension - that any limb controller must regulate, an old and general solution to holding a joint.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Like the stretch reflex, this arc depends on Schwann-cell myelin for its afferent and motor conduction speed and on ventral-horn astrocytes to keep its busy motoneurons supplied and buffered.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Golgi-arc dysfunction contributes to the abnormal force regulation and stiffness of spasticity and clasp-knife phenomena after upper motor neuron lesions, where the give-way response is pathologically altered; force-feedback loss also accompanies the large-fibre sensory neuropathies that strip proprioception.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Whole-muscle tension via Ib afferents firing in proportion to active force; convergent cutaneous, joint, and descending signals onto the Ib interneuron.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Graded inhibition (or, in locomotion, facilitation) of the homonymous and synergist motoneurons.

• STATE.

◦ Ib interneuron excitability and the current sign of the reflex (autogenic-inhibitory versus locomotor-excitatory).

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Two central synapses; central delay a few milliseconds; Ib conduction velocity roughly 80 to 120 metres per second.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Force-tracking over tens of milliseconds; glycinergic inhibitory synaptic decay several to tens of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Altered force regulation and clasp-knife give-way in spasticity; loss of tension feedback in large-fibre neuropathy.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named muscle_force_governor: it would subscribe to a per-actuator force estimate and publish an inhibitory (or, in a locomotor state, facilitatory) adjustment to that actuator's drive, with a sign switch controlled by a behavioural-state input.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a torque-limiting current clamp in a motor controller, the protective loop that caps actuator effort.

Where it differs is that the biological loop can reverse the sign of its feedback under load-bearing conditions, so it is a context-switchable force controller rather than a one-way limiter.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

It is the reflex that inhibits a muscle in proportion to its own force through a single interposed inhibitory neuron - the sign flip that distinguishes force feedback from the length feedback of the stretch reflex.


CHAPTER 46. THE VESTIBULO-OCULAR THREE-NEURON ARC (Semicircular-Canal-to-Eye-Muscle Reflex) (The World-Steadying Loop) (NON-COG)

Fix your eyes on this word and shake your head no; the page stays sharp, held still by a circuit that moves your eyes exactly opposite your head, faster than you could ever do on purpose.

It runs on just three neurons in series and completes in about ten milliseconds - the fastest sensorimotor loop the human body possesses.

Its whole job is to cancel head motion at the eye, so that the image on your retina does not smear while you move.

World-steadying names its function: keeping the seen world stationary on the retina against every turn of the head.

Loop names its form, a closed reflex from the balance organs straight to the eye muscles and back through vision's stability.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The vestibulo-ocular reflex (VOR) computes an eye rotation equal and opposite to the head rotation, so gaze stays fixed in space while the head moves.

It is a velocity-to-velocity transform with a gain of very nearly minus one: for every degree per second the head turns one way, the eyes are driven the same number of degrees per second the other way.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE and speed are its defining virtues; the computation is trivial, but doing it fast enough to beat visual blur is everything.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The graph is three nodes in series, per the arc's name.

Node one is the semicircular canal afferent (part of cranial nerve VIII, the vestibulocochlear nerve), signalling head angular velocity.

Node two is a second-order neuron in the vestibular nuclei of the brainstem.

Node three is an extraocular motoneuron in one of the eye-muscle nuclei (the oculomotor, trochlear, or abducens nuclei, cranial nerves III, IV, and VI).

The edges: excitatory from canal afferent to the vestibular nucleus neuron; from there an excitatory (crossing) projection to the motoneurons of the appropriate eye muscle on one side, paired with an inhibitory projection to the antagonist eye muscle's motoneurons - a push-pull arrangement that turns one eye muscle on while relaxing its opponent.

Each canal is paired with the specific eye-muscle pair whose pulling plane matches the canal's sensing plane, so head rotation in any plane is decomposed and routed to exactly the muscles that can oppose it; a parallel indirect pathway through the cerebellum and the neural integrator adds the position-holding and calibration signals.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The canal afferent is a fast, tonically firing neuron whose baseline discharge rises and falls with head velocity; its personality is a high, symmetric resting rate that lets it signal rotation in both directions by modulation around a set point, giving the reflex its bidirectional speed.

The second-order vestibular nucleus neuron is a fast-relaying, sign-inverting-and-distributing cell that routes the velocity signal to the correct motoneuron pools with minimal delay; some are pure relays, others integrate.

The extraocular motoneuron drives some of the fastest muscles in the body, built for high-frequency firing and rapid, fatigue-resistant contraction.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The afferent-to-vestibular-nucleus and excitatory nucleus-to-motoneuron synapses are glutamatergic on fast alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors; the inhibitory arm onto antagonist motoneurons uses gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) and glycine.

The synapses are optimised for speed and reliability - large, secure contacts with fast kinetics - because the reflex's value is entirely in its short latency; the cerebellar side loop supplies the plastic synapses that calibrate the gain.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is compact and entirely within the head: a few centimetres from inner ear through brainstem to eye muscle, three neurons long, the smallest physical span of any arc in this part.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

There are a fixed, small number of canal-to-muscle channels - three canals per ear, each paired with its matching eye-muscle pair, wired bilaterally - so the reflex is not a mass-repeated module but a small set of precisely arranged fixed circuits, augmented by the linear (otolith) VOR for translation.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The vestibular nuclei of the medulla and pons, the central hub where second-order neurons route head-velocity signals to the eye.

• The oculomotor, trochlear, and abducens nuclei of the brainstem, whose motoneurons drive the extraocular muscles.

• The vestibulocerebellum (flocculus and paraflocculus), the side loop that continuously calibrates the reflex's gain.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this arc the brainstem loses its gaze-stabilising reflex, and the visual world smears with every head movement - the oscillopsia and blurring reported by patients who have lost vestibular function.

The eye-movement system would keep its voluntary and tracking functions but lose the fast, automatic compensation that makes vision usable during walking, running, and every turn of the head.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is a near-unity-gain velocity inverter: eye velocity equals about minus 0.9 to minus 1.0 times head velocity across the behaviourally important frequency range, with a small phase lead that compensates for the loop's own delay.

The reflex works over head rotations from a fraction of a hertz up to several hertz, a range voluntary tracking cannot cover, precisely because the three-neuron arc is so short.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The total reflex latency is about 7 to 15 milliseconds, commonly cited near 8 to 12 milliseconds, with eye movement lagging head movement by under 10 milliseconds - the fastest sensorimotor loop in the human body.

The three-synapse central delay is only a few milliseconds; the rest is transduction and neuromuscular transmission.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The reflex is suppressed when eyes and head move together to track a target (VOR cancellation), and its gain is context-set by the cerebellum; velocity storage in the vestibular nuclei extends its low-frequency response beyond the canal's own mechanics.

In disease the two sides become unbalanced, producing the spontaneous nystagmus of acute vestibular failure.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The VOR is the textbook model of cerebellar-dependent motor learning: wearing magnifying or reversing spectacles drives the flocculus to reset the reflex's gain over hours to days (VOR adaptation), keeping vision stable as the body and its optics change with age and injury.

This calibration is the cerebellar cortical template of entry 42 doing its supervised-learning job on a reflex.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The angular VOR (from the semicircular canals) counters rotation; the linear or translational VOR (from the otolith organs) counters head translation and depends on viewing distance; the three-neuron arc is the rotational core, with slower, more computational pathways added for the linear case.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The canal-to-muscle wiring is laid down prenatally with precise plane-matching between each canal and its eye-muscle pair, and the reflex is functional early in life, its gain then continuously recalibrated by visual experience through the cerebellum.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The three-neuron VOR is one of the most ancient and conserved circuits in vertebrates, present wherever there are eyes and a vestibular apparatus; its extreme conservation reflects the unchanging physics of the problem - image stability requires an equal-and-opposite eye movement, computed fast.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The circuit depends on the heavily myelinated, fast-conducting vestibular and oculomotor axons and on brainstem glia; its calibrating cerebellar loop depends in turn on the Purkinje and granule cell machinery of entry 42.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Vestibular neuritis, Meniere disease, bilateral vestibulopathy (with its disabling oscillopsia), and gain asymmetries producing nystagmus and vertigo are the disorders of this arc; clinically its integrity is tested by the head-impulse test, which reveals a corrective catch-up saccade when the reflex fails.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Head angular velocity via semicircular canal afferents; head translation via otolith afferents; visual error and gain commands from the cerebellum.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Push-pull drive to the extraocular motoneurons producing an eye rotation opposite the head.

• STATE.

◦ Vestibular nucleus firing balance between the two sides; velocity-storage integrator state; current cerebellar gain setting.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Three neurons in series; total latency about 7 to 15 milliseconds; gain about minus 0.9 to minus 1.0; effective bandwidth up to several hertz.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Central synaptic delay a few milliseconds; velocity storage several to tens of seconds; adaptation over hours to days.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Oscillopsia in bilateral vestibulopathy; spontaneous nystagmus and vertigo in acute unilateral vestibular loss.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named gaze_stabilisation_loop: it would subscribe to a head angular-velocity estimate and publish an equal-and-opposite eye-velocity command, with a scalar gain and a separate slow error input for calibration.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a feedforward image-stabilisation controller, such as the inertial-measurement-unit-driven gimbal stabiliser on a camera drone that counter-rotates the sensor against platform motion.

Where it differs is that its gain is not fixed but continuously retuned by a supervised cerebellar side loop from visual-slip error, so it is a self-calibrating feedforward stabiliser rather than a fixed one.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

Three neurons, about ten milliseconds, and an eye movement precisely equal and opposite to the head - no other reflex is this short, this fast, or this exactly compensatory.


CHAPTER 47. THE BAROREFLEX ARC (Arterial-Pressure Negative-Feedback Reflex) (The Blood-Pressure Thermostat) (NON-COG)

Stand up quickly and, for the second before you feel faint, a brainstem circuit is already fighting to keep the blood in your head - speeding your heart, tightening your vessels - against gravity's pull.

It senses the stretch of your great arteries beat by beat and adjusts heart and vessels to hold pressure steady, the way a thermostat holds a room's temperature.

This is the fastest and most important of the autonomic feedback loops, working continuously and invisibly every second of your life.

Blood-pressure names the regulated variable, the arterial pressure the reflex defends.

Thermostat names its form, a negative-feedback controller with a set point that corrects deviations in both directions.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The baroreflex computes the error between actual arterial pressure and a set point, and drives autonomic corrections - heart rate, cardiac contractility, and vessel tone - to cancel that error within a heartbeat or two.

Its transform has negative sign: a rise in pressure produces slowing and vasodilation, a fall produces speeding and vasoconstriction, so the loop opposes any deviation and stabilises perfusion, especially against posture changes.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The graph is a brainstem loop with a sensory input, a central integrator, and two opposing autonomic outputs.

The input nodes are baroreceptor afferents - stretch sensors in the carotid sinus (via the sinus nerve of Hering, a branch of the glossopharyngeal nerve, cranial nerve IX) and the aortic arch (via the aortic nerve joining the vagus, cranial nerve X).

These afferents make excitatory (glutamatergic) synapses onto the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS), the medulla's cardiovascular integration hub.

From the NTS the loop splits into two signed pathways: an excitatory projection to the parasympathetic cardiac neurons (the nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus), which slow the heart; and a sympatho-inhibitory pathway in which the NTS excites the caudal ventrolateral medulla (CVLM), which in turn sends a GABAergic inhibitory edge to the rostral ventrolateral medulla (RVLM), the source of sympathetic vasomotor tone.

Because rising pressure excites the NTS, which both excites the vagus and (through the CVLM) inhibits the RVLM, a pressure rise simultaneously slows the heart and withdraws vasoconstriction - the two-armed negative feedback that defines the reflex.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The baroreceptor afferents are stretch-sensitive neurons whose firing tracks both mean pressure and its rate of rise, so they signal not just how high the pressure is but how fast it is changing - a proportional-plus-derivative sensor.

The NTS neurons are integrating relay cells that combine baroreceptor input with chemoreceptor, cardiac, and respiratory signals, coordinating the reflex with breathing (the source of respiratory sinus arrhythmia).

The CVLM neurons are GABAergic inhibitory cells whose tonic output holds the RVLM in check, and the RVLM presympathetic neurons are pacemaker-like drivers whose ongoing firing sets the body's background vasoconstrictor tone; the cardiac vagal neurons are the fast brake on heart rate.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Baroreceptor-to-NTS and NTS-to-CVLM synapses are glutamatergic on alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors; the crucial CVLM-to-RVLM synapse is GABAergic, and much of the reflex's tuning happens at this inhibitory relay.

The vagal output to the heart's sinoatrial node is cholinergic (acetylcholine on muscarinic receptors, fast because of a direct potassium-channel link), while the sympathetic output is a two-neuron chain ending in noradrenaline on the heart and vessels; the NTS is also a rich target of neuropeptide and hormonal modulation.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a body-spanning loop: sensors in the neck and chest, an integrator in the medulla a centimetre or two across, and effectors reaching the heart and the entire arterial tree - a single distributed control system rather than a repeated small module.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

There is essentially one baroreflex, bilaterally arranged, with the carotid and aortic sensor populations feeding a shared brainstem hub - not a mass-replicated motif but a singular, central regulatory circuit.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The carotid sinus and aortic arch, the peripheral Layer 9 addresses housing the arterial stretch sensors.

• The nucleus tractus solitarius of the medulla, the central integrator receiving all baroreceptor input.

• The caudal and rostral ventrolateral medulla, the relay and the sympathetic command centre that set vasomotor tone.

• The nucleus ambiguus and dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, the parasympathetic cardiac output.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this arc the medulla loses beat-by-beat blood-pressure control, and pressure swings wildly with posture and activity - the orthostatic hypotension and fainting of baroreflex failure, and the pressure lability that makes standing dangerous.

The brainstem would keep the heart beating and vessels toned, but lose the fast corrective feedback that keeps the brain perfused when you stand, strain, or bleed.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is negative feedback with a sigmoid pressure-to-output curve: over the operating range, output autonomic activity changes roughly linearly with pressure error, saturating at very high and very low pressures; the reflex's sensitivity is measured as baroreflex gain in milliseconds of heart-period change per millimetre of mercury.

The loop acts within one to two heartbeats on the heart-rate arm (fast, vagal) and over several seconds on the vascular arm (slower, sympathetic), correcting deviations of tens of millimetres of mercury.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The vagal (parasympathetic) arm responds within a single cardiac cycle, under a second, because acetylcholine acts on the sinoatrial node almost instantly; the sympathetic arm responds over several seconds because of its slower ganglionic and noradrenergic transmission.

This two-speed signature lets the reflex both parry sudden pressure drops and set steady-state tone.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The set point is not fixed: it is reset upward in chronic hypertension and during exercise, and shifts with sleep, emotion, and the respiratory cycle; the reflex's gain falls with age and in heart failure.

Resetting is why the baroreflex defends a high pressure in a chronic hypertensive as diligently as it defends a normal one in a healthy person.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The baroreflex undergoes both rapid resetting (over minutes, shifting its operating point) and chronic resetting (over days to weeks, in sustained hypertension), plasticity that occurs at the afferent, central, and effector levels and that unfortunately lets high pressure become the defended norm.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Related brainstem reflexes share the NTS hub: the chemoreflex (responding to blood oxygen and carbon dioxide), the cardiopulmonary reflexes from low-pressure receptors, and the Bezold-Jarisch reflex; the arterial baroreflex is the fast, high-pressure arm of this family.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The baroreflex matures over the perinatal period and infancy, its gain rising as the autonomic nervous system develops; the NTS and ventrolateral medullary circuits are specified early in brainstem development.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Arterial pressure regulation by a brainstem negative-feedback loop is conserved across vertebrates with a closed high-pressure circulation; the motif is the cardiovascular instance of the general homeostatic thermostat the framework identifies throughout the autonomic system.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The circuit depends on brainstem astrocytes, which in the NTS and ventrolateral medulla actively sense carbon dioxide and modulate the reflex, and on the specialised baroreceptor endings whose mechanotransduction (via PIEZO ion channels) converts vessel stretch into afferent firing.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Baroreflex failure (after neck surgery, radiation, or in some neurodegenerations) causes volatile hypertension and fainting; reduced baroreflex sensitivity is a marker of poor prognosis in heart failure and after myocardial infarction; carotid sinus hypersensitivity causes syncope; and impaired baroreflex resetting contributes to sustained hypertension.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Arterial stretch (pressure and its rate of change) from carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors; chemoreceptor and respiratory signals at the NTS.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Vagal (cardio-inhibitory) drive to the sinoatrial node; sympathetic vasomotor and cardiac drive via the RVLM.

• STATE.

◦ Current set point; NTS integration state; RVLM background firing; respiratory phase.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Baroreflex gain roughly on the order of 10 to 20 milliseconds per millimetre of mercury (falling with age); vagal arm under one second, sympathetic arm several seconds.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Cardiac vagal response within one cardiac cycle; sympathetic vascular response over seconds; central resetting over minutes to weeks.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Baroreflex failure with volatile hypertension and syncope; reduced sensitivity in heart failure; impaired resetting in chronic hypertension.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named pressure_setpoint_regulator: it would subscribe to a measured arterial-pressure signal and a set point, and publish two opposing effector commands - a fast parasympathetic brake and a slower sympathetic drive - to null the error.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a proportional-integral controller with an adjustable set point regulating a plant around a target.

Where it differs is that its set point is itself plastic and resets toward whatever pressure is chronically sustained, so the controller can be captured by a pathological operating point rather than defending a fixed one.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A loop whose one sensor is arterial stretch and whose two opposing outputs - fast vagal braking and slower sympathetic tone - always move to cancel a pressure change is the blood-pressure thermostat and nothing else.


CHAPTER 48. THE VAGO-VAGAL LOOP (Gut-to-Brainstem-to-Gut Vagal Reflex) (The Digestion Autopilot) (NON-COG)

Swallow a mouthful and, without any awareness on your part, your stomach relaxes to receive it, seconds before the food arrives - a reflex that both listens to the gut and commands it, over the same nerve.

The vagus nerve carries the sensing fibres up to the brainstem and the commanding fibres back down, closing a loop that runs your digestion on autopilot.

It is the circuit context of the framework's vagal layer-skipping channel - the body's private line between gut and brainstem, bypassing the spinal cord entirely.

Digestion names the domain it governs, the mechanical and secretory work of the stomach and upper gut.

Autopilot names its manner, an automatic regulator that keeps digestion running with no conscious input at all.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The vago-vagal loop computes the appropriate motor and secretory state of the upper gut from its own sensory condition - distension, chemistry, and content - and commands relaxation, contraction, or secretion to match.

Its signature computation is receptive relaxation (gastric accommodation): sensing the arrival or anticipation of food, it actively relaxes the stomach so that volume can rise without pressure rising, a feedback that keeps the organ's wall tension regulated.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The graph is a brainstem loop carried entirely by the vagus nerve, hence vago-vagal.

The input node is the vagal afferent from the gut wall (mechanoreceptors and chemoreceptors), whose cell bodies lie in the nodose ganglion and which make excitatory (glutamatergic) synapses onto the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) in the medulla.

The NTS integrates and projects, largely via GABAergic and glutamatergic connections, onto the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (DMV), the source of parasympathetic preganglionic outflow.

The DMV's efferent (cholinergic) fibres run back down the vagus to the enteric nervous system in the gut wall, synapsing on two opposing populations of postganglionic enteric neurons: an excitatory (cholinergic) pathway that contracts the muscle and a separate inhibitory (nitrergic, using nitric oxide, and peptidergic) pathway that relaxes it.

The loop closes through the gut: the motor response changes wall tension and content, which the vagal afferents re-sense, making the whole a continuous feedback controller; the dual excitatory and inhibitory efferent limbs let the same descending command either squeeze or relax, depending on which enteric pathway the NTS-DMV circuit selects.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The vagal afferent is a slowly and tonically firing sensory neuron whose personality is patient, sustained signalling of gut state rather than fast phasic alarm, matching the slow timescale of digestion.

The NTS neuron is an integrating hub cell, the same class that serves the baroreflex, here weighing gut sensation against hormonal satiety signals and coordinating the response.

The DMV preganglionic neuron is a pacemaker-influenced cholinergic output cell whose ongoing firing sets background parasympathetic tone to the viscera; its two downstream enteric targets - the excitatory cholinergic and the inhibitory nitrergic motor neurons - give the loop its push-pull control over gut muscle.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Vagal-afferent-to-NTS synapses are glutamatergic; the NTS-to-DMV connection is a mix of glutamatergic excitation and strong GABAergic inhibition, and this GABAergic tone is the main dial setting the loop's output.

The DMV-to-enteric synapse is cholinergic (nicotinic), and the final enteric motor output to smooth muscle is either cholinergic (contraction) or nitrergic and peptidergic - using nitric oxide and vasoactive intestinal peptide - for relaxation; the NTS-DMV junction is heavily modulated by circulating hormones such as cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide-1, and ghrelin.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance spans from the gut wall, up the vagus (a nerve running the length of the neck and chest), through a medullary circuit a few millimetres across, and back down to the gut - a long, slow, body-spanning loop matched to the slow tempo of digestion.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The loop is essentially singular and bilateral, a shared brainstem circuit serving the whole upper gastrointestinal tract; it is regionally specialised along the gut (oesophagus, stomach, proximal small intestine) rather than mass-replicated.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The nucleus tractus solitarius of the medulla, the sensory integration hub for gut afferents.

• The dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus, the parasympathetic command nucleus for the viscera.

• The stomach, oesophagus, and proximal small intestine, the peripheral Layer 9 addresses where sensing and motor effect occur, in partnership with the enteric nervous system.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this loop the upper gut loses its brainstem-coordinated reflexes - receptive relaxation, the gastrocolic and enterogastric reflexes, and reflex acid secretion - and digestion becomes uncoordinated with swallowing and satiety.

The medulla would keep the vagus as a conduit but lose the closed sense-and-command loop that lets the stomach anticipate and accommodate a meal; gastric emptying and accommodation would be disordered.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is slow negative feedback on gut wall tension and content: rising distension drives, via the NTS-DMV circuit, an increase in the inhibitory nitrergic output that relaxes the wall and holds pressure roughly constant as volume rises - the pressure-volume regulation of accommodation.

The same circuit switches to net excitatory output to drive contraction and emptying when the content and timing are right, so the loop is a state-selecting controller, not a fixed reflex.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The loop operates on the slow timescale of digestion - seconds to minutes - far slower than the somatic reflexes, because both its afferent signalling and its smooth-muscle effectors are inherently slow.

Receptive relaxation, for instance, precedes and accompanies swallowing over seconds; secretory and motility changes play out over minutes.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The loop's output is gated by the GABAergic NTS-DMV synapse and set by circulating hormones, so the same gut distension produces different responses in the fasted versus fed state, and in hunger versus satiety.

This hormonal and state dependence is why the vago-vagal circuit is a central node in appetite and gut-brain signalling.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The NTS-DMV connection is plastic, its strength reset by hormones, prior afferent activity, and metabolic state - a plasticity that adapts digestion to diet and that is a target of current obesity and diabetes research (including how gut hormone mimetics act partly through this circuit).

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Named vago-vagal reflexes include receptive relaxation and gastric accommodation, the enterogastric reflex (slowing gastric emptying when the small intestine is loaded), reflex control of acid and enzyme secretion, and the emetic reflex's afferent limb; each is a regional tuning of the same sense-integrate-command loop.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The vagal circuits and their enteric targets are established during development from vagal neural crest (which populates the gut) and brainstem neurogenesis; the loop is functional at birth, supporting suckling and early feeding, and matures with diet.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Brainstem-gut vagal reflexes are ancient and conserved across vertebrates, reflecting the deep evolutionary partnership between the central nervous system and the semi-autonomous enteric nervous system; the vagus is the private channel the framework highlights as bypassing the spinal relay.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The circuit depends on the enteric glia and the interstitial cells of Cajal (the gut's pacemaker cells) at its effector end, and on brainstem astrocytes at the NTS-DMV hub; the enteric nervous system provides the local circuitry the vagal command modulates rather than fully controls.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Impaired vago-vagal control contributes to gastroparesis (delayed emptying, common in diabetes with vagal neuropathy), functional dyspepsia and impaired accommodation, and the dumping syndrome after vagal injury or gastric surgery; vagal afferent signalling is also central to nausea and to the satiety failures studied in obesity.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Gut distension and chemistry via vagal afferents; circulating satiety and hunger hormones (cholecystokinin, glucagon-like peptide-1, ghrelin) at the NTS.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Vagal efferent commands selecting excitatory (contract, secrete) or inhibitory (relax, accommodate) enteric motor pathways.

• STATE.

◦ NTS integration state; DMV background tone; fed-versus-fasted hormonal context; GABAergic gate setting.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Loop timescale seconds to minutes; effector smooth muscle, not striated; output sign selectable (contract versus relax).

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Receptive relaxation over seconds; motility and secretory adjustments over minutes; hormonal state changes over minutes to hours.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Gastroparesis and impaired accommodation in vagal neuropathy; dumping syndrome after vagal injury; disordered satiety in obesity.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named visceral_state_regulator: it would subscribe to slow interoceptive signals (organ distension, chemistry) and hormonal context, and publish a selected motor or secretory program to the local effector network, choosing between opposing (contract versus relax) outputs.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a supervisory controller that sets the mode of a lower autonomous subsystem rather than commanding it directly - an arbitration layer over a semi-autonomous agent.

Where it differs is that it modulates, rather than replaces, a fully capable local controller (the enteric nervous system), and its arbitration is gated by hormonal and metabolic state, so it is a slow, state-dependent supervisor over an autonomous peripheral agent.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A reflex whose sensing and commanding limbs travel the same nerve, looping gut to brainstem to gut without ever touching the spinal cord, is the vago-vagal loop and no other.


CHAPTER 49. THE SYMPATHETIC GANGLION DIVERGENCE MOTIF (Preganglionic-to-Postganglionic Fan-Out) (The Alarm Distribution Board) (NON-COG)

When you are startled, a handful of commands leaving your spinal cord blossom into a body-wide surge - pupils wide, heart pounding, skin cold - because each command neuron fans out to dozens of targets at once.

The relay station where this happens is the sympathetic ganglion, a distribution board that takes a few incoming lines and copies each onto many outgoing ones.

It is divergence (entry 2) installed in the autonomic wiring, and it is why fight-or-flight is fast, coordinated, and total rather than piecemeal.

Alarm names the response it distributes, the sympathetic fight-or-flight activation.

Distribution board names its form, a relay that fans one input line out to many output lines, amplifying and broadcasting the signal.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The sympathetic ganglion divergence motif computes amplification-by-copying: it takes the firing of one preganglionic neuron and distributes it, with gain, onto many postganglionic neurons, converting a modest central command into a widespread peripheral response.

Its second computation is temporal broadening: peptide co-transmission alongside the fast transmitter stretches the postganglionic response in time, so a brief central burst produces a sustained peripheral effect.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The graph is a fan-out (divergence) with convergence mixed in.

The input node is the preganglionic sympathetic neuron, whose cell body sits in the intermediolateral column of the thoracolumbar spinal cord and whose axon runs out to a sympathetic ganglion.

Each preganglionic axon makes excitatory (cholinergic) synapses onto many postganglionic neurons - the divergence - and each postganglionic neuron also receives convergent input from several preganglionic axons.

The postganglionic neurons then project their (noradrenergic, mostly) axons onward to the target organs; the topology is therefore many-from-one and one-from-many at the same node, a fan-out board with overlap, and the essential signed edges are all excitatory from pre- to postganglionic.

A subset of ganglion cells receives an inhibitory or modulatory influence from small intensely fluorescent interneurons, adding a minor local gain-control edge.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The preganglionic neuron is a cholinergic command cell whose personality is that of a broadcaster: its single axon is built to drive many followers, so its firing is copied rather than merely relayed.

The postganglionic neuron is an integrating relay whose large excitatory input has a high safety factor for the strong synapses but requires summation of the weaker ones, so it filters as well as relays - only a fraction of its synaptic inputs, roughly a fifth to a third, actually trigger its spikes.

The small intensely fluorescent cell is a local dopaminergic interneuron that provides slow inhibitory modulation, a minor tuning voice on the board.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The preganglionic-to-postganglionic synapse uses acetylcholine on fast nicotinic receptors for the primary, secure transmission, with slower muscarinic and peptidergic (for example, luteinising-hormone-releasing-hormone-like and neuropeptide-Y) components that produce slow excitatory and late-slow postsynaptic potentials.

This layered fast-plus-slow transmission is the fabric's signature: the nicotinic component copies each spike, while the peptide component stretches the response over seconds, broadening the alarm in time.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One ganglion is a discrete structure from a few millimetres to a couple of centimetres, containing thousands to hundreds of thousands of postganglionic neurons; the superior cervical ganglion, the best-studied, holds on the order of a million neurons in humans.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The instances are the sympathetic ganglia themselves: the paired paravertebral chain running the length of the spine (including the superior, middle, and stellate cervical ganglia) and the prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric) of the abdomen - a few dozen major ganglia, each a divergence board for its territory.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The paravertebral sympathetic chain ganglia, distributing sympathetic outflow to the head, body wall, and thoracic organs.

• The prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior mesenteric, inferior mesenteric), distributing to the abdominal and pelvic viscera.

• The adrenal medulla, a modified ganglion where preganglionic fibres drive chromaffin cells to pour adrenaline into the blood - divergence taken to the hormonal extreme.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this motif the sympathetic outflow loses its amplification and coordination, and fight-or-flight becomes weak and fragmentary rather than a fast, body-wide surge.

Each ganglion would relay one-to-one instead of one-to-many, so the small number of central preganglionic neurons could no longer command the vast peripheral target field; the response would be neither strong enough nor synchronous enough to matter.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is divergent amplification with temporal broadening: one preganglionic input is copied onto many postganglionic outputs (a fan-out on the order of 1 to 10 up to 1 to 100 or more, depending on ganglion and method of counting), and the peptide co-transmission converts brief input bursts into prolonged output.

The convergence mixed in means each postganglionic cell needs a threshold amount of input to fire, so the board also performs a gating and pattern-recombination step rather than pure copying.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Fast nicotinic transmission produces postganglionic spikes within milliseconds; the muscarinic slow excitatory potential lasts seconds, and the peptidergic late-slow potential lasts tens of seconds to minutes - a three-timescale signature that lets the ganglion both relay quickly and sustain a prolonged state.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

At low preganglionic firing the ganglion relays faithfully; at high firing the slow and peptidergic components build up, raising postganglionic excitability and sustaining output - a use-dependent shift from relay to amplifier that matches the escalating demands of an alarm response.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

Ganglionic synapses show activity-dependent plasticity and long-term facilitation, and the ganglion's connectivity is refined during development; the balance of fast and slow transmission can be reset by prior activity and by injury-induced sprouting.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Variants include the paravertebral chain ganglia (rapid, widespread distribution), the prevertebral ganglia (which also contain their own reflex circuitry integrating gut afferents), and the adrenal medulla (hormonal broadcast); the enteric prevertebral ganglia blur into the peripheral reflex circuitry of the next chapter.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Sympathetic neurons derive from the neural crest and are specified by transcription factors and by nerve growth factor signalling from their targets, which also sets how many postganglionic cells survive and thus the divergence ratio; target-derived support matches the board's size to the tissue it serves.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The ganglionic amplifier is a conserved feature of the vertebrate autonomic nervous system, the peripheral solution to commanding a large body from a small central outflow - divergence, entry 2 of this catalogue, installed in flesh as an amplifying distribution board.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Satellite glial cells wrap each ganglion neuron and regulate its environment, and Schwann cells myelinate the preganglionic inputs; after injury, satellite glia and macrophages modulate ganglionic excitability, contributing to some chronic pain states.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Ganglionic transmission fails in autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy (antibodies against the ganglionic nicotinic receptor), producing widespread autonomic failure; the motif is also the target of surgical sympathectomy for hyperhidrosis, and its dysregulated sprouting contributes to some sympathetically maintained pain.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Preganglionic cholinergic drive from the intermediolateral column, each axon diverging onto many ganglion cells.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Postganglionic (mostly noradrenergic) drive fanned out to target organs; adrenaline to the bloodstream from the adrenal medulla.

• STATE.

◦ Postganglionic excitability, raised by accumulated slow and peptidergic transmission; local modulation by small intensely fluorescent cells.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Divergence ratio roughly 1 to 10 up to 1 to 100 or more; superior cervical ganglion on the order of a million neurons; only about 20 to 30 percent of synaptic inputs are suprathreshold.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Nicotinic transmission milliseconds; slow muscarinic potential seconds; peptidergic late-slow potential tens of seconds to minutes.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Autoimmune autonomic ganglionopathy; the intended failure of therapeutic sympathectomy; sympathetically maintained pain from aberrant sprouting.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named command_broadcast_amplifier: it would subscribe to a small number of high-level activation lines and publish that activation, copied and gain-scaled, onto a large fan-out of effector channels, with a slow-decay component that sustains the broadcast in time.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a broadcast or fan-out node in a message-passing graph, or the global neuromodulatory broadcast used to switch a whole network into an alert regime.

Where it differs is the layered fast-plus-slow transmission that both copies each spike immediately and stretches the response over seconds, so the module is a broadcast amplifier with built-in temporal low-pass persistence rather than a pure copy operation.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A relay station where each incoming line is copied onto dozens of outgoing ones and stretched in time by peptide co-transmitters is the sympathetic ganglion, the autonomic system's amplifying distribution board.


CHAPTER 50. THE ENTERIC PERISTALTIC CIRCUIT (THE LAW OF THE INTESTINE) (Polarised Ascending-Excitatory, Descending-Inhibitory Reflex) (The Squeeze-Behind, Relax-Ahead Wave) (NON-COG)

Watch a wave of a meal move through the gut and you are watching a nervous system think without a brain: the gut wall squeezes behind the bolus and opens ahead of it, propelling the contents along entirely on its own.

The circuit that does this lives in the wall of the gut, needs no input from the brain or spinal cord, and was named a century ago the law of the intestine.

It is a complete, polarised reflex - direction built into its wiring - assembled from ordinary motifs in the one place in the body where a full reflex runs outside the central nervous system.

Squeeze-behind names its ascending excitatory arm, contracting the muscle above the bolus.

Relax-ahead names its descending inhibitory arm, relaxing the muscle below the bolus.

Wave names the result, a travelling ring of contraction-and-relaxation that carries the contents onward, restarting itself at each new position.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The enteric peristaltic circuit computes direction: it detects a local distension and produces a spatially asymmetric motor response - contraction on the oral (upstream) side and relaxation on the anal (downstream) side - that moves the contents in one direction, aborally.

This polarised response is the elementary unit of propulsion; repeated at each successive position as the bolus advances, it produces the continuous travelling wave of peristalsis, the whole computation being a built-in sense of which way is downstream.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The graph is a polarised reflex assembled from intrinsic sensory neurons, two oppositely directed interneuron chains, and two classes of motor neuron.

The input node is the intrinsic primary afferent neuron (IPAN), a sensory neuron in the gut wall responding to distension and mucosal stimulation.

From the IPAN the graph splits by direction: an ascending (oral) pathway of excitatory interneurons that drive excitatory (cholinergic) motor neurons, contracting the circular muscle above the bolus; and a descending (anal) pathway of interneurons that drive inhibitory (nitrergic and peptidergic) motor neurons, relaxing the circular muscle below the bolus.

The signed edges are: IPAN excitatory onto both interneuron chains; ascending interneurons excitatory onto excitatory motor neurons; descending interneurons (using in part slow excitatory transmission through purinergic P2Y1 receptors) onto inhibitory motor neurons; excitatory motor output cholinergic (contract); inhibitory motor output nitrergic (relax).

The polarity - ascending chains projecting orally, descending chains projecting anally, some spanning up to 40 millimetres - is hard-wired into the geometry of the interneuron projections, which is why the reflex has an intrinsic direction and the wave always moves the same way.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The intrinsic primary afferent neuron is a large, multipolar, plateau-generating cell (the Dogiel type II neuron) whose long-lasting after-depolarisation lets it sustain firing after a brief stimulus, giving the reflex its persistence and helping recruit its neighbours through mutual excitation.

The ascending and descending interneurons are relay and integrating cells whose oppositely directed projections encode the reflex's polarity; the cholinergic ascending interneurons in the human colon can project up to about 40 millimetres orally, extending the reach of the squeeze-behind arm.

The excitatory motor neuron is a cholinergic contractor and the inhibitory motor neuron a nitrergic and peptidergic relaxer; their opposition, switched by position relative to the bolus, is the heart of the wave.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Fast enteric transmission uses acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors and adenosine triphosphate on purinergic receptors; slow transmission to interneurons during descending inhibition uses purinergic P2Y1 receptors, and the intrinsic afferents drive slow excitatory potentials that sustain the reflex.

The final excitatory motor output is cholinergic (with the peptide tachykinins) onto smooth muscle; the inhibitory output uses nitric oxide, vasoactive intestinal peptide, and adenosine triphosphate, acting on the smooth muscle through the interstitial cells of Cajal, the gut's pacemaker interface.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One functional instance is a segment of gut a few centimetres long, its circuitry embedded in the myenteric plexus between the muscle layers, with interneuron projections spanning up to about 40 millimetres in each direction - the reflex is short-range but overlapping, tiling the whole length of the gut.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The circuit is repeated continuously along the entire gastrointestinal tract, from oesophagus to rectum, embedded in an enteric nervous system of some 200 to 600 million neurons - as many as in the spinal cord - so the peristaltic motif runs in effectively uncountable overlapping copies down metres of gut.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The myenteric (Auerbach's) plexus of the small and large intestine, the principal motor network housing the peristaltic reflex.

• The submucosal (Meissner's) plexus, which contributes secretory and mucosal reflex arms coordinated with propulsion.

• The stomach and oesophagus, where polarised enteric reflexes participate in gastric mixing and oesophageal peristalsis alongside vagal control.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this circuit the gut loses its intrinsic propulsion, and contents no longer move without external command - the functional obstruction of aganglionic bowel, where the missing enteric circuit leaves the segment unable to relax and propel.

The gut wall would keep its muscle and its slow-wave pacemaker but lose the polarised, self-restarting reflex that turns local distension into directed transport; the organ would be a tube that cannot swallow its own contents.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transform is a spatial derivative made motor: a local distension is mapped to opposite-signed motor outputs on its two sides (contract above, relax below), and the moving bolus continually re-triggers the reflex at each new position, producing a propagating wave whose velocity is set by the interneuron chain and pacemaker dynamics.

In numbers, peristaltic waves in the human gut travel on the order of centimetres per second (varying widely by region and content), each polarised reflex acting over a few centimetres and handing off to the next.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The reflex operates on the slow timescale of smooth muscle - contractions lasting seconds - and its wave restarts at each position, so a bolus is carried in a series of slow, overlapping steps rather than one fast movement.

Underlying slow waves from the interstitial cells of Cajal set a rhythmic background (a few cycles per minute in the stomach, faster in the small intestine) on which the reflex acts.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The enteric network switches between distinct motor programs - propulsive peristalsis during and after a meal, and the migrating motor complex (the housekeeper wave) that sweeps residue along during fasting - the same circuitry reconfigured by state and by input from the vagus and hormones.

The circuit can run entirely autonomously but is modulated by the vago-vagal loop of the previous chapter.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The enteric nervous system shows plasticity in response to diet, inflammation, and the microbiome, remodelling its circuits over time; enteric neurogenesis and circuit adaptation continue into adult life, and inflammation can durably alter the reflex's excitability.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The motif appears as classical peristalsis (propulsion), segmentation (mixing, with contractions that do not propagate), the migrating motor complex (fasting housekeeper), and the peristaltic reflex of the oesophagus and colon; each is a regional and state-dependent tuning of the polarised ascending-excitatory, descending-inhibitory template.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The enteric nervous system arises from vagal and sacral neural crest cells that migrate to colonise the whole gut and differentiate into its sensory, inter-, and motor neurons; failure of this migration to reach the distal bowel leaves an aganglionic segment (Hirschsprung disease), the developmental proof of the circuit's necessity.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The enteric nervous system is evolutionarily ancient, present in the earliest bilaterians with a through-gut, and is often called the first brain; the polarised peristaltic reflex is one of biology's oldest complete reflex arcs, predating the centralised nervous system it now merely coordinates with.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Enteric glial cells support and modulate the neurons and help maintain the gut barrier, and the interstitial cells of Cajal are the obligatory pacemaker interface between the enteric neurons and the smooth muscle, without which the reflex cannot translate into coordinated contraction.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Hirschsprung disease (congenital aganglionosis) causes functional obstruction; achalasia reflects loss of the inhibitory nitrergic motor neurons in the oesophagus; chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction, slow-transit constipation, and the dysmotility of diabetic and inflammatory enteric neuropathies all reflect failure of this circuit.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Local distension and mucosal stimulation via intrinsic primary afferent neurons; modulatory vagal and hormonal input.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Ascending excitatory (cholinergic contraction) motor drive orad; descending inhibitory (nitrergic relaxation) motor drive aborad.

• STATE.

◦ Current motor program (propulsive, segmenting, or migrating motor complex); interstitial-cell-of-Cajal slow-wave phase; network excitability.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Interneuron projection reach up to about 40 millimetres; wave velocity on the order of centimetres per second; slow-wave rhythm a few to about a dozen cycles per minute by region.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Smooth-muscle contractions over seconds; intrinsic afferent after-depolarisation seconds; program switching over minutes.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Hirschsprung disease, achalasia, and chronic intestinal pseudo-obstruction from loss or dysfunction of the enteric neurons.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

Propose a module named polarised_transport_reflex: it would subscribe to a spatially localised load signal along a one-dimensional array of actuators and publish opposite-signed motor commands on the two sides of the load (drive upstream, release downstream), re-triggering at each new load position to produce a travelling wave.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a distributed cellular-automaton or local-rule controller, in which a global transport behaviour emerges from identical short-range rules with a built-in directional bias, needing no central coordinator.

Where it differs is that the directionality is wired into the geometry of the connections rather than imposed by a clock or a controller, so the module is a fully decentralised, self-restarting transport reflex - the clearest catalogue example of a complete computation running with no central unit at all.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A complete, direction-built-in reflex - contract behind, relax ahead - running entirely in the wall of the gut with no help from brain or spinal cord is the enteric peristaltic circuit, the only place in the body where a full reflex lives wholly outside the central nervous system.

END OF PART SEVEN.


PART EIGHT. THE SENSORY FRONT-END MOTIFS

Between the raw physics of the world and the interpreted scene that reaches awareness stands a small set of specialised filters, and this part catalogues eight of them.

Each one is a wiring diagram that performs a single early transformation on a sensory signal - carving an edge, splitting brightening from darkening, pooling photons for the night, reading the direction of motion, sorting smells into channels, sharpening those channels, subtracting one ear from the other, and turning the ear's own amplifier up or down.

None of these motifs thinks, and so every entry in this part carries the tag (NON-COG), meaning it serves early filtering rather than cognition.

Yet the caution stated at the head of the outline applies with full force here, because everything these filters pass onward becomes the raw material from which perception, and then thought, is later assembled.

The reader should hold both facts at once: the circuits below are magnificent pieces of pre-processing machinery, and they are also the ground floor on which the cognitive motifs of Parts One through Six do their work.


CHAPTER 51. CENTRE-SURROUND ANTAGONISM (Concentric Opponent Receptive Field Motif) (The Edge-Carving Circuit) (NON-COG)

Shine a small spot of light on one patch of retina and a nearby cell brightens its firing; widen that spot into the ring around the patch and the same cell falls quiet, as if the light in the middle and the light in the surround were fighting.

That fight is the first computation the nervous system ever performs on light, and it is what lets you see an edge rather than a wash of brightness.

Centre names the small excitatory heart of the receptive field, the patch of photoreceptors that drives the cell one way.

Surround names the antagonistic ring around it, wired with the opposite sign so that uniform light cancels and only differences survive.

Antagonism names the subtraction itself, the deliberate opposition of centre against surround that makes the cell a difference detector rather than a light meter.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The centre-surround motif is a concentric opponent receptive field in which a cell is driven by light falling on a small central zone and driven the opposite way by light falling on a surrounding annulus, so that its output reports the difference between the two.

It computes spatial contrast, which is to say it responds strongly to edges, spots and gradients while ignoring uniform illumination, and this is the reason vision begins as a map of boundaries rather than a photograph.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the cone photoreceptor, the horizontal cell, the bipolar cell and, downstream, the retinal ganglion cell.

The central edge runs from a small group of cones directly onto a bipolar cell by a sign-conserving or sign-inverting glutamate synapse, forming the excitatory centre.

The surround edge runs laterally: cones across a wide area excite a horizontal cell through sign-conserving glutamate synapses, and that horizontal cell feeds back an inhibitory (sign-inverting) signal onto the central cones and forward onto the bipolar cell dendrites, so that light in the surround opposes the centre response.

The horizontal-cell feedback edge is negative and spatially broad; the direct cone-to-bipolar edge is fast and spatially narrow; the algebraic result at the bipolar cell, and again at the ganglion cell, is centre minus surround.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The cone photoreceptor is a slow, graded, non-spiking cell that releases glutamate continuously in the dark and reduces release in light, and its tonic, analogue personality means the whole circuit works in smooth voltages rather than spikes.

The horizontal cell, a wide-field, gap-junction-coupled, slowly integrating interneuron, averages light over a large area and feeds it back with a delay, and its sluggish, pooling personality is exactly what builds a broad, blurred surround out of a sharp centre.

The cone bipolar cell is the first cell to carry an explicit centre-surround signal, and depending on its glutamate receptor it inverts or preserves the cone sign, setting up the ON and OFF families treated in Chapter 52.

The retinal ganglion cell, typically a midget or parasol type in the human, is the spiking output cell that inherits the centre-surround field and transmits it to the brain, converting the graded difference into a train of action potentials.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The cone-to-horizontal-cell and cone-to-bipolar synapses use glutamate released at ribbon synapses, specialised structures that sustain the high, graded release rate these analogue cells demand.

The surround is built by horizontal-cell feedback onto cones, mediated in humans and other mammals by a mixture of mechanisms including a pannexin-1 hemichannel and pH-dependent ephaptic (electrical-field) signalling that shifts the cones' calcium channels, rather than by a conventional transmitter alone.

Horizontal cells are joined to one another by connexin-mediated gap junctions, the electrical couplings that let them pool light over hundreds of micrometres and set the width of the surround.

The characteristic weights are set in development and adjusted by ambient light and by dopamine, which uncouples the horizontal-cell network and so shrinks the surround in bright conditions.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a single ganglion cell's receptive field, in the human fovea a centre only a few micrometres to tens of micrometres across drawing on one or a few cones, with a surround several times wider.

In the peripheral retina one instance may pool dozens to hundreds of photoreceptors, so the physical size of a single motif ranges from roughly ten micrometres to several hundred micrometres of retinal surface.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The human retina holds on the order of one to one and a half million ganglion cells, and essentially every one carries a centre-surround field, so instances number in the millions per eye.

They tile the entire retina in overlapping mosaics, densest at the fovea, where centres are smallest for high acuity, and sparsest in the far periphery, where centres are largest for sensitivity.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The retina, in both the outer plexiform layer (where horizontal cells build the surround) and the inner retina, where it is the founding computation of every visual signal leaving the eye.

• The dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus, whose relay cells inherit and sharpen a centre-surround field before passing it to cortex.

• The dorsal column nuclei and somatosensory relays, where an analogous lateral-inhibition surround sharpens the map of touch, showing the motif is not unique to vision.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Delete this motif from the retina and the eye would still report how bright each point is, but it would lose all sense of where one thing ends and another begins, because contrast, not luminance, is what the surround extracts.

The visual world would collapse into a foggy field of brightness with no borders, and every later stage that depends on edges - form, texture, object boundaries - would have nothing to work with.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transfer function is subtractive at heart and is classically modelled as a difference-of-Gaussians: the response equals a narrow positive Gaussian weighting of the centre minus a broad, weaker negative Gaussian weighting of the surround.

In real numbers the surround typically cancels sixty to ninety per cent of the response to a full-field uniform light, so a cell firing at, say, forty spikes per second to a spot may fall to a few spikes per second when the surround is co-illuminated.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The centre response is fast, following the cone signal within a few to some tens of milliseconds, while the horizontal-cell surround arrives with a delay of roughly ten to fifty milliseconds, and this timing gap gives the field a transient, edge-emphasising character in time as well as space.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

In bright (photopic) conditions dopamine uncouples horizontal cells and narrows the surround, favouring acuity; in dim conditions the network couples more widely, broadening the surround and pooling light for sensitivity.

The motif thus has at least two standing regimes, a high-acuity daylight state and a high-sensitivity twilight state, switched by ambient luminance through neuromodulator tone.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The circuit is not a learning device in the synaptic-memory sense, but its gain adapts continuously to background light and contrast, a slow homeostatic re-scaling that keeps the difference signal within range.

Developmentally, the width and strength of the surround are tuned by early visual experience, and abnormal early input can leave the antagonism mis-set.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The motif comes in an ON-centre form (excited by light in the centre, inhibited by light in the surround) and an OFF-centre form (the reverse), and in colour-opponent variants in which the centre and surround are driven by different cone types, adding a spectral difference to the spatial one.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The outer retinal circuitry self-assembles before and shortly after birth as cones, horizontal cells and bipolar cells stratify into the outer plexiform layer, with spontaneous retinal waves helping refine the concentric geometry before the eyes open.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Lateral inhibition producing a centre-surround field is one of the oldest and most conserved computations in the animal kingdom, found from the compound eye of the horseshoe crab (where Hartline first measured it) to the vertebrate retina, evidence that difference detection is a near-universal solution to early sensory coding.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Müller glia, the retina's principal support cells, buffer the potassium and neurotransmitter released by this continuously active analogue circuit and maintain the extracellular pH on which horizontal-cell feedback depends, so the surround itself is metabolically supported by glia.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Loss or distortion of centre-surround processing accompanies retinal degenerations such as retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration, and horizontal-cell dysfunction (for example in some forms of congenital stationary night blindness affecting the outer retina) degrades contrast sensitivity even when acuity charts look normal.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Cone photocurrent from the centre cones, graded, 0 to a few tens of millivolts of hyperpolarisation.

◦ Pooled cone signal from the surround via horizontal cells, weighted over roughly 100 to 500 micrometres.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A graded bipolar-cell voltage and, downstream, a ganglion-cell spike train of roughly 0 to 200 spikes per second encoding centre-minus-surround contrast.

• STATE.

◦ Horizontal-cell coupling strength (surround width), adaptation level, dopamine tone.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Centre diameter roughly 5 to 100 micrometres; surround diameter roughly 3 to 6 times the centre; surround cancellation 60 to 90 per cent.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Centre latency a few to tens of milliseconds; surround feedback delay roughly 10 to 50 milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Retinitis pigmentosa and age-related macular degeneration degrade the mosaic; horizontal-cell or outer-retinal disease flattens contrast sensitivity; loss of the surround yields washed-out, edge-blind vision.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named concentric_contrast_extractor would subscribe to a two-dimensional array of luminance samples and publish a contrast map, computing each output as a narrow positive weighting minus a broad negative weighting of its input neighbourhood.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is the difference-of-Gaussians or Laplacian-of-Gaussian filter, and the centre-surround kernels of the first layer of a convolutional neural network, which learn almost exactly this shape.

The biological motif differs in being analogue and graded rather than clocked, in adapting its surround width to ambient light in real time, and in building the subtraction partly through non-synaptic ephaptic feedback rather than pure weighted summation.

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A cell that fires to a spot in one place and falls silent when the light spreads to a ring around it, built by a slow wide-field horizontal cell feeding back against a fast narrow cone input - the concentric difference detector that turns light into edges.


CHAPTER 52. THE ON-OFF PUSH-PULL SPLITTER (Sign-Inverting and Sign-Conserving Bipolar Divergence) (The Bright-and-Dark Fork) (NON-COG)

A single cone in the dark leaks a steady drizzle of glutamate onto the bipolar cells beneath it, and when light strikes, that drizzle slackens; two kinds of bipolar cell listen to the very same drizzle and draw opposite conclusions, one reading the dimming as "brighter", the other as "darker".

From one photoreceptor's single signal the retina thus manufactures two complementary channels, and from that fork the whole opponent architecture of vision descends.

ON names the channel that depolarises to light, built by a sign-inverting receptor that turns "less glutamate" into "more excitation".

OFF names the channel that depolarises to darkness, built by a sign-conserving receptor that passes the cone's signal through unchanged.

Push-pull names the opponent pairing, the fact that the two channels move in opposite directions to the same event so that increments and decrements of light are each carried by a dedicated line.

Splitter names the divergence itself: one input wire in, two opposite-signed output wires out.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The ON-OFF splitter is a divergence motif at the cone-to-bipolar synapse in which one photoreceptor's graded glutamate signal is read by two receptor systems of opposite sign, producing an ON bipolar cell that depolarises to light increments and an OFF bipolar cell that depolarises to light decrements.

It computes the rectified separation of a signal into its positive-going and negative-going parts, doubling the dynamic range and speed with which brightening and darkening can each be represented.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:
