The single node upstream is the cone; two parallel nodes downstream are the ON bipolar cell and the OFF bipolar cell.

The cone-to-ON-bipolar edge is sign-inverting: glutamate acts on a metabotropic receptor of the mGluR6 (metabotropic glutamate receptor type 6) type that, when bound, closes a cation channel, so that light (less glutamate) opens the channel and depolarises the ON cell.

The cone-to-OFF-bipolar edge is sign-conserving: glutamate acts on ionotropic alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA)-type and kainate-type receptors (fast excitatory glutamate receptors) that open cation channels directly, so that darkness (more glutamate) depolarises the OFF cell.

Both edges originate from the same presynaptic ribbon, and the two channels remain segregated into distinct sublaminae of the inner retina, ON bipolar terminals in the inner sublamina and OFF terminals in the outer.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The cone photoreceptor supplies the shared, tonic, graded glutamate signal, and its high steady release rate in darkness is the resting condition the whole fork is defined against.

The ON cone bipolar cell carries a metabotropic, comparatively slow inverting synapse, and its personality is that of a lagging sign-flipper, which is why the ON pathway is slightly slower than the OFF pathway.

The OFF cone bipolar cell carries fast ionotropic receptors and so responds more briskly, a quicker, more faithful relay of the cone's own polarity.

Downstream, ON and OFF ganglion cells (midget and parasol types in the human) inherit the split and feed separate ON and OFF channels all the way to cortex.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The fabric is the cone ribbon synapse, where a single glutamate release site faces both mGluR6-bearing ON dendrites and AMPA/kainate-bearing OFF dendrites within an invaginating triad.

In the ON dendrite the mGluR6 receptor is coupled through a G-protein cascade to the TRPM1 (transient receptor potential melastatin 1) cation channel, the actual gate that opens to light.

The OFF dendrite uses conventional fast ionotropic glutamate receptors placed at flat contacts just outside the invagination.

The weights are largely fixed by receptor identity rather than learned, which is why the sign of each channel is a developmental commitment rather than an adjustable parameter.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a single cone pedicle with its associated ON and OFF bipolar dendrites, a structure only a few micrometres across containing on the order of a dozen or more ribbon release sites feeding both channels.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

There are roughly six million cones in the human retina, and every cone pedicle is a splitter feeding both an ON and an OFF pathway, so instances number in the millions.

The rod pathway of Chapter 53 injects its signal into this same ON/OFF machinery downstream, so the split ultimately serves the entire retina.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The retina, at the outer plexiform layer cone synapse, where the ON/OFF division of all subsequent visual processing is created.

• The inner plexiform layer, whose ON and OFF sublaminae keep the two channels physically separate through to the ganglion cells.

• By functional analogy, the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus, which maintains separate ON and OFF relay channels to cortex.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove the splitter and the retina would have only one polarity of response, halving its ability to signal decrements and slowing its reaction to one direction of change; night driving, reading dark text on light, and detecting a shadow would all suffer.

The visual system's characteristic even-handedness toward brightening and darkening - its ability to see a dark object on a light ground as readily as the reverse - is precisely what this fork provides.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is a signed split with half-wave rectification: the ON channel outputs the positive part of the light change and the OFF channel outputs the negative part, each roughly threshold-linear above its baseline.

In real terms a cone hyperpolarisation of a few millivolts to a light increment produces depolarisation in the ON bipolar and hyperpolarisation in the OFF bipolar, and the two together reconstruct the full signed signal from two positive-only lines.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The OFF channel, using fast ionotropic receptors, leads the ON channel, which uses a slower metabotropic cascade, by a few milliseconds, a small but reliable asymmetry measurable in the timing of ON and OFF responses throughout the visual system.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Under steady light both channels sit at a maintained baseline from which they push in opposite directions; under flicker they alternate, the ON channel marking each brightening and the OFF channel each darkening.

Adaptation shifts the operating point of both channels together so the fork stays centred on the prevailing luminance.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The sign of each channel is fixed by receptor expression and is not plastic, though the overall gain of the split adapts to background light; this is a hard-wired divergence rather than a learned one.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

There are roughly a dozen distinct cone bipolar types in the primate retina, split into ON and OFF families of several members each, differing in kinetics (transient versus sustained) and in the spatial extent they pool, so the fork is really a family of parallel forks tuned to different temporal and spatial scales.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The ON and OFF dendrites sort themselves onto the correct receptor complements and stratify into the correct inner-retinal sublaminae during late fetal and early postnatal development, guided by molecular cues and refined by spontaneous activity.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The mGluR6-TRPM1 sign-inverting mechanism is ancient and conserved across vertebrates, and the ON/OFF division it creates is a general strategy for representing a bidirectional signal with unidirectional (positive-firing) neurons, a constraint every nervous system shares.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Müller glia again buffer the extracellular environment of this tonically active synapse, and the specialised architecture of the cone pedicle, with its glial ensheathment, keeps the ON and OFF postsynaptic elements correctly apposed.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Mutations in the ON pathway - in the genes for mGluR6, TRPM1 or their signalling partners - cause the complete form of congenital stationary night blindness, in which the ON channel is silenced while the OFF channel survives, a clean natural knock-out of one prong of the fork.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Cone glutamate release, graded, high in darkness and falling with light.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ ON bipolar depolarisation to light increments and OFF bipolar depolarisation to light decrements, each a positive-only graded signal.

• STATE.

◦ Adaptation operating point; baseline release rate.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ ON latency slower than OFF by a few milliseconds; roughly a dozen bipolar subtypes; two segregated inner-retinal sublaminae.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ OFF ionotropic response order of a few milliseconds; ON metabotropic response order of tens of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Complete congenital stationary night blindness (mGluR6/TRPM1 loss) silences the ON channel; loss of either channel halves the retina's response to that polarity of change.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named signed_channel_splitter would subscribe to a single signed input stream and publish two positive-only streams, one carrying the rectified positive part and one the rectified negative part.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is the pair of rectified linear units applied to a signal and its negation, the standard trick for representing a signed quantity with non-negative activations.

The biological motif differs in implementing the two signs with genuinely different receptor machinery (metabotropic versus ionotropic), which gives the two channels different speeds rather than the identical kinetics an artificial split would have.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

One presynaptic ribbon facing two postsynaptic dendrites that read the same glutamate with opposite-signed receptors - the single point in the visual system where brightening and darkening become two separate wires.


CHAPTER 53. THE ROD CONVERGENCE (SCOTOPIC POOLING) PATHWAY (Piggyback Rod Signal Injection Motif) (The Photon-Pooling Night Line) (NON-COG)

On a moonless night a single photon striking a single rod can be felt by the brain, and the trick that makes such absurd sensitivity possible is not a better detector but a wider net: thousands of rods pour their faint whispers into a shared line, so that a signal too small to hear alone becomes a shout when summed.

The price of that summation is acuity, which is why night vision is grainy and colourless, and the circuit that strikes this bargain borrows the cone system's wiring rather than building its own.

Rod convergence names the fan-in, the funnelling of many rods onto few relay cells so that their tiny signals add.

Scotopic pooling names the function, scotopic meaning vision in near-darkness, pooling meaning the summation of photons across space and time that buys sensitivity.

Pathway names the fact that this is a dedicated relay chain - rod to rod bipolar to AII amacrine to cone bipolar - that injects the rod signal into the pre-existing cone circuitry rather than running to the brain on its own.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The rod convergence pathway is a high-convergence relay that pools the outputs of many rods through a dedicated rod bipolar cell and a specialised AII amacrine cell, then injects the pooled signal into the cone ON and OFF pathways for transmission to the brain.

It computes spatial and temporal summation for sensitivity, trading the fine resolution of the cone system for the ability to detect a handful of photons in near-total darkness.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the rod, the rod bipolar cell, the AII amacrine cell, and the ON and OFF cone bipolar cells.

The rod-to-rod-bipolar edge is a sign-inverting glutamate synapse (using the same mGluR6, metabotropic glutamate receptor type 6, mechanism as the ON cone bipolar) with high convergence, roughly twenty rods onto one rod bipolar in the primate.

The rod-bipolar-to-AII edge is an excitatory glutamate synapse, again convergent, roughly twenty rod bipolars onto one AII amacrine cell.

The AII then splits the signal two ways: onto the ON cone bipolar it makes a sign-conserving electrical synapse (a gap junction), and onto the OFF cone bipolar it makes a sign-inverting inhibitory glycine synapse, so that the pooled rod signal enters both the ON and OFF cone channels with the correct polarity.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The rod is an exquisitely sensitive, slow, saturating photoreceptor able to register single photons, and its slowness and saturation are exactly the properties a summing night detector needs.

The rod bipolar cell is a dedicated, high-gain, sign-inverting relay found only in this pathway, and its narrow job of amplifying and pooling rod input gives the scotopic line its enormous gain.

The AII amacrine cell is a fast, sometimes spiking, glycinergic interneuron that acts as the pathway's switchboard, and its dual output - electrical to ON, chemical-inhibitory to OFF - is what lets one relay serve both polarities; voltage-gated sodium channels in the AII speed its scotopic response.

The cone ON and OFF bipolar cells lend their existing axons to carry the rod signal onward, so the night line reaches the ganglion cells without any private wiring of its own.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The rod-to-rod-bipolar synapse is an invaginating ribbon synapse using glutamate onto mGluR6-TRPM1 (transient receptor potential melastatin 1) machinery.

The AII-to-ON-cone-bipolar contact is an electrical synapse built from connexin-36 gap junctions, a bidirectional low-resistance coupling that passes the signal without inversion.

The AII-to-OFF-cone-bipolar contact is a chemical glycine synapse, glycine being the inhibitory transmitter that inverts the sign for the OFF channel.

The connexin-36 coupling is itself modulated by light and dopamine, which adjusts the balance of rod and cone signals as the eye moves between night and day.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance, from rods through a single AII amacrine cell, pools on the order of several hundred to a few thousand rods (roughly 20 rods per rod bipolar times roughly 20 rod bipolars per AII), spanning a retinal patch tens to a couple of hundred micrometres across.

By the ganglion cell, convergence of these pooled units can reach several thousand and, in the far periphery, up to on the order of ten thousand rods feeding one ganglion cell.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The human retina holds roughly 90 to 120 million rods and a correspondingly large population of rod bipolar and AII amacrine cells, so instances of the motif number in the millions, absent from the rod-free central fovea and densest in a ring around it.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The retina, throughout the rod-rich parafovea and periphery, where it provides all vision below the cone threshold.

• The inner plexiform layer, where the AII amacrine cell distributes the pooled signal into the ON and OFF cone strata.

• By downstream inheritance, the scotopic channels of the lateral geniculate nucleus and visual cortex, which receive the pooled rod signal repackaged in cone-pathway wiring.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Take away this pathway and vision would simply stop at dusk, because the cone system cannot register the few photons available at night; the retina would be blind below moonlight.

The graininess and colourlessness of night vision are the signature of the bargain this circuit strikes, and they are the price the region pays for being able to see at all in the dark.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is spatial and temporal summation followed by high-gain amplification: the pooled response is approximately the sum of many single-rod signals, so sensitivity rises roughly in proportion to the number of rods pooled while spatial resolution falls in the same proportion.

In real numbers, pooling on the order of a thousand rods lets the system integrate single-photon events that each shift a rod by a fraction of a millivolt into a detectable summed signal, at the cost of blurring detail across that same patch.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The rod response is slow, integrating over roughly 100 to 300 milliseconds, and this long integration time is itself part of the sensitivity bargain - the circuit sums photons over time as well as space, which is why dim objects must be viewed steadily to be seen.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The pathway has a fully scotopic regime (deep dark, maximal pooling, connexin-36 coupling set for sensitivity) and a mesopic regime (twilight, where rod and cone signals mix and dopamine begins to uncouple the network), handing over entirely to the cone system in daylight.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The pathway does not learn, but its gain adapts across many orders of magnitude of light through modulation of the rod bipolar synapse and the AII gap junctions, a continuous automatic gain control rather than synaptic memory.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Beyond this primary rod pathway there are secondary routes - rods coupling directly to cones through gap junctions, and rods contacting certain OFF cone bipolars directly - that carry rod signals at higher light levels, so scotopic pooling is layered rather than single.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Rods are generated late and in vast numbers, and the rod bipolar and AII cells wire to them and to the cone bipolars after the cone circuitry is already laid down, consistent with the pathway's piggyback design.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The dedicated rod pathway is a mammalian elaboration built on top of an older cone-based retina, an evolutionary retrofit that let early nocturnal mammals exploit the night without inventing a whole new output stage.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The retinal pigment epithelium regenerates the enormous quantity of visual pigment the rods consume, and Müller glia support the metabolically demanding, tonically active rod synapses; without pigment regeneration the night line cannot reset.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Rod-specific degenerations such as retinitis pigmentosa destroy this pathway first, producing night blindness and tunnel vision years before central cone vision fails; vitamin A deficiency impairs pigment regeneration and blunts the same pathway reversibly.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Single-photon rod signals, each a fraction of a millivolt, from hundreds to thousands of rods.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A pooled, amplified signal injected into ON cone bipolars (electrically) and OFF cone bipolars (via glycine).

• STATE.

◦ Connexin-36 coupling strength; adaptation gain; dopamine tone.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Roughly 20 rods per rod bipolar; roughly 20 rod bipolars per AII; up to about 10,000 rods per ganglion cell in the periphery.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Rod integration roughly 100 to 300 milliseconds; AII response accelerated by voltage-gated sodium channels.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Retinitis pigmentosa (rod loss) and vitamin A deficiency cause night blindness; AII or connexin-36 dysfunction disrupts scotopic signalling.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named scotopic_pooling_relay would subscribe to a large array of weak, noisy detector signals and publish a single summed, high-gain output routed into an existing downstream channel with the correct sign for each branch.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is average pooling combined with automatic gain control, and the practice of summing many weak measurements to raise signal-to-noise before feeding a shared classifier.

The biological motif differs in routing its pooled output through two different synapse types (electrical to one branch, inhibitory-chemical to the other) so that a single relay serves opposite-signed downstream channels, and in trading resolution for sensitivity dynamically as light changes.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A dedicated bipolar and a single glycinergic amacrine that gathers thousands of rods and splices their summed whisper into the cone system's wiring through a gap junction on one side and an inhibitory synapse on the other - the night line that borrows the day system's cables.


CHAPTER 54. THE DIRECTION-SELECTIVITY CIRCUIT (Asymmetric Starburst Inhibition Motif) (The Motion-Reading Wiring) (NON-COG)

Some ganglion cells in your retina fire hard when a shape drifts one way across them and stay almost silent when the identical shape drifts the other way, and they compute this in just two synapses, before the signal has left the eye.

The secret is not speed but geometry: a star-shaped interneuron whose every arm prefers motion outward is wired to veto the ganglion cell precisely when, and only when, motion runs in the forbidden direction.

Direction names the quantity computed, the axis and sense of visual motion.

Selectivity names the asymmetry of the response, strong to the preferred direction and suppressed to the opposite, or null, direction.

Circuit names the fact that this is an emergent property of wiring, not of any single cell's machinery - it lives in how the starburst cell and the ganglion cell are connected.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The direction-selectivity circuit is a retinal motif in which starburst amacrine cells provide asymmetric, direction-tuned inhibition to a direction-selective ganglion cell, so that motion in the null direction is vetoed by well-timed inhibition while motion in the preferred direction escapes it.

It computes the direction of visual motion locally, reporting which way an image is moving across a patch of retina before any cortical processing.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the bipolar cells (excitatory drive), the starburst amacrine cells (directional inhibition), and the direction-selective ganglion cell (output).

Bipolar cells excite both the starburst dendrites and the ganglion cell directly with glutamate, an untuned excitatory edge.

Each starburst dendritic arm is itself directionally tuned, responding best to motion travelling from the cell body outward toward the arm's tip, an emergent property of the arm's own dendritic processing.

The critical edge is asymmetric and inhibitory: the ganglion cell receives GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) synapses preferentially from starburst arms pointing in the ganglion cell's null direction, so that null-direction motion recruits strong, well-timed inhibition onto the ganglion cell while preferred-direction motion does not.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The starburst amacrine cell is a radially symmetric, GABA-and-acetylcholine co-releasing interneuron whose dendritic arms act as semi-independent, outward-preferring motion detectors, and this per-arm directionality is the computational heart of the motif.

The direction-selective ganglion cell is a spiking output cell whose selectivity comes entirely from which starburst arms it listens to, a cell that inherits its preference from its wiring rather than its biophysics.

The cone bipolar cells supply the shared excitatory drive and the slight timing differences (sustained versus transient types) that the starburst arms exploit to build their directional tuning.

The starburst cell's dual transmitter personality matters: its acetylcholine is a fast, untuned boost to excitation, while its GABA is the directionally tuned, slightly slower veto, and the temporal offset between them is essential to the computation.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

Excitation onto starburst and ganglion cells is glutamatergic at ribbon synapses from bipolar cells.

The starburst output is a co-release of GABA (onto GABA-A receptors, fast chloride channels) and acetylcholine (onto nicotinic receptors) from the distal dendrites, with the GABAergic, direction-tuned synapses placed selectively on null-side ganglion-cell dendrites.

The vesicular GABA transporter loads GABA into the starburst terminals, and deleting it degrades the tuned inhibition, confirming that the GABA arm carries the direction signal.

There are no axons in this motif; the starburst cell is axonless and computes and outputs entirely within its dendritic tree, a dendrite-only inhibitory device.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a single direction-selective ganglion cell with the ring of starburst cells whose null-side arms converge on it, a structure a few hundred micrometres across integrating dozens of starburst arms.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Direction-selective ganglion cells make up a few per cent of the roughly one to one and a half million human ganglion cells, tiling the retina in four subtypes tuned to four cardinal directions, so instances number in the tens of thousands per direction.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The retina, in the inner plexiform layer, where it is the first place motion direction is explicitly represented.

• The accessory optic system and pretectum, which receive the ON direction-selective ganglion cells and use their signals to stabilise the eyes and drive the optokinetic reflex.

• By projection, the superior colliculus and, in primates, the lateral geniculate nucleus and cortex, which inherit early motion signals.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this circuit the retina would report that something is moving but not which way, forcing the whole burden of direction computation onto the cortex and crippling the fast subcortical reflexes that keep gaze steady.

The optokinetic reflex, which locks your eyes onto a moving world so the image does not smear, depends directly on the retina already knowing the direction of motion, so losing this motif would blur every moving scene.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is a direction-tuned gating: the ganglion cell's response is an excitation multiplied down by inhibition whose strength depends on motion direction, well approximated as preferred-direction excitation minus a large null-direction inhibitory conductance.

In real numbers the firing to preferred-direction motion can exceed the null-direction firing by several fold to more than ten fold, a deep modulation achieved in two synaptic steps with sub-100-millisecond timing.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The computation is fundamentally about timing: in the null direction the starburst inhibition arrives coincident with or just before the excitation and cancels it, while in the preferred direction the inhibition lags and misses, and the whole space-time comparison plays out over tens of milliseconds as the image sweeps across the dendrites.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The circuit operates across a wide range of speeds and contrasts, with the preferred speed set by the dendritic filtering of the starburst arms; at very low or very high speeds the directional tuning weakens as the timing relationship breaks down.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The asymmetric wiring is largely established developmentally and is not a substrate for ongoing learning, though the precise starburst-to-ganglion connectivity is refined by activity during a critical period before eye opening.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

There are ON, OFF and ON-OFF direction-selective ganglion cells, the ON-OFF type tuned to four cardinal directions for image motion and the ON type tuned to three directions for the slower motion signals that drive gaze stabilisation.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The asymmetric GABAergic wiring from null-side starbursts self-organises before vision, guided by molecular recognition cues and by spontaneous retinal waves, one of the clearest cases of a precise functional asymmetry built without visual experience.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Retinal direction selectivity is widespread across vertebrates, and the starburst amacrine cell is one of the most conserved interneurons of the inner retina, evidence that reading motion at the earliest possible stage is an old and valuable trick.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Müller glia support the inner-retinal synapses of the motif and regulate the chloride and GABA environment on which the tuned inhibition depends.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Selective disruption of starburst signalling degrades the optokinetic reflex and motion vision, and congenital nystagmus and certain optokinetic deficits have been linked to abnormal development of this early motion circuitry.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Untuned glutamatergic excitation from bipolar cells onto starburst arms and the ganglion cell.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A direction-tuned ganglion-cell spike train, strong for preferred-direction motion, suppressed for null-direction motion.

• STATE.

◦ Momentary dendritic voltage of each starburst arm; the timing relationship between excitation and inhibition.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Preferred-to-null firing ratio several fold to greater than 10 fold; four cardinal directions represented; a few per cent of ganglion cells.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Excitation-inhibition timing offset and dendritic sweep on the order of tens of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Loss of tuned starburst GABA release abolishes direction selectivity and degrades the optokinetic reflex; developmental miswiring is linked to nystagmus.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named motion_direction_gate would subscribe to a moving input array and publish a direction-tuned response, implementing an asymmetric spatiotemporal filter in which a delayed inhibitory tap positioned on the null side cancels excitation only for one direction of motion.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a Reichardt or motion-energy detector, or a spatiotemporal convolution kernel oriented in the space-time plane, the standard building blocks of computer motion estimation.

The biological motif differs by computing the direction inside a single axonless dendritic tree using co-released fast excitation and slower tuned inhibition, achieving the space-time asymmetry with wiring geometry rather than explicit delay lines.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

An axonless star-shaped cell whose every arm prefers outward motion, wired so that only the arms pointing the wrong way inhibit the ganglion cell - a motion detector built from geometry and timing in two synapses inside the eye.


CHAPTER 55. THE OLFACTORY GLOMERULAR MODULE (Convergent Receptor-Identity Sorting Motif) (The One-Smell Pixel) (NON-COG)

Scattered across the roof of your nose are millions of sensory neurons, each expressing just one kind of odorant receptor, and all the neurons that happen to share the same receptor - no matter where they sit - send their axons to the same tiny ball of neuropil in the olfactory bulb.

The result is that a chaotic sheet of receptors is sorted into an orderly map, one ball per receptor type, so that each smell becomes a specific pattern of lit-up balls, like a picture painted in labelled dots.

Olfactory names the sense, smell, the chemical detection of airborne molecules.

Glomerular names the anatomical unit, the glomerulus, a spherical tangle of neuropil where incoming axons meet the bulb's output cells.

Module names the repeated, self-similar nature of the unit - the bulb is a field of these balls, each a complete little processing station for one receptor identity.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The olfactory glomerular module is a convergence-and-normalisation motif in which all sensory neurons expressing a single odorant-receptor gene converge onto one (or a few) glomeruli, where their signal is pooled, averaged and normalised against neighbouring glomeruli by local interneurons before being read out by the bulb's principal cells.

It computes a sorted, denoised, gain-controlled representation of odorant identity, turning a noisy scatter of receptor activations into a clean channel per receptor type.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the olfactory sensory neurons, the glomerulus itself (as a shared neuropil node), the mitral and tufted (principal output) cells, and the periglomerular interneurons.

Thousands of sensory neurons of one receptor identity send excitatory glutamate axons that converge onto a single glomerulus, forming a massive fan-in edge.

Within the glomerulus these axons excite the primary dendrites of the mitral and tufted cells, whose single apical dendrite ramifies in exactly one glomerulus, a one-glomerulus-per-principal-cell rule.

Periglomerular interneurons form inhibitory (GABAergic and dopaminergic) edges both within a glomerulus (controlling its gain) and between glomeruli (lateral normalisation), and short-axon cells extend this interglomerular inhibition further across the map.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The olfactory sensory neuron is a small, individually noisy, single-receptor detector, and it is precisely because each one is unreliable that thousands must converge to average out their noise.

The mitral cell is a large principal output neuron with one glomerular tuft, an integrator that reads the pooled signal of one receptor channel and relays it to the cortex; its personality as a high-convergence read-out cell is what turns thousands of weak inputs into one strong signal.

The tufted cell is a smaller principal cell serving a similar role with different projection targets and a lower threshold, providing a more sensitive parallel read-out of the same glomerulus.

The periglomerular cell is a small inhibitory interneuron, some co-releasing dopamine, that sets the gain of its glomerulus and enforces competition between glomeruli, the local normaliser of the module.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The sensory-neuron-to-mitral synapse is glutamatergic onto alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors within the glomerular neuropil.

Periglomerular inhibition uses gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) onto GABA-A receptors, with dopamine (acting on D2 receptors on sensory terminals) providing presynaptic gain control that turns down input at high odour concentrations.

The glomerulus is a defined ball of neuropil wrapped by astrocytes, which delimit it and confine signalling within it.

Intraglomerular gap junctions couple some mitral and tufted cells belonging to the same glomerulus, synchronising the read-out of a single channel.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a single glomerulus, a sphere roughly 50 to 200 micrometres across in humans, receiving the axons of on the order of thousands of sensory neurons and feeding on the order of some tens of mitral and tufted cells.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The human olfactory bulb contains on the order of a few thousand glomeruli (estimates vary widely, from roughly 1,000 to several thousand, with wide interindividual variation and decline with age), roughly matching the number of functional odorant-receptor genes, which is on the order of 400 in humans.

They tile the surface of each olfactory bulb in a layer, forming a chemotopic map that is broadly conserved between individuals.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The olfactory bulb, where it is the fundamental processing unit of smell, one module per odorant-receptor identity.

• The accessory olfactory bulb, where an analogous glomerular convergence sorts pheromonal signals from the vomeronasal organ.

• By strong analogy, the antennal lobe of insects, the invertebrate homologue built on the same one-receptor-one-glomerulus plan.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without the glomerular module the bulb would receive an unsorted jumble of noisy receptor signals with no way to pool or normalise them, and smell would be both far less sensitive and far less able to tell one odour from another across changing concentrations.

The very idea of an odour as a reproducible pattern of activity - the thing that lets you recognise coffee whether faint or strong - depends on this sorting and normalising step.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is convergent averaging followed by divisive normalisation: the glomerular output is the pooled sensory input divided by a term reflecting the total activity across neighbouring glomeruli, which yields concentration-tolerant identity coding.

In real numbers, pooling thousands of noisy inputs sharply improves signal-to-noise, and the interglomerular division keeps each channel's output within range as overall odour concentration varies over orders of magnitude.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

Odour input is naturally chunked by the sniff cycle (a few sniffs per second), and the glomerular module reads out each sniff as a burst, with the relative timing of glomerular activation across a sniff carrying part of the odour code.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The module has a low-concentration regime, where sensitivity and pooling dominate, and a high-concentration regime, where dopaminergic and GABAergic gain control suppress input to prevent saturation, keeping the identity code stable across concentration.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The periglomerular and granule interneuron populations are continuously renewed by adult neurogenesis, giving the bulb an unusual capacity for experience-dependent remodelling of its inhibitory tuning across life.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Glomeruli differ by the receptor they serve and by their transmitter complement of surrounding interneurons; the main olfactory and accessory olfactory (vomeronasal) glomeruli are the principal variant classes.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The convergence is built by an axon-guidance program in which the odorant receptor protein itself, together with activity, instructs each sensory axon to find the glomerulus shared by its receptor identity, one of biology's most striking examples of molecularly guided self-sorting.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The one-receptor-one-glomerulus plan is deeply conserved, appearing in essentially the same form in the insect antennal lobe and the vertebrate olfactory bulb, a convergent or ancient solution to sorting a huge combinatorial receptor repertoire.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes wrap each glomerulus and define its borders, buffering transmitter and confining signalling, while the constant supply of new interneurons from the subventricular zone via the rostral migratory stream sustains the module's inhibitory machinery.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Loss of smell (anosmia) from viral infection (including certain respiratory viruses), head trauma, or neurodegeneration reflects damage to sensory neurons or their glomerular targets, and olfactory deficits are among the earliest signs of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, in which bulbar circuitry degenerates early.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Excitatory glutamate from thousands of single-receptor-identity sensory axons per glomerulus.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Mitral and tufted cell spike trains, one channel per receptor identity, to the olfactory cortex.

• STATE.

◦ Periglomerular inhibitory tone; dopaminergic presynaptic gain; sniff phase.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Roughly 1,000 to a few thousand glomeruli per bulb; roughly 400 receptor genes; thousands of sensory neurons per glomerulus; glomerulus 50 to 200 micrometres.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Sniff cycle a few hundred milliseconds; synaptic responses milliseconds to tens of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Anosmia from sensory-neuron loss or bulbar degeneration; early olfactory loss in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named receptor_identity_sorter would subscribe to a large population of noisy single-label detector signals and publish one pooled, normalised channel per label, routing all inputs of a given identity to a shared summing-and-normalising node.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a scatter-add or embedding-pooling operation followed by divisive (softmax-like) normalisation across channels, the standard way to turn sparse labelled events into a dense normalised feature vector.

The biological motif differs in that the sorting itself is achieved physically by molecularly guided axon targeting rather than by an index lookup, and in that its normalisation is continuously re-tuned by lifelong neurogenesis.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A single ball of neuropil that gathers the axons of thousands of scattered sensory neurons sharing one receptor gene and hands their pooled, normalised signal to a principal cell with exactly one dendrite in exactly one ball - the anatomical pixel of smell.


CHAPTER 56. THE DENDRODENDRITIC RECIPROCAL INHIBITION MOTIF (Two-Way Dendritic Synapse Sharpening Motif) (The Axonless Handshake) (NON-COG)

At most synapses signals run one way, from an axon to a dendrite, but in the olfactory bulb two dendrites meet and talk in both directions across a single junction: the output cell excites an interneuron's spine, and that very same spine inhibits it straight back.

There is no axon anywhere in the exchange, and the whole conversation - excite, then be inhibited - happens at one contact, sharpening each odour signal against its neighbours.

Dendrodendritic names the anatomy, a synapse between two dendrites rather than the usual axon-to-dendrite arrangement.

Reciprocal names the two-way traffic, excitation one way and inhibition the other across the same paired contact.

Inhibition names the function, the granule cell's GABAergic quieting of the mitral cell that produces both self-inhibition and lateral inhibition of neighbours.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The dendrodendritic reciprocal inhibition motif is a two-way synapse between the lateral dendrite of an olfactory bulb mitral (or tufted) cell and the spine of a granule cell, in which the mitral dendrite excites the granule spine and the granule spine inhibits the mitral dendrite back, at the same junction.

It computes recurrent self-inhibition (a mitral cell damping itself) and lateral inhibition (a mitral cell damping its neighbours through shared granule cells), sharpening and decorrelating odour representations and synchronising principal cells into rhythms.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the mitral (or tufted) cell lateral dendrite and the granule cell spine; there is no axon in the motif at all.

One edge is excitatory: the mitral dendrite releases glutamate onto the granule spine, depolarising it.

The reciprocal edge is inhibitory: the same depolarised granule spine releases GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) back onto the same mitral dendrite, at the same paired synaptic contact, within milliseconds.

Because one granule cell contacts the lateral dendrites of many mitral cells, activity in one mitral cell can, through the granule cell, inhibit distant mitral cells, forming the lateral-inhibition edge across the bulb.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The mitral (or tufted) cell is the excitable principal cell whose long lateral dendrites broadcast excitation across the bulb and receive the returning inhibition, and its readiness to fire is exactly what the motif reins in.

The granule cell is an axonless GABAergic interneuron, the most numerous cell in the bulb, whose spines each act as a semi-independent input-output unit; its personality as a distributed, spine-by-spine processor is what lets one granule cell mediate many separate reciprocal handshakes at once.

The granule cell integrates slowly and can release GABA both by fast local spikes and by slow, asynchronous, calcium-dependent mechanisms, giving the inhibition both a prompt and a lingering component.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The fabric is a paired synapse within a single granule-cell spine: a glutamatergic mitral-to-granule contact (onto alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) and, importantly, N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptors) immediately adjacent to a GABAergic granule-to-mitral contact (onto GABA-A receptors).

The NMDA receptors on the granule spine are central, because their calcium entry can drive GABA release locally without a full granule-cell action potential, allowing the spine to act on its own.

The two synaptic specialisations sit micrometres apart on the same spine, and the whole exchange is confined to that spine, an unusually local piece of synaptic machinery.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a single reciprocal synaptic pair on one granule-cell spine, a submicrometre structure, though the functional unit - one granule cell linking many mitral dendrites - spans tens to hundreds of micrometres.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

Granule cells outnumber mitral cells by roughly 50 to 100 to one, and each granule and mitral cell bears very large numbers of these reciprocal contacts, so instances in the human bulb number in the many millions, distributed throughout the external plexiform layer.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The main olfactory bulb, in the external plexiform layer, where it sharpens and synchronises the output of the glomerular modules of Chapter 55.

• The accessory olfactory bulb, where the same mitral-granule reciprocal arrangement processes pheromonal signals.

• The retina, as a close analogue, where amacrine-cell dendrodendritic reciprocal synapses perform comparable local inhibition, showing the motif is not unique to olfaction.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this motif the bulb's principal cells would fire without mutual restraint, odour representations would be broad and overlapping rather than sharp and separable, and the gamma-frequency synchrony that helps bind and time olfactory signals would be lost.

The bulb would lose its ability to make similar smells distinct, so that closely related odours would blur together the way an image blurs without lateral inhibition.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is recurrent and lateral subtractive inhibition: each mitral cell's output is reduced by an amount proportional to its own activity (self-inhibition) and to the activity of its neighbours routed through shared granule cells (lateral inhibition), sharpening contrast between odour channels.

The self-inhibition follows the mitral cell's excitation within a few to some tens of milliseconds, converting a maintained excitation into a briefer, contrast-enhanced, rhythmically patterned output.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The reciprocal loop operates on a millisecond-to-tens-of-milliseconds timescale and is the engine of olfactory bulb gamma oscillations (roughly 40 to 100 cycles per second), organising principal-cell firing into precise time slots, with an additional slow, asynchronous inhibitory component lasting hundreds of milliseconds.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The motif can operate in a fast, spike-driven mode that produces prompt lateral inhibition and gamma rhythm, and a slow, subthreshold, NMDA-and-calcium-driven mode that produces lingering, graded inhibition, with the balance set by input strength and neuromodulation.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The mitral-to-granule synapse shows long-term potentiation and depression and, crucially, granule cells are continuously replaced by adult neurogenesis, so the inhibitory network is remodelled by experience throughout life, tuning odour discrimination to the animal's history.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Analogous dendrodendritic reciprocal synapses appear between mitral cells and periglomerular cells in the glomerular layer, between amacrine and bipolar cells in the retina, and among thalamic interneurons, each a variant of the same two-way dendritic contact.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Granule cells are generated prenatally and then continuously through life from the subventricular zone, migrating to the bulb and forming reciprocal synapses as they mature, so the motif is under constant construction.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Dendrodendritic reciprocal inhibition is an ancient feature of the olfactory system and appears in modified form in the retina and thalamus, an old solution to the problem of local inhibition where space or wiring economy forbids a dedicated axon.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes in the external plexiform layer buffer the glutamate and GABA of these densely packed synapses and, through glutamate uptake, shape the NMDA-dependent component of the granule-cell response.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Disruption of bulbar inhibition and of the neurogenic supply of granule cells impairs odour discrimination and is implicated in the early olfactory deficits of Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease, where granule-cell populations and their reciprocal synapses are affected.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Glutamate from mitral and tufted lateral dendrites onto granule-cell spines.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ GABAergic self- and lateral inhibition returned onto the same and neighbouring mitral dendrites.

• STATE.

◦ Granule-spine calcium and voltage; balance of fast and slow release modes.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Granule-to-mitral ratio roughly 50 to 100 to 1; gamma rhythm roughly 40 to 100 cycles per second.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Fast reciprocal inhibition a few to tens of milliseconds; slow asynchronous component hundreds of milliseconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Loss of granule-cell inhibition blurs odour discrimination and abolishes bulbar gamma; early granule-cell loss in Parkinson's and Alzheimer's disease.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named reciprocal_lateral_sharpener would subscribe to a set of channel activations and publish the same channels after subtracting a self-and-neighbour inhibition computed at the very node that carries the excitation, fusing the forward and inhibitory operations into one bidirectional edge.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is lateral inhibition or a local competitive normalisation layer, but implemented with tied, co-located forward and backward weights rather than separate layers.

The biological motif differs in dispensing with an axon entirely and in letting each synaptic spine act as an independent processor, so inhibition is computed and delivered at the same point in space, with a plasticity supplied by lifelong replacement of the inhibitory cells themselves.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A single dendritic spine that receives glutamate and returns GABA to the very dendrite that excited it, with no axon anywhere in the loop - the two-way handshake that sharpens smells at the point of contact.


CHAPTER 57. THE INTERAURAL LEVEL SUBTRACTION MOTIF (Excitation-Minus-Inhibition Loudness-Comparison Motif) (The Louder-Ear Subtractor) (NON-COG)

A sound coming from your right is a little louder in your right ear than your left, because your head casts an acoustic shadow, and a small nucleus in your brainstem exists to measure exactly that difference by pitting the two ears against each other.

Excitation from the near ear pushes a cell to fire; inhibition from the far ear, arriving through a sign-flipping relay, pushes back, and the cell's firing rate reports which ear won and by how much - a running subtraction that localises high-pitched sounds.

Interaural names the comparison, between the two ears.

Level names the cue used, the loudness or intensity difference between the ears, as opposed to the timing difference used by the delay-line motif of entry 21.

Subtraction names the computation itself, excitation from one ear minus inhibition from the other.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The interaural level subtraction motif is a brainstem circuit in the lateral superior olive in which a principal cell receives excitation driven by the ipsilateral (same-side, near) ear and inhibition driven by the contralateral (opposite-side, far) ear, so its firing rate encodes the difference in loudness between the two ears.

It computes the interaural level difference, the primary cue for localising high-frequency sounds in the horizontal plane, and is the loudness-difference partner to the timing-difference (delay-line) motif of the medial superior olive.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the ipsilateral cochlear nucleus, the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (the sign-flipping relay), and the lateral superior olive principal cell.

The excitatory edge runs from the ipsilateral cochlear nucleus (spherical and globular bushy cells) directly onto the lateral superior olive principal cell with glutamate, driven by the near ear.

The inhibitory edge runs indirectly: the contralateral cochlear nucleus excites the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body with glutamate (via a fast, secure calyx synapse), and that nucleus then inhibits the lateral superior olive principal cell with glycine, so the far ear's signal arrives sign-inverted.

The two edges are tonotopically matched, meaning excitation and inhibition serving the same sound frequency converge on the same principal cell, so the subtraction is done frequency by frequency.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The lateral superior olive principal cell is the subtractor, a cell that behaves as a temporal differentiator, comparing the instant-by-instant balance of excitation and inhibition; its rapid, non-integrating personality is what lets the subtraction track ongoing sound level.

The spherical and globular bushy cells of the cochlear nucleus are fast, temporally precise relays that preserve the loudness and timing of the auditory-nerve input, delivering a clean copy of each ear's signal.

The principal neuron of the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body is a high-speed sign-inverter driven by the calyx of Held, one of the largest and fastest synapses in the brain, whose reliability lets the far-ear inhibition arrive almost as promptly as the near-ear excitation despite the extra synapse.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The ipsilateral excitation uses glutamate onto alpha-amino-3-hydroxy-5-methyl-4-isoxazolepropionic acid (AMPA) receptors optimised for speed.

The trapezoid-body relay is the calyx of Held, a giant glutamatergic synapse engineered for near-failure-free, high-frequency transmission.

The inhibitory input to the lateral superior olive uses glycine onto glycine receptors, the fast inhibitory transmitter of the brainstem, and this glycinergic inhibition is precisely timed to oppose the excitation.

The relative strengths and timing of the excitatory and inhibitory synapses are refined by activity during development to keep the subtraction balanced across frequencies.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is a single lateral superior olive principal cell with its matched excitatory and inhibitory inputs at one characteristic frequency, a microcircuit spanning the small S-shaped nucleus a few millimetres across.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The lateral superior olive contains on the order of thousands of principal cells per side, arranged tonotopically, so the motif is instantiated a few thousand times per hemisphere, one set per frequency band, biased toward high frequencies where level cues are strongest.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The lateral superior olive of the brainstem, the sole primary site of interaural level difference computation.

• The medial nucleus of the trapezoid body, the obligatory glycinergic relay that supplies the far-ear inhibition.

• By projection, the inferior colliculus, which integrates the level-difference output with the timing-difference output to build a full map of auditory space.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this motif the brainstem could not localise high-frequency sounds, and the auditory system would be left only with the low-frequency timing cues of the medial superior olive, badly degrading the ability to tell where a sound is coming from.

The everyday act of turning toward a voice or a snapping twig on your right depends on this running subtraction, and its loss would flatten the auditory world into a source-less wash.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is subtractive: firing rate rises with ipsilateral (near-ear) level and falls with contralateral (far-ear) level, well approximated as a sigmoidal function of the difference in decibels between the ears.

In real numbers a lateral superior olive cell typically shifts from near-maximal to near-zero firing over an interaural level difference of roughly 10 to 20 decibels centred near its balance point, giving a steep readout of source azimuth.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The circuit works in near-real time, with the glycinergic inhibition arriving within a fraction of a millisecond of the excitation thanks to the fast calyx relay, and the principal cell responds to the ongoing moment-to-moment balance rather than integrating over long windows.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

Across its dynamic range the cell operates as a graded subtractor; at the extremes (sound far to one side) it saturates at maximum or minimum firing, and its most informative regime is the steep transition around the midline where small azimuth changes produce large rate changes.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The excitation-inhibition balance is calibrated during a developmental critical period, and the glycinergic inhibition undergoes long-term plasticity that keeps the subtraction accurate as the head grows and the acoustic shadow changes.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

Recent work shows the lateral superior olive contains several principal-cell types supporting somewhat different localisation strategies, and low-frequency lateral superior olive cells can also be sensitive to interaural timing, blurring the classic level-only picture.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The tonotopic matching of excitation and inhibition is established before hearing onset through spontaneous activity and then refined by experience, and the glycinergic projection is initially depolarising before switching to inhibitory as the circuit matures.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

The excitation-minus-inhibition plan of the lateral superior olive is conserved across mammals and is especially elaborated in small-headed, high-frequency-hearing species, reflecting that level cues dominate when a head is too small to produce useful timing cues.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

Astrocytes and the specialised perineuronal and myelin environment of the auditory brainstem support the extreme speed and reliability this timing-critical subtraction demands, and dense myelination of the trapezoid-body pathway minimises the delay of the inhibitory arm.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Damage to the brainstem olivary complex, and disorders of glycinergic transmission, impair sound localisation, and age-related and noise-induced high-frequency hearing loss degrades the very inputs this level-difference circuit depends on.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Glutamatergic excitation from the ipsilateral (near) ear; glycinergic inhibition from the contralateral (far) ear via the trapezoid body.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ A firing rate encoding interaural level difference, sent to the inferior colliculus.

• STATE.

◦ Momentary balance of excitatory and inhibitory conductance.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Operating range roughly 10 to 20 decibels of interaural level difference; thousands of cells per side; tonotopically ordered, high-frequency-biased.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Excitation-inhibition timing difference a fraction of a millisecond; response essentially instantaneous.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Glycinergic dysfunction or olivary damage impairs localisation; high-frequency hearing loss removes the cue this motif reads.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named interaural_level_subtractor would subscribe to two intensity streams (near and far channels) and publish their signed difference passed through a steep sigmoid, one comparison per frequency band.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is a difference unit or a subtractive gating layer, the elementary "A minus B" comparator that underlies many contrast and disparity computations.

The biological motif differs in achieving the subtraction with a fast glycinergic inhibitory arm routed through an extra sign-inverting relay engineered (the calyx of Held) to add almost no delay, so that a chemically inhibitory pathway can still perform a near-instantaneous subtraction.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A brainstem cell excited by the near ear and inhibited, through a single lightning-fast sign-flipping relay, by the far ear, so that its firing rate reads out which ear hears the sound louder - the loudness subtractor that locates high-pitched sound.


CHAPTER 58. THE EFFERENT GAIN-CONTROL LOOP OF THE COCHLEA (Olivocochlear Amplifier-Damping Motif) (The Turn-Down-the-Ear Loop) (NON-COG)

The inner ear is not a passive microphone but an active amplifier, its outer hair cells wriggling in time with sound to boost faint vibrations a thousandfold, and the brain reserves the right to turn that amplifier down.

A loop of neurons runs from the brainstem back out to the cochlea and, by releasing acetylcholine onto the outer hair cells, quiets their dance - protecting the ear in loud noise and helping it pick a voice out of a crowd.

Efferent names the direction, outward, from brain to sense organ, the reverse of the usual afferent flow.

Gain-control names the function, the adjustment of amplification, the same idea as the volume knob on an amplifier.

Loop names the closed feedback: sound drives the brainstem, which drives the cochlea, which changes the sound it sends back - a controlled sensor whose sensitivity is itself a regulated variable.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The efferent gain-control loop is a feedback circuit in which medial olivocochlear neurons in the brainstem project back onto the outer hair cells of the cochlea and, by inhibiting them, reduce the gain of the cochlear amplifier.

It computes an adaptive turn-down of hearing sensitivity, set by the ambient sound level and by attention, that protects the ear from overstimulation and improves the detection of signals in background noise.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

The nodes are the auditory-nerve afferents, the cochlear nucleus, the medial olivocochlear neurons (in the superior olivary complex), and the outer hair cells of the cochlea.

The forward sensing edge runs from the cochlea through the auditory nerve to the cochlear nucleus, which excites the medial olivocochlear neurons, closing the sound-driven reflex arc.

The efferent edge runs from the medial olivocochlear neurons back out along the auditory nerve to the outer hair cells, an inhibitory cholinergic synapse.

There is also a lateral olivocochlear component that projects onto the afferent dendrites beneath the inner hair cells, adjusting the gain of the afferent synapse rather than the amplifier itself, and the medial reflex has both an ipsilateral and a crossed (contralateral) limb.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The outer hair cell is the cochlear amplifier, a cell that changes length in time with sound (electromotility) to boost basilar-membrane vibration, and its wriggling gain is exactly the variable this loop controls.

The medial olivocochlear neuron is a cholinergic feedback neuron, relatively slow to build its effect, whose sustained firing sets a standing level of amplifier suppression rather than a fast spike-by-spike control.

The type II spiral ganglion afferent, which senses outer-hair-cell activity and damage, helps drive the reflex, giving the loop a route to respond to potentially injurious sound.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The efferent synapse onto the outer hair cell uses acetylcholine acting on an unusual alpha-9/alpha-10 nicotinic receptor that admits calcium, which then opens calcium-activated potassium channels (of the SK type), hyperpolarising and stiffening the outer hair cell and shunting its electromotility.

The net effect is inhibitory despite the excitatory-sounding transmitter, because the potassium efflux quiets the cell.

The lateral olivocochlear terminals onto afferent dendrites use a cocktail of transmitters (including dopamine and peptides) to modulate afferent excitability and offer some protection against excitotoxicity.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is the set of efferent terminals contacting a small group of outer hair cells at one cochlear location, part of a system of only a few hundred to roughly a thousand medial olivocochlear neurons per side serving the whole cochlea.

NUMBER AND DISTRIBUTION OF INSTANCES:

The human medial olivocochlear system comprises on the order of hundreds to about a thousand neurons per side, distributing terminals along the entire length of the cochlear spiral, densest in the mid-frequency regions.

WHERE IT IS INSTALLED (THE LAYER 9 MAP):

• The cochlea, at the outer hair cells (medial efferents) and the afferent dendrites beneath the inner hair cells (lateral efferents), where the gain adjustment is applied.

• The superior olivary complex of the brainstem, where the olivocochlear neurons originate and where the sound-driven reflex is closed.

• The cochlear nucleus, the relay that turns afferent sound input into the drive for the efferent neurons.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Without this loop the cochlea would run its amplifier at a fixed maximum gain, more easily damaged by loud sound and less able to suppress steady background noise that masks a wanted signal.

The familiar ability to follow one conversation in a noisy room, and the ear's built-in protection against sustained loud sound, both draw on this efferent turn-down, so its loss leaves hearing more fragile and more easily masked.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transformation is negative feedback gain control: efferent activity subtracts from the cochlear amplifier's gain roughly in proportion to sound level, compressing the cochlea's response and shifting its operating point.

In real numbers medial olivocochlear activation can reduce cochlear gain by on the order of 10 to 20 decibels, effectively turning the amplifier down by up to about a factor of ten at the frequencies it targets.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The reflex is comparatively slow, building over tens of milliseconds to seconds after sound onset and decaying over a similar course, so it acts as a running adjustment to the recent acoustic environment rather than a fast, moment-to-moment control.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

The loop has a quiet-environment regime, in which the amplifier runs at high gain for maximum sensitivity, and a loud-or-noisy regime, in which efferent drive turns the gain down for protection and unmasking; attention and arousal can bias the loop even before sound level changes.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The strength of efferent feedback is shaped during development and by acoustic experience, and a well-functioning efferent system in early life appears important for normal maturation of the cochlear amplifier and for resistance to noise damage.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

The system divides into the medial olivocochlear component (onto outer hair cells, myelinated, the amplifier control) and the lateral olivocochlear component (onto afferent dendrites, unmyelinated, the afferent-gain and protective control), each a distinct variant of the efferent motif.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

Efferent fibres transiently contact inner hair cells before hearing onset and help pattern the spontaneous activity that tunes the developing auditory system, later retracting to their mature outer-hair-cell targets.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Efferent control of hair cells is ancient and present throughout vertebrates, and the alpha-9/alpha-10 nicotinic receptor of the hair cell is an evolutionarily old acetylcholine receptor repurposed for inhibition, evidence that controlling one's own sensor is a deep design principle.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

The cochlea's supporting cells, the stria vascularis that maintains the endolymphatic potential powering the amplifier, and the blood supply of the inner ear all underwrite the amplifier whose gain this loop regulates.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

A weak efferent system is associated with greater vulnerability to noise-induced hearing loss and with poorer speech-in-noise performance, and loss of the outer hair cells themselves (from noise, ageing, or ototoxic drugs) removes the amplifier the loop is meant to control, a common cause of hearing loss.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Sound-driven excitation from the cochlear nucleus (and type II afferents) reporting ambient level; descending attentional bias.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Cholinergic inhibition onto outer hair cells reducing amplifier gain, and modulation of afferent dendrites.

• STATE.

◦ Standing efferent firing rate; current amplifier gain set point.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Gain reduction on the order of 10 to 20 decibels; hundreds to about 1,000 medial neurons per side.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Onset and decay over tens of milliseconds to seconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Weak efferent feedback raises vulnerability to noise damage and worsens speech-in-noise; outer-hair-cell loss removes the controlled amplifier entirely.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

A konnectome module named sensor_gain_regulator would subscribe to a running estimate of input level (and a top-down attention signal) and publish a gain-reduction command back onto the sensor's own front-end amplifier, closing a negative-feedback loop around the input stage.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is automatic gain control or adaptive input normalisation, and top-down attentional gating applied at the earliest sensory layer.

The biological motif differs in that the controlled element is a mechanical amplifier (hair-cell electromotility) rather than a numeric gain, and in that its inhibition is delivered by an excitatory transmitter (acetylcholine) turned inhibitory by a specialised calcium-activated potassium mechanism, a hardware trick with no direct software counterpart.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A loop that runs from the brainstem back out to the ear and releases acetylcholine to quiet the outer hair cells' active dance, turning the cochlea's own amplifier down in noise - the sensor whose sensitivity the brain holds in its own hand.


PART NINE. THE NEUROENDOCRINE MICROCIRCUITS

The framework has insisted from its first volume that the endocrine system is not an annex bolted onto the nervous system but one more province of a single architecture, and Layer 8 is where that claim is paid in full.

The motifs of this part are wiring diagrams exactly like those of the cortex and the cord, drawn from the same alphabet of convergence, feedback, reciprocal inhibition, and coupled oscillation, but their wires are sometimes blood vessels and their spikes are sometimes pulses of hormone.

A releasing-hormone cascade is a fan-out amplifier; a hormone axis is a closed negative-feedback loop; the KNDy network is a relaxation oscillator; the milk-ejection circuit is a burst synchroniser; the suprachiasmatic clock is a pacemaker network - each of these is a motif already catalogued in earlier parts, now installed at a glandular address and reading out in micrograms rather than millivolts.

The one-architecture claim is that you do not need a second theory of the body to understand hormones, only the same theory pointed at a slower clock and a chemical output line.

Every chapter in this part is tagged (NON-COG), because these circuits regulate the internal milieu rather than perform cognition, and so their code sections collapse to a single sentence; but the reader should notice that they are built of the identical parts that, wired elsewhere, do think.

That is the lesson of Layer 8 restated in the language of glands: old parts, new problem, one architecture.


CHAPTER 59. THE HYPOPHYSIOTROPIC CASCADE AMPLIFIER (Portal-Coupled Three-Stage Endocrine Fan-Out) (The Chemical Amplifier) (NON-COG)

A whisper of hormone leaves a few thousand hypothalamic cells, falls into a private set of veins no wider than a thread, and by the time its message reaches the ankles it has been made a million times louder.

This is the master motif of the neuroendocrine system: three chemical stages in series, each one adding gain, converting a nervous decision into a body-wide chemical command.

It is the circuit that lets the brain, which speaks in millivolts, give orders to organs that listen only in hormones.

Hypophysiotropic names the function: acting on (tropic) the hypophysis, the older name for the pituitary gland.

Cascade names the topology: a stage drives a stage drives a stage, each downstream of the last.

Amplifier names the computation: small input, large output, with a defined gain.

WHAT IT IS AND WHAT IT COMPUTES:

The hypophysiotropic cascade amplifier is a three-stage chemical fan-out that turns a nanogram-scale hypothalamic signal into a milligram-scale peripheral hormone response, a total amplification of roughly a millionfold.

Its computation is multiplication with gain: output equals input multiplied by the product of three stage gains, so that a change of a few nanograms of releasing hormone becomes a change of micrograms of pituitary trophic hormone and then milligrams of final glandular hormone.

It is the neuroendocrine embodiment of the divergence, or fan-out, primitive of Part One, drawn across three tissues and coupled by a specialised bloodstream rather than by axons.

THE WIRING DIAGRAM:

There are three nodes in series and one dedicated transport edge that makes the whole thing possible.

Node one is the parvocellular (small-bodied) neurosecretory neuron of the hypothalamus, which releases a releasing hormone, for example corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH), thyrotropin-releasing hormone (TRH), or gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), from its terminals in the median eminence.

The transport edge is the hypophyseal portal system, a private capillary-to-capillary vascular link: blood collects the releasing hormone from a first capillary bed in the median eminence and carries it directly down the pituitary stalk to a second capillary bed in the anterior pituitary, so the signal reaches its target undiluted by the general circulation - this edge is paracrine-hormonal in sign and strongly positive.

Node two is the anterior pituitary endocrine cell, for example the corticotroph, thyrotroph, or gonadotroph, which responds by secreting a trophic hormone (adrenocorticotropic hormone, thyroid-stimulating hormone, or the gonadotropins) into the systemic blood - a positive hormonal edge.

Node three is the peripheral target gland, for example the adrenal cortex, thyroid, or gonad, which secretes the final effector hormone (cortisol, thyroxine, or the sex steroids) into the whole body - again a positive hormonal edge.

Every edge in the forward path is excitatory; the inhibitory feedback edges that wrap around this cascade are the subject of Chapter 60 and are deliberately excluded here.

THE CELLULAR CAST AND THEIR PERSONALITIES:

The first player is the parvocellular neurosecretory cell of the hypothalamic paraventricular and other nuclei, drawn from the Layer 6 neuron catalogue's Part Seven of neuroendocrine cells; its personality is that of a phasic, pulse-firing secretory neuron whose bursts of action potentials are converted into discrete boluses of releasing hormone, so the amplifier is fed in pulses, not a steady drip.

The second players are the anterior pituitary endocrine cells catalogued in the other-cells manuscript, Chapters 51 to 57: the corticotroph, thyrotroph, gonadotroph, somatotroph, lactotroph, and their kin; each is a secretory workhorse whose personality is dose-following amplification, translating the concentration of releasing hormone it senses into a proportionally larger output of trophic hormone.

Supporting these are the folliculostellate cells (Chapter 57 of the other-cells catalogue), star-shaped non-endocrine cells that couple the endocrine cells into a communicating web and lend the gland a coordinated, all-together responsiveness rather than a scatter of independent secretors.

The pituicytes, the specialised glia of the posterior pituitary (also in the other-cells catalogue), belong properly to the magnocellular system of Chapter 62 but are named here for completeness as the glial personality of the gland.

The peripheral gland cells (adrenocortical, thyroid follicular, gonadal steroidogenic cells) are slow, biosynthetic personalities: they take minutes to hours to build steroid or thyroid hormone, which sets the long tail of the cascade's timing.

THE SYNAPTIC AND JUNCTIONAL FABRIC:

The fabric here is largely not synaptic but neurovascular and paracrine, which is the motif's defining oddity.

At node one the parvocellular terminal forms a neurohaemal junction: the axon ending abuts a fenestrated (window-perforated) portal capillary and releases peptide by exocytosis into the blood rather than onto a postsynaptic cell.

The releasing peptides act on G-protein-coupled receptors on the pituitary cells - the CRH receptor, TRH receptor, and GnRH receptor - most of them Gq-coupled, raising intracellular calcium and driving secretion.

Within the pituitary the folliculostellate cells are joined by connexin-43 gap junctions, and the endocrine cells communicate by paracrine factors and calcium waves rather than classical synapses.

At node three the trophic hormones act on their own G-protein-coupled receptors (the melanocortin-2 receptor for adrenocorticotropic hormone, the thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor, the luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone receptors), coupled to Gs and cyclic adenosine monophosphate.

The characteristic weights are set by receptor number and portal-vessel geometry, and they are plastic on timescales of hours to days through receptor up- and down-regulation.

SCALE OF ONE INSTANCE:

One instance is an entire axis, spanning three organs: on the order of ten thousand parvocellular neurons of a given type at the top, a defined population of one pituitary cell class (numbering from tens of thousands to a few million cells depending on the axis) in the middle, and a whole peripheral gland weighing grams at the bottom.

The physical span from hypothalamic cell body to peripheral effector is the height of the head and torso, but the functional coupling of the top two stages is compressed into the few millimetres of the pituitary stalk by the portal shortcut.
