• The entire cerebral cortex, where the unit delivers the fuel for the brain's most energy-hungry tissue and generates the signal read by functional magnetic resonance imaging.

• The cerebellum, where dense granule-cell activity demands tightly coupled flow.

• The hippocampus, where metabolic support sustains the plasticity of memory circuits.

• The retina, a metabolically extreme tissue with its own tightly regulated coupling.

• The subcortical grey matter and brainstem generally, wherever neurons fire and must be fed.

HOW IT COLOURS ITS REGIONS:

Remove this motif and each region keeps its neurons but starves them under load: activity would continue for seconds on local reserves and then falter as oxygen and glucose ran short, and sustained thought or perception in that patch would become metabolically impossible.

What the region loses is endurance - the ability to work hard for more than a moment - and, to the outside observer, the very signal by which we detect that it is working at all.

THE INPUT-OUTPUT TRANSFORMATION:

The transfer function is a delayed, saturating feedforward gain from neural activity to blood flow: a rise in local activity produces, after a lag of one to two seconds, a proportional rise in local blood flow that peaks around four to six seconds and then returns to baseline, saturating at high activity.

In plain terms, the unit reads how hard the tissue is working and opens the fuel valve by a matching amount, a low-pass, delayed version of the activity it serves rather than a faithful copy.

TEMPORAL SIGNATURE:

The response is deliberately slow relative to spikes: onset lag about one second, peak at four to six seconds, and a return over several more seconds, with an early fast component (partly direct neuronal and pericyte-mediated) and a later sustained component that depends on astrocyte calcium.

This sluggishness is the fundamental temporal limit of blood-flow-based brain imaging.

DYNAMIC REGIMES AND STATES:

In the resting regime, tonic pericyte and smooth-muscle tone set a baseline flow.

In the functional-hyperaemia regime, local activity dilates vessels and raises flow.

In the autoregulatory regime, the same actors hold flow constant against changes in blood pressure.

In the dysfunctional regime, seen in hypertension, small-vessel disease, and Alzheimer disease, coupling weakens and the flow response is blunted or delayed.

PLASTICITY AND LEARNING:

The unit does not learn or store information; its adaptations are physiological and structural - angiogenesis (growth of new vessels) in response to sustained demand or hypoxia, and slow changes in vascular tone and reactivity with exercise, ageing, and disease.

This is adjustment of plumbing to load, not the acquisition of memory.

VARIANTS AND SUBTYPES:

An astrocyte-dependent variant dominates the sustained, arteriolar phase.

A pericyte-mediated capillary variant produces the earliest and most local dilation.

A direct neuronal variant, driven by nitric-oxide or peptide-releasing interneurons, gives the fastest response and can bypass the astrocyte.

Regional vascular specialisations tune the motif to local demand, most extremely in the retina.

DEVELOPMENT AND ASSEMBLY:

The vasculature invades the brain during development guided by neural and glial signals, and pericytes and astrocyte endfeet assemble onto the vessels to build the neurovascular unit and the blood-brain barrier together.

Coupling matures postnatally as neural activity, astrocyte endfeet, and vascular tone come into register.

EVOLUTIONARY PROVENANCE:

Matching local blood flow to local metabolic demand is a general feature of vascularised tissue, but the brain's version is unusually fast, precise, and glia-mediated, elaborated as brains grew large and metabolically expensive and could no longer be fed by uniform perfusion.

SUPPORT SYSTEM:

This motif is itself a support system - the fuel supply for every neuronal and glial motif in the catalogue - and it partners closely with the astrocyte grid of Chapter 68, which shares the endfeet, and with the tripartite island of Chapter 69, which shares the glutamate-sensing step.

DISEASES AND DISORDERS:

Neurovascular uncoupling is an early feature of Alzheimer disease and vascular cognitive impairment, where a blunted flow response starves active tissue and may drive damage.

Hypertension and diabetes stiffen and dysregulate the unit, chronic small-vessel disease impairs it, and acute failure underlies aspects of stroke and of the cortical spreading depolarisation that turns healthy dilation into harmful constriction.

SYSTEMS INTERFACE:

• SUBSCRIBES (INPUTS).

◦ Local neural activity sensed as glutamate release and as neuromodulator and interneuron signals.

◦ Local metabolic state (oxygen, glucose, carbon dioxide, adenosine) and arterial blood pressure.

• PUBLISHES (OUTPUTS).

◦ Local vessel dilation (or constriction) and a matching change in cerebral blood flow, typically a rise of tens of percent.

◦ The blood-oxygen-level-dependent signal read by functional imaging.

• STATE.

◦ Pericyte and smooth-muscle contractile tone, astrocyte endfoot calcium, vessel diameter, local metabolite levels.

• PARAMETERS.

◦ Onset lag about 1 second; peak 4 to 6 seconds; flow increase tens of percent; unit span tens to a couple of hundred micrometres.

• TIME CONSTANTS.

◦ Astrocyte calcium seconds; dilation onset about 1 second; peak 4 to 6 seconds; recovery several seconds.

• FAILURE MODE.

◦ Neurovascular uncoupling in Alzheimer disease and vascular cognitive impairment; blunted coupling in hypertension and diabetes; inverted response in spreading depolarisation.

THE KONNECTOME NOTE:

For the konnectome the module name is demand_driven_resource_allocator.

It would subscribe to a local_compute_load signal from every active module in a region and publish a resource_delivered token, throttling how sustainably neighbouring modules can keep running, on a seconds clock.

Its closest artificial-intelligence analogue is dynamic power-and-compute allocation or load-based resource scheduling in a distributed system, and the biological motif differs in being feedforward and anticipatory (it dilates before the reserve is exhausted) and in that the very act of allocation, the blood-flow change, is what external observers measure as the proxy for computation itself.

ENGLISH READABLE CODE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

CODE SAMPLE:

This section does not apply to this microcircuit type for the reason that this motif serves a substrate or regulatory role rather than a cognitive-computational role, and is tagged (NON-COG).

WHAT MAKES IT UNMISTAKABLE:

A chain that runs from a firing synapse through an astrocyte's vascular endfoot to a relaxing pericyte and a widening arteriole, opening the local blood supply one to two seconds after the tissue starts to work - the servant circuit that carries no thought yet is the only part of thinking a brain scanner can see.


THE COGNITIVE SCOREBOARD

Of the seventy-one chapters of this volume, thirty-two carry the (COG) tag, and their distribution is the volume's final lesson.

• Parts One through Three are cognition's instruction set: the elementary loops (Chapters 1, 2, 4, 5, 6), the addressed inhibitory repertoire (Chapters 7, 8, 9, 13, 14, 15), and every competitive and normalising motif (Chapters 16 through 19).

• Part Four splits by what the clock times: the oscillators that bind cortical ensembles (Chapters 22, 23, 24) and the sequence chain (Chapter 28) are (COG); the oscillators that drive muscles, breath, and hormones (Chapters 25, 26, 27) are not.

• Part Five is the memory suite, (COG) throughout (Chapters 29, 30, 32, 33, 34, 35) except the motor integrator (Chapter 31) and the sleep-wake switch (Chapter 36).

• Part Six, the great composites, is (COG) in five of six chapters (37 through 41), with the cerebellar template (Chapter 42) as the calibrating exception.

• Parts Seven, Eight, and Nine - the reflex arcs, the sensory front-ends, and the entire neuroendocrine suite - are (NON-COG) without exception: magnificent machinery, none of it thinking.

• Part Ten seats two non-neuronal motifs at the cognitive table (Chapters 69 and 70), the tripartite synaptic island and the microglial pruning loop, in agreement with the tags their member cells carry in the Layer 6 companion volume.

Three closing observations, in the systems spirit of the whole corpus.

First, the downward lesson: no motif in this volume computes anything that its cellular cast does not permit.

The fast-spiking basket cell makes feedforward inhibition fast; the plateau-holding neuron makes attractors stable; the bursting neurosecretory cell makes hormone pulses possible - the personality of the Layer 6 cell is the parameter set of the Layer 8 motif.

Second, the upward lesson: no region in the Layer 9 manuscript does anything except by hosting some arrangement of the motifs in this volume.

A region's celebrated faculty - seeing, choosing, remembering, regretting - is always and only its particular installation of generic diagrams, wired to particular inputs and outputs.

That is why the framework says a region is defined by its interfaces: the internals are the same parts catalogue everywhere.

Third, the engineering lesson, for konnectome: this volume is a parts library.

Every chapter's SYSTEMS INTERFACE block is a module specification - what it subscribes to, what it publishes, its state, parameters, time constants, and failure modes - and every KONNECTOME NOTE names the module and its nearest artificial intelligence analogue.

The seventy-one motifs are the complete instruction set with which nature builds every faculty in the Layer 9 manuscript; a synthetic cognitive architecture that implements this library, and then wires instances of it according to the Layer 9 interface map, is following the only proven blueprint for a general intelligence.

The neurons think, the other cells make thinking possible - and the motifs are HOW the thinking is done.
